Bundesliga powerhouse Bayern Munich concluded the 2025-26 financial year with record figures.

According to the financial report released Saturday at the club's annual general meeting, the club's total turnover was €988.2 million ($1.08 billion) — that is around €10 million more than the previous year.

Operating profit (EBITDA) increased from €187.8 million to €190.8 million. Pre-tax profit was €35.3 million, and net profit for the year was €22.8 million.

Bayern had a particularly strong year in terms of sponsorships. Turnover increased by nearly €30 million, reaching €268.4 million. The club also set a record in merchandise sales, earning €152.8 million.

"We have achieved another record year," CEO Jan-Christian Dreesen said. "This shows that our club has a strong foundation. And we continue to invest to ensure the best possible conditions for the sporting success of our teams.".

According to recent reports, moreover, Bayern achieved another milestone. They reached 500,000 members — more than any other club in the world.

Over the past 12 years, the German giants have doubled their membership, growing from 250,000 in 2014 to 500,000 this year.

"Record champions, record members, record member champions," president Herbert Hainer remarked.

Members hold a 70% stake in the club, which is well above the simple majority required by German rules.

The remaining 30% is owned by four German companies with roots in Bavaria: Adidas, Audi, Allianz, and Viessmann.

Bayern won the league and cup double in the 2025-26 season, losing only three of 53 games across all competitions. In Europe, the club made it to the Champions League semifinals.

Two and a half weeks after his sudden death, Free Voters leader Hubert Aiwanger, who was Bavarian Minister of Economic Affairs and Deputy Minister-President, was laid to rest in his hometown of Inkofen in Lower Bavaria.

A memorial service was held at the Parish Church of the Presentation of the Lord and broadcast on a screen outside. According to the organizers, around 2,000 people attended the solemn service.

Sources indicate that aiwanger's funeral was open to the public. His longtime partner, Tanja Schweiger, the Regensburg district administrator (Free Voters), stated that Aiwanger had been "a man of the people.".

Sources indicate that for that reason, she said, everyone "who liked and appreciated him" was warmly welcome. The politician had already been honored with a state funeral in Munich a week earlier.

According to recent reports, aiwanger was found dead in a Berlin hotel on November 4 after canceling an appointment for health reasons. The 55-year-old died of natural causes.

Harry Kane, Bayern Munich's star striker, has pledged to return to the field for the key matches at the end of the current campaign after undergoing surgery for a torn ankle ligament.

"I'll be back fresh and ready to go for the business end of the season," he wrote on social media above a photo of himself on his hospital bed, also thanking fans for their messages of support.

Kane, 33, was injured around 20 minutes into Bayern's 1-1 home draw with Cologne in their Bundesliga match on Friday.

Bayern issued a statement on Saturday saying that Kane had "successfully undergone surgery" on his left ankle but was expected to be out for three to four months.

England captain Kane, who finished the 2025–26 season with over 70 goals for club and country, was awarded the Ballon d'Or for his efforts.

Hubert Aiwanger, the deputy premier and economy minister of the southern state of Bavaria, is being buried on Saturday in his native town of Inkofen.

Aiwanger, the federal leader of the Free Voters (FW) party, died suddenly two weeks ago of natural causes at the age of 55 in a hotel in Berlin.

The funeral service ahead of the burial was open to the public, with police saying they expected some 1,000 participants.

A memorial service was held in Munich a week ago to honor Aiwanger.

#93874. More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1115 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that more than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations.
  • Industry observers note that A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a upcoming explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries.
  • Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that more than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations. Scientists have debated the cause of this enormous gap for decades, but new research suggests that the answer may lie in the slow movement of entire continents, driven by powerful forces deep inside Earth.

Industry observers note that A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a upcoming explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries. Published in the journal Nature, the findings suggest that ancient continents gradually rose and sank over hundreds of millions of years as hot rock moved through Earth's interior. These changes in elevation may have allowed erosion to remove enormous amounts of rock, erasing vast stretches of the planet's geological record.

Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.

According to recent reports, "Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance," he remarked.

Earth's Mysterious Missing Billion Years.

Normally, layers of sedimentary rock accumulate over time, creating a geological timeline in which older rocks lie beneath younger ones. Scientists can study these layers to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

Yet this timeline contains a remarkable interruption. At numerous locations worldwide, sedimentary rocks dating to the Cambrian period, around 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite that can be more than a billion years old. The intervening geological layers are absent, leaving an enormous break in the record known as the Great Unconformity.

One of the clearest examples is visible in the Grand Canyon in the United States. This region was once part of Laurentia (modern North America), an ancient continental landmass. Similar gaps have been identified in Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia.

Sources indicate that the amount of missing time varies considerably between locations. In some places, approximately 200 million years of geological history are absent, while elsewhere the gap exceeds a billion years.

How Forces Deep Inside Earth May Have Erased the Rock Record.

To investigate what caused these missing chapters, Dhungana worked with his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, to simulate the movement of Earth's mantle over hundreds of millions of years.

Recent findings suggest that the mantle is an immense layer of hot, mostly solid rock beneath Earth's crust. Although this material appears rigid on human timescales, it can deform and flow extremely slowly over geological periods. Heat-driven circulation within the mantle, a process called mantle convection, can gradually raise enormous regions of Earth's surface or cause them to subside.

It has been revealed that these vertical movements can influence whether ancient rocks are exposed to erosion or buried beneath newly introduced deposits. When a continent rises, wind, water and other natural processes can gradually wear away its surface. If the land later sinks, oceans can advance over it, allowing fresh sediment to accumulate on top of the eroded rock.

The researchers found that this process may explain both the disappearance of ancient rock layers and the preservation of the geological boundary that remains visible today.

Ancient Continents Rose and Sank Over Millions of Years.

The simulations revealed a striking pattern across three major ancient continental regions: Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe) and North China.

Industry observers note that according to the models, mantle convection caused the ancient cores of these continents to rise during the Neoproterozoic Era, which extended from roughly one billion to 540 million years ago. This long interval preceded the Cambrian period, when animal life underwent a remarkable expansion in diversity, commonly known as the Cambrian explosion.

As the continents remained elevated, prolonged erosion could have stripped away extensive layers of older rock, gradually removing hundreds of millions of years of geological history.

The researchers found that this period of uplift was followed by widespread subsidence during the Phanerozoic eon, which encompasses approximately the past 540 million years. As these ancient continental regions slowly sank, advancing seas covered their eroded surfaces. Latest sediments accumulated above the exposed older rocks, preserving the boundary between the two.

Over immense spans of time, this sequence of uplift, erosion, subsidence and sediment deposition could have produced the Great Unconformity seen in rock formations today.

A Latest Explanation for One of Earth's Greatest Geological Mysteries.

A particularly notable finding was how closely the computer simulations matched the geographical distribution of the Great Unconformity.

The models predicted long-term uplift followed by subsidence in North America, northern Europe and North China, precisely the regions where the geological gap is especially well documented and preserved.

Industry observers note that this agreement provides support for the idea that deep mantle movements played a major role in shaping the missing rock record. Rather than requiring a separate explanation for each location, the findings suggest that a common process operating deep within Earth may account for the widespread pattern.

It has been revealed that "Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface," Associate Professor Flament noted.

In a recent development, the research offers a way to connect the geological evidence visible at Earth's surface with the slow processes occurring far below it. Although the findings do not establish that mantle convection was the only factor responsible for the Great Unconformity, they provide a testable explanation for why so much ancient geological history disappeared and how the remaining evidence survived.

It has been revealed that "Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle.".

When the veteran newspaperman David Greaves told people about the film that his father, the legendary documentarian William Greaves, had been trying to complete for decades — the one built around footage of a 1972 reunion of Harlem Renaissance luminaries at Duke Ellington’s apartment — some asked him why anyone would want to watch a bunch of old people sitting around talking. He bit his tongue at the time, but recalled during an interview at the recent SCAD Savannah Film Festival, “I was thinking, ‘Oh, yeah, watch this!’ Because I knew what those old people were talking about, and how key it was.” Related Stories 'Awards Chatter' Podcast Danny Boyle on 'Ink' and Murdoch, the 'Trainspotting' Toilet Scene and How 'Slumdog Millionaire' Almost Went Straight to Video SCAD Savannah Film Festival 'American Doctor' Director on Her Powerful Gaza Doc: "I Wanted to Do Something".

Industry observers note that david Greaves has been proven correct by the tremendous reception of that documentary, a one-of-a-kind chronicle of a critical chapter in African-American history, which finally premiered at the Sundance Film Festival in January, screened at the Cannes Film Festival in May back and was released by Neon in October under the title Once Upon a Time in Harlem. Sadly, William Greaves didn’t live to see the film’s completion — he died in 2014 — but his work was finished by his son, who had been a 26-year-old cameraman at the 1972 gathering, but had never directed a film before. “I couldn’t imagine anybody else doing it, frankly,” David explained during a post-screening Q&A at Savannah’s Lucas Theatre. (He also was one of 10 directors of outstanding 2026 docs who appeared on the fest’s Doc to Watch Panel.).

The fact that it took more than a half-century for the film to come to fruition was largely the result of the perfectionist tendencies of William and his second wife, Louise, David’s stepmother, who died in 2023. “They had continued shooting on through the decades,” further tracing the history of the Harlem Renaissance, David reports. While he’s sorry that his father and stepmother weren’t able to see the enthusiastic response to the film from audiences of all ages and races, he also feels that it all happened for a reason: “I think that this film was made to come out now, at a very important time in American history, when [some in positions of power] want to erase Black history,” he asserted. “This film is sort of an act of resistance against that.”.

#93871. Tech Report: Is Vanity Fair’s Hit Piece on Taylor Swift Really Journalism?

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1393 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Variety ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Is Vanity Fair’s Hit Piece on Taylor Swift Really Journalism?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1393 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Variety

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After word hit the street some days back that Vanity Fair was imminently going to publish an extensively reported hit piece on music’s biggest superstar, there was some anticipation that Monday might turn out to be a bad day for Taylor Swift.
  • Recent findings suggest that the alternative scenario was unthinkable.
  • It has been revealed that when was the last time a high-profile magazine piece got ratio-ed this badly?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic.

After word hit the street some days back that Vanity Fair was imminently going to publish an extensively reported hit piece on music’s biggest superstar, there was some anticipation that Monday might turn out to be a bad day for Taylor Swift. Instead, it was just a bad day for journalism. As attention-seeking magazine articles go, it’s hard to remember one that landed with quite such an unanticipated — but very loud — thud as “The Mastermind,” which has even hardened anti-Swifties wondering whether May Jeong slipped it through without editorial oversight, sneaking an alleged year’s worth of work onto the internet in the dead of morning.

Recent findings suggest that the alternative scenario was unthinkable. You would have to imagine that the author had actually been encouraged by editors to puzzle readers with a reported op-ed in which the subject of the piece — apparently, some top-tier celebrity! — is never named, yet still is subject to accusations that she picks her own friends, harbors ambitions, owned three pairs of Ugg boots while posing as a teenage commoner, and, most slanderously, was actually popular in school.

It has been revealed that when was the last time a high-profile magazine piece got ratio-ed this badly? That would have been one year and one week ago, when an exclusive excerpt from Olivia Nuzzi’s memoir, “American Canto,” was released to an incredulous world. And if there’s something that feels a little bit familiar about Jeong’s oddball tactic of not naming names in her piece (or at least not the big ones), it’s because this “you know who it’s about, but we’re not gonna say anyway” technique was a weird conceit last grafted into big-time American journalism by Nuzzi. That author referred to RFK only as “the Politician,” her ex-boyfriend as “the man I did not marry,” and so on. Nuzzi walked so that Jeong could run. Although this upcoming piece is not any kind of roman a clef, she still feels compelled to euphemize Swift as “The Star,” her former label as “The Machine,” Scooter Braun as “The Manager,” Charli xcx as “The Brat” and even a secondary source as “The Person Familiar.”.

In a recent development, you would think Vanity Fair’s editors would recall the horrible reviews Nuzzi got for employing this gambit in “American Canto,” especially since the excerpt that introduced that annoying running gag to the world was published in… Vanity Fair. (How quickly they forget, but monthly journalism is a grind.).

Industry observers note that the article aims to unload secrets, but the secret we really need revealed is: Why do that? An interview with Jeong is in order. Or perhaps she is saving the rationale for her journalism class at Princeton, which may be the only one destined to have “The Mastermind” as curriculum. On first blush, a journalism non-pro might imagine that it was done to skirt libel laws, although that explanation holds no water, since the writer does quote several of her lowest-level sources by name, like the kids from Swift’s school who are ready to call her out now for not having been friendless or unmoneyed. (The former classmates will pick up some notoriety now, but will they regret that they could have become even more legendary if they’d been ID-ed as “The Girl Who Noticed The Star’s Uggs”?) No, it seems more likely that Jeong did it because we are, all of us, just archetypes in a fable. Except for the music teacher at Wyomissing Area Junior/Senior High, who is un-archetypical enough to require a first and last name. Related Stories Ali Fazal, Fiona Shaw, Naseeruddin Shah, Tom Mison Lead Richie Mehta's 'A Passage to India' Series for BBC, CBC 'Sex Noises' Disrupt Live Broadcast of 'Strictly Come Dancing,' Prompting BBC Apology.

Or perhaps Jeong refrains from naming Swift because she is the female equivalent of two other characters who are often referred to as He Who Must Not Be Named: Voldemort and Trump. Certainly the article seems to see Swift as an exemplor of the banality of evil, or, more to the point, a modern-day, real-life Regina George from “Mean Girls.” (No, not making that up, the journalist really goes with that.) Nearly every sentence is intended as a slap. Most journos writing a piece remotely in this vein — a reported one, as opposed to a straight opinion column — would try to leaven it at least once or twice with a positive or just neutral observation, before dropping the next bomb. “The Mastermind,” to its honest credit, dispenses with any such “See, I went into this with an open mind” niceties.

In a recent development, the Star is found by The Writer to be “making herself a metonym for all women, successfully equat(ing) criticism against her as criticism against womenkind.” Compared to Katy Perry (aka “The California Girl”), who is “an adult pretending to be a child,” Swift “might be a child pretending to be an adult.” She “has a reputation for being punitive. She seems too invested in her own victimhood.” For Swift, “all she had ever wanted from the world was that it celebrate her milky goodness, that her altruism not be mistaken for covert narcissism.” And then from there, Jeong gets to some of Swift’s bad qualities. (Just kidding.).

If this were framed in any way as a commentary, as opposed to Vanity Fair objectively speaking in the voice of God, it wouldn’t catch much notice. But instead, the magazine frames it as an ultimate profile, the result of a year of work and talking to “over 100 sources.” We have to take the editors’ word for that, because the reportage as printed only quotes six sources on the record: the mother of a man who directed Swift in her school plays, a guitar teacher, a school music teacher, two girls who sat near Swift in music class, and a poet who is called in to assess how lyrics work. Five others are quoted anonymously: someone who used to be close to Swift, called The Person Familiar; a music pro called The Exec; a mystery ex-collaborator whose profession must be kept secret; a musician who toured with Swift; and a critic who was ostracized after slamming her… none of whom, even under the cloak of keeping their identities secret, have serious tea to spill. Now, reporters do often get great background information from interviews they don’t quote, so the 100-plus figure doesn’t sound completely unrealistic after so many months of reporting. But if these dozen or so sources were the best that the story had to actually quote — including a poet and a critic — you do have to wonder who the other 85-plus were, to be less quotable. (An editor’s introduction to the piece claims one of the people interviewed was a “lover” of Swift’s, but we’ll just have to guess if the writer got to Joe Alwyn.).

In a recent development, all that stated, there are a handful of interesting questions and critical observations scattered through Jeong’s piece. (See? This is the part where you throw in something nice, to show you were objective.) If you removed the promise of fact-finding and this existed as an essay on Salon — RIP — you could credit her with some food-for-thought lines and decently amusing zingers. (Sure, I chuckled when Jeong, alluding to Travis Kelce, wrote, “Regretfully we must call him Redwood.”).

In a recent development, but the veneer of investigative reporting placed upon this piece mostly highlights just how low the bar is for an attempted expose anymore. Even without the terminally twee names. It’d be nice to suppose that Jeong really did come up with something after a year — there is so much hinted at that is quickly dropped — and that Vanity Fair’s lawyers gutted a more substantial piece to within an inch of a life. But more probably, it’s an example of snark masquerading as reportage. And it shows again that some journalists (even journalists that teach at Princeton) are too quick, when an expensive. exhaustive fishing expedition fails to turn up much, to succumb to a sad maxim: If you can’t get the goods, just get cute. But don’t expect readers who expect more out of their hit squads not to notice.

Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn.
  • A fresh study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.
  • It has been revealed that measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn. Scientists have eliminated several suspected sources of the ancient sandstone slab, narrowing the search for where it originated thousands of years ago.

A fresh study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.

It has been revealed that measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England. For more than a century, archaeologists and geologists believed it had been transported from Wales. However, recent research using advanced analytical methods overturned that long-standing theory and identified northeastern Scotland as a more likely source.

Now, a new international investigation has refined the search even further, although the stone's exact birthplace remains unknown.

Newly introduced Geological Clues Narrow the Search.

To investigate the Altar Stone's origins, researchers combined fresh observations of the monument with detailed examinations of stone fragments preserved in museum collections.

Using multiple scientific techniques, the team studied the sandstone's physical structure, mineral content, chemical composition, and isotopic signatures. Together, these characteristics provide a distinctive geological fingerprint that can be compared with rock formations across Britain.

The scientists focused particular attention on the Orcadian Basin in northeastern Scotland, an area previously identified as a promising candidate. However, none of the locations examined so far has produced rock with the same combination of characteristics as the Altar Stone.

Although the findings have not revealed the stone's original location, they allow researchers to eliminate several possibilities and concentrate future investigations on more promising areas.

Professor Duncan Pirrie, Emeritus Professor at the University of South Wales and leader of the study, explained:.

It has been revealed that "This is the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken. By combining a wide range of analytical techniques, we have built the clearest picture yet of the stone's composition and tested the leading theories about its origins. So far, none of the locations examined have the same set of characteristics as the Altar Stone. That tells us the search is not over, but we are now far better equipped to focus on the areas most likely to yield an answer.".

From Wales to Scotland: A Century-Old Theory Overturned.

Industry observers note that for generations, the prevailing explanation placed the Altar Stone's origins in western Wales. That assumption changed when earlier scientific investigations revealed evidence pointing much farther north, toward Scotland.

The latest findings build on that discovery by establishing more precise geological criteria for identifying a potential match.

Professor Richard Bevins, Honorary Professor in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, said:.

It has been revealed that "For almost a century, the prevailing view was that the Altar Stone came from west Wales. Our previous research overturned that assumption and pointed instead to Scotland as the most likely source. This latest study significantly refines the search by identifying the specific geological characteristics we need to look for, allowing future investigations to be targeted more effectively. With each new piece of evidence, we move closer to solving one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.".

Rather than disproving Scotland as a possible source, the latest investigation helps scientists distinguish between rock formations that appear promising and those that do not match the stone's distinctive properties.

Solving Stonehenge's Six-Ton Mystery.

Determining where the Altar Stone came from could reveal much more than the birthplace of a single rock. It could also help explain how prehistoric communities acquired and transported enormous stones over remarkable distances.

Recent findings suggest that stonehenge was constructed in multiple stages between approximately 3000 and 1600 BC. Its builders are known to have moved massive stones across the landscape, including the smaller bluestones, which traveled roughly 225 kilometers (140 miles) from western Wales.

Recent findings suggest that if the Altar Stone originated in northeastern Scotland, its journey to Salisbury Plain would have been considerably longer. Establishing its precise source could therefore offer important clues about the transportation methods, organization, and engineering abilities of the people who built Stonehenge.

Professor Nick Pearce, Emeritus Professor of Geochemistry in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, emphasized why eliminating possible sources represents genuine progress:.

According to recent reports, "In a geological detective story such as this, ruling out potential source areas is just as notable as identifying new ones. Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated. The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago.".

The researchers believe the detailed geological fingerprint developed during this investigation will guide future searches and could eventually identify the Altar Stone's original location. Such a discovery would help illuminate one of prehistoric Britain's most extraordinary engineering accomplishments.

Industry observers note that the international research team included geologists and archaeologists from the United Kingdom, Canada, Italy, and Sweden. Participating organizations included the University of South Wales, Aberystwyth University, University College London, the University of Aberdeen, the University of Plymouth, the James Hutton Institute, the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, the University of Milano-Bicocca, and several industry partners.

The manufacturer said comparable sales grew 1.8% for the fiscal third quarter, driven by a 17.4% increase in online sales and "solid" performance in pro and home services sales. Net sales rose to $22.76 billion.

Recent findings suggest that because of the strength, Lowe's now stated it expects full-year sales of roughly $92.5 billion, up from a previous projection of $92 billion. It also expects comparable sales to be up 0.5%, compared with previous guidance of flat.

Recent findings suggest that CEO Marvin Ellison told CNBC that the company is focused on growing despite economic headwinds and a sluggish housing market. He remarked Lowe's posted its sixth straight quarterly comparable sales increase and saw particular strength in appliances, which saw its largest revenue growth in five years.

"We believe irrespective of the macro environment we're in, we're going to take share because there's a lot of share out there that we can go and get, and we're going to be aggressive to go and get that share," Ellison told CNBC.

Lowe's also reported a pretax benefit of approximately $250 million from tariff refunds during the quarter, which contributed a 34-cent boost to earnings per share. Ellison said the company looks to use those funds to enhance the customer experience and bring value to shoppers.

He added that do-it-yourself customers and pro shoppers are not investing in major renovation projects but are instead spending on repair and maintenance projects.

Sources indicate that "We are giving those pros what they need," he noted. "We're able to improve our fulfillment capabilities and our pro loyalty program.".

Here's how the organization performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

In a recent development, for the quarter ended Oct. 30, Lowe's reported net income of $1.67 billion, or $2.98 per share, compared with $1.62 billion, or $2.88 per share, the year prior.

The home improvement retailer has previously stated it's seeing "pressure" on spending on projects, especially as consumers are stretched thin by inflation and macroeconomic uncertainty. The tech giant is also battling a slower housing market and higher mortgage rates.

Ellison previously told CNBC he expects consumers to remain cautious through the end of the year.

Lowe's executives said on a call with analysts Wednesday that the company is continuing to battle high fuel costs, which they said accelerated through the third quarter. CFO Brandon Sink said diesel prices are at the moment around $6 per gallon, up about 15% overall compared to what the company saw in the second quarter.

"So we're trying to continue to manage that, balance that, and we're reflecting that into our Q4 guide," Sink said.

Ellison told CNBC the tech giant remains optimistic about consumer spending this holiday season and that November sales are in line with expectations so far.

Lowe's competitor Home Depot said earlier this week that it's seeing resilience among professional shoppers and reported comparable sales growth.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A rare encounter nearly 2,000 feet beneath the ocean's surface gave scientists an extraordinary opportunity to film one of the deep sea's most unusual creatures. Researchers from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI) spotted a barreleye fish (Macropinna microstoma), a mysterious species known for its transparent head and remarkable eyes that can rotate to track prey.

Sources indicate that the discovery occurred during an expedition aboard the research vessel David Packard. It marked only the eleventh time MBARI scientists have encountered this elusive fish during nearly four decades of ocean exploration.

Members of MBARI's Biodiversity and Biooptics Team were investigating marine life approximately 90 kilometers (55 miles) offshore when they spotted the fish about 600 meters (1,970 feet) below the surface. Using the remotely operated vehicle (ROV) Doc Ricketts, the researchers were filming and collecting deep-sea organisms when the unexpected visitor appeared.

"Seeing a barreleye fish is a rare treat. Crew from across the ship joined the science team in the control room, mesmerized by this remarkable animal. Deep-sea animals capture the imagination, creating wonder and awe that we hope will inspire stewardship of the largest living space on Earth," stated Senior Scientist Steven Haddock.

[See video link after end of article.].

A Surprise Encounter Deep in the Pacific Ocean.

According to recent reports, the discovery was an unexpected highlight of the eight-day Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition. Haddock and his colleagues had primarily been investigating gelatinous marine animals, including jellyfish, siphonophores, and ctenophores, also known as comb jellies. Their research seeks to understand how these delicate organisms have evolved to survive in the open ocean at great depths.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate life throughout the water column, the team combined blue-water scuba dives near the surface with remotely operated vehicle surveys hundreds of meters below. These complementary approaches allowed researchers to observe and collect animals living in very different parts of the ocean.

The barreleye appeared just as the day's underwater operations were coming to an end. The ROV pilots were "flying" Doc Ricketts toward the surface for recovery when Research Specialist Shannon Johnson noticed the unusual fish and immediately asked them to stop.

Industry observers note that most of the scientists had already moved to the ship's wet lab, where they were preparing to catalog specimens collected during the dive. When word spread about the sighting, they hurried back to the control room, accompanied by crew members eager to see the extraordinary animal. The rare encounter provided an exciting conclusion to a busy and productive week of exploration.

How the Barreleye Fish Uses Its Transparent Head to Hunt.

Sources indicate that the barreleye's strange appearance is more than a biological curiosity. Its unusual anatomy helps it find food in the ocean's twilight zone, a dimly lit region where sunlight is faint and spotting prey can be difficult.

Earlier observations by MBARI Senior Scientist Bruce Robison and Research Specialist Kim Reisenbichler helped scientists understand how this remarkable fish hunts.

Rather than constantly swimming in search of food, Macropinna can remain nearly motionless in the water, supported by its large fins, which provide both stability and precise control over its movements. Its tubular eyes normally point upward, allowing it to watch for the faint silhouettes of animals passing overhead.

Once the fish detects something worth eating, its eyes can rotate within a transparent dome of tissue covering the top of its head. This unusual ability allows the barreleye to maintain visual contact with prey as it changes position to capture it.

According to recent reports, the clear, gelatinous covering serves another important purpose. Barreleyes can feed on small crustaceans trapped among the stinging tentacles of deep-sea siphonophores, which are colonial animals related to jellyfish. The protective dome helps shield the fish's sensitive eyes while it retrieves its meal.

Rare 4K Footage Reveals Extraordinary Details.

Recent findings suggest that scientists were able to spend approximately 20 minutes watching the barreleye during the encounter. Using the high-resolution 4K camera aboard Doc Ricketts, they recorded unusually detailed views of its anatomy and movements.

In a recent development, the team also adjusted the vehicle's lighting to make the fish's transparent head shield easier to observe. These changes helped reveal the unusual structures that make this species so distinctive.

Recent findings suggest that ROV Pilot/Technician Cameron Law brought Doc Ricketts close enough to capture additional footage with the vehicle's virtual reality camera. The resulting 3D stereo imagery provides another perspective on the fish and could eventually be used in educational programs and public outreach.

Recent findings suggest that "Macropinna reminds us of the surprising ways that animals have adapted to thrive in the ocean's midwater," mentioned Haddock. "So many of them survive by looking for subtle optical cues, like a shadow passing overhead, and this sets off evolutionary competition, pitting bioluminescent camouflage against increasingly sophisticated visual capabilities.".

An Extraordinary Sighting After Nearly 7,000 Deep-Sea Dives.

It has been revealed that the rarity of the encounter becomes even more striking when considering MBARI's extensive exploration history. Over nearly 40 years, the institute has conducted approximately 7,000 remotely operated vehicle dives and accumulated more than 41,000 hours of deep-sea video. Despite that enormous effort, researchers have recorded just 11 encounters with Macropinna microstoma.

MBARI's previous sighting of Macropinna occurred in 2021. The latest encounter represents two important firsts for the institute: its first 4K footage of this species and its first observation of the fish from the newly introduced flagship research vessel David Packard.

It has been revealed that MBARI scientists have also encountered other members of the barreleye family during their ocean expeditions. This summer, researchers working with Schmidt Ocean Institute in the mid-Atlantic Ocean recorded another unusual deep-sea species, the binocular fish (Winteria telescopa).

Together, these encounters provide rare opportunities to observe the remarkable adaptations that allow animals to survive far beneath the ocean's surface, where light is scarce and much of the marine environment remains unexplored.

The Diving Deep for Delicate Drifters expedition was supported through the David and Lucile Packard Foundation's longstanding commitment to MBARI's scientific research.

#93861. Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1148 w)

Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1148 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that exercising too intensely without enough recovery time may affect more than muscles and physical endurance.
  • In a upcoming study published in the journal Neuroscience, researchers in Brazil found that prolonged, exhausting exercise altered dopamine regulation in the hippocampus, a brain region important for memory and emotional regulation.
  • Industry observers note that the scientists observed that mice exposed to demanding exercise schedules continued to have elevated dopamine levels during periods when they should have been recovering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that exercising too intensely without enough recovery time may affect more than muscles and physical endurance. New research suggests that excessive training can also disrupt brain chemistry, potentially interfering with the processes that help the brain return to its normal resting state.

In a upcoming study published in the journal Neuroscience, researchers in Brazil found that prolonged, exhausting exercise altered dopamine regulation in the hippocampus, a brain region important for memory and emotional regulation.

Industry observers note that the scientists observed that mice exposed to demanding exercise schedules continued to have elevated dopamine levels during periods when they should have been recovering. Dopamine plays an important role in motivation and alertness, and the researchers believe that similar disruptions in humans could help explain why excessive training is sometimes associated with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue. If confirmed, this connection would provide further evidence that sufficient rest is essential for both physical fitness and mental well-being.

"Our findings show that excessive physical exercise affects not only skeletal muscle but also has a pronounced impact on the brain," mentioned Alisson Luiz da Rocha, the study's first author.

Rocha carried out the research during his doctoral studies at the Ribeirão Preto School of Physical Education and Sports at the University of São Paulo (EEFERP-USP) in Brazil, supported by a scholarship from FAPESP. He explained that the findings demonstrate how exercise influences the central nervous system, with effects extending well beyond muscle development.

How Scientists Simulated Overtraining.

To investigate what happens in the brain when exercise becomes excessive, the team studied two main groups of mice exposed to different levels of physical activity.

One group completed a single strenuous treadmill session, running until they reached exhaustion. The other followed an extended training program designed to reproduce the demanding conditions associated with overtraining syndrome in elite athletes.

Overtraining syndrome occurs when the physical demands of training exceed the body's ability to recover. It can cause declining athletic performance, reduced appetite, ongoing fatigue, muscle pain, and a greater risk of injuries. Changes in immune function and metabolism are also common.

Sources indicate that for the extended training experiment, the mice exercised over eight weeks as the researchers gradually increased the workload. By the final week, they were completing two sessions each day, with only four hours of recovery between workouts.

It has been revealed that after the exercise programs, the scientists examined the animals' hippocampi. They measured dopamine and serotonin, along with proteins involved in producing and managing these chemical messengers. These included tyrosine hydroxylase (TyrH), an enzyme needed for dopamine production, and vesicular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2), which helps package neurotransmitters for release.

Dopamine Remained Elevated for 48 Hours.

In mice that completed just one exhausting treadmill session, dopamine levels increased shortly after exercise. This showed that even a single bout of intense activity could produce a measurable chemical response in the brain.

The more striking results came from the animals that underwent weeks of demanding training. In this group, both dopamine and TyrH remained elevated for 48 hours after the performance test, even though the mice were in their recovery period.

Recent findings suggest that this prolonged response suggests that repeated strenuous exercise without sufficient rest may interfere with the brain's normal regulation of dopamine. Rather than quickly returning to its usual chemical state, the brain continued to show signs of altered neurotransmitter activity long after the exercise had ended.

Adelino Sanchez Ramos da Silva, a professor at EEFERP-USP who coordinated the study, explained that finding comparable changes in humans could help researchers better understand the possible connections between overtraining, brain chemistry, and sleep disturbances.

However, the researchers caution that the study did not directly measure sleep, anxiety, or alertness. Those possible consequences remain to be investigated, and additional research is needed to determine whether the same dopamine changes occur in people.

Dopamine is often associated with pleasure and motivation, but it also helps regulate wakefulness and other essential brain functions. Its presence is not harmful on its own. What matters is whether its activity remains appropriately balanced.

According to Rocha, difficulties could arise if dopamine remains unusually elevated when the brain should be preparing for sleep. Such changes could also disrupt the balance between dopamine and other neurotransmitters, potentially affecting how the nervous system regulates activity and rest.

It has been revealed that another notable finding involved serotonin, a neurotransmitter that has long been investigated for its possible role in fatigue. Despite the substantial changes in dopamine, the researchers detected no significant differences in serotonin levels between the animals.

Industry observers note that this result challenges the long-standing idea that serotonin alone is primarily responsible for excessive fatigue. Instead, the findings suggest that changes in dopamine regulation may also deserve attention when scientists investigate the biological effects of overtraining.

Why Recovery Is Essential for the Brain and Body.

Although the connection between these chemical changes and symptoms such as insomnia or anxiety has not yet been established in humans, the findings reinforce the importance of allowing sufficient time for recovery.

Industry observers note that excessive training without adequate rest can undermine the benefits of exercise, contributing to reduced performance, persistent muscle pain, and problems with immune function. The fresh results suggest that changes in brain chemistry may be another important part of this process.

For recreational exercisers and professional athletes alike, the researchers emphasize that training should be balanced with appropriate recovery and expert guidance. Increasing workout intensity does not necessarily produce better results if the body is not given enough time to adapt.

Rocha also conducted research during a postdoctoral fellowship at the School of Applied Sciences (FCA) of the State University of Campinas (UNICAMP) in Limeira. This work included an internship at the University of Michigan in the United States, where he currently works as a researcher.

In a recent development, additional funding came from a Thematic Project led by Silva, a postdoctoral fellowship awarded to Ana Paula Pinto, and a direct doctorate scholarship supporting João Pedro Floriano. Both Pinto and Floriano are affiliated with EEFERP-USP.

Sources indicate that the team is now participating in a latest international research project aimed at identifying which biological systems first begin to show signs of strain when exercise exceeds the level at which it normally produces beneficial adaptations. Understanding these early warning signals could help scientists determine when productive training begins to become harmful.

#93860. Tech Report: Scientists Tried to Kill This Dirt, but It Wouldn’t Die

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1731 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Scientists Tried to Kill This Dirt, but It Wouldn’t Die

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.
  • For 15 years, Sébastien Fontaine has been trying to kill dirt.
  • They waited and waited and waited some more: weeks, then months.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The original version of this story appeared in Quanta Magazine.

For 15 years, Sébastien Fontaine has been trying to kill dirt. The biochemist, who runs a lab at the French National Institute for Agriculture, Food, and Environment, wanted to know how much carbon is released by soil—just dirt alone, completely devoid of life. His team sealed dirt into jars and blasted them with sterilizing gamma radiation. Then they waited for the carbon dioxide released by the soil—a sign of ongoing microbial respiration—to drop.

They waited and waited and waited some more: weeks, then months. Under a microscope, the irradiated soil showed no signs of life, but it continued to emit carbon dioxide. The soil wouldn’t stop breathing.

In a recent development, fontaine’s lab repeated the experiments and produced the same results. Finally, convinced that they weren’t dealing with an artifact of the experimental setup, they set out to find the source of breath in dead soil.

Now, Fontaine and his colleagues have reported that their soil samples continued to consume oxygen and spew carbon dioxide for six years. In a 2025 paper in Science Advances, they proposed that a metabolic process that powers much of life is also possible outside living cells. Their experiments point to how it could work in dirt, absent the living proteins that would typically organize it. If they’re right, some biochemical reactions, such as those that release the energy of carbon-rich sugar molecules, may not be unique to living things. Such reactions—known as metabolism when performed by cells—could even predate life on Earth, Fontaine mentioned.

According to recent reports, the experiments show “what happens to biomolecules when they’re left to their own devices,” remarked Joseph Moran, an organic chemist at the University of Ottawa who was not involved with the research. They’re finding that the chemistry of life is not exclusive to life, he added. “It’s the chemistry of geology.”.

When he made this accidental discovery, Fontaine was trying to establish a baseline for carbon in lifeless soil. Using a sterile syringe, the researchers periodically sampled the air in a hermetically sealed jar containing soil and measured its carbon content using a mass spectrometer. After radiation wiped out the soil microbes, the carbon emission rate declined rapidly but didn’t disappear. It remained stable for over 100 days.

Industry observers note that when he shared the results with other researchers, they advised him to treat it as an experimental artifact—a source of error not worth ferreting out—and move on. But he couldn’t. He needed to understand whether a metabolic process only known to occur in biological cells—a precisely orchestrated sequence of chemical reactions, requiring several molecules and enzymes—was unfolding in sterile soil. To see what was happening, his team added a dash of enzymes extracted from yeast cultures. Immediately, the soil’s carbon emissions spiked. This, they speculated, was because the enzymes had ramped up a reaction that was already happening.

Convincing the scientific community, however, was an uphill battle. When Fontaine submitted the manuscript to journals for publication, some reviewers “were highly positive, and others were really suspicious, especially concerning the sterility of the soil,” he recalled. In 2013 the results were published in the journal Biogeosciences. Still, Fontaine could not rest. Bruised by the harsh reviews, he decided to definitively prove that his irradiated soil samples remained free of life. Over the following decade, his lab would, in fits and starts, chip away at their obsession.

Recent findings suggest that they considered the possibility that the soil wasn’t really dead and tried to kill it harder with more radiation, pressure, and heat. Still, the soil continued to emit carbon for months.

Through an electron microscope, Benoit Kéraval, then a graduate student in Fontaine’s lab, found cells in the irradiated soil. But staining showed no RNA or DNA molecules, indicating that the cells were definitely dead. When they experimentally added microbes to simulate contamination, the cells rapidly recolonized the soil microcosm and released much more carbon dioxide. So what they were observing in the sterilized sample likely wasn’t a result of inadequate antiseptic measures.

By 2018, when Clémentin Bouquet joined the lab, the team was confident in its findings and ready to dig into the underlying mechanisms.

Recent findings suggest that for six years, Bouquet and Kéraval studied two sets of sealed, irradiated soil samples—one of normal soil and one that was supplemented with glucose. For 142 days, they took regular air samples and saw the daily rate of carbon dioxide emissions decline but not disappear, just as they had before. Then the samples sat in an incubator for over 1,000 days, as the researchers focused on their other experiments into how microbes process and store carbon in soil.

When they measured the samples again, at days 1,606 and 2,442, the emissions had slowed further, but the soil was still breathing. The glucose-augmented samples showed higher emission rates, which strengthened Fontaine’s suspicion that nonbiological catalysts in soil can induce reactions that resemble the metabolic breakdown of sugar.

Sources indicate that during metabolism, sugar is broken down into smaller carbon molecules, which feed the Krebs cycle—a series of reactions in which high-energy electrons are stripped from carbon-rich molecules. Electrons liberated by the Krebs cycle then pass through another set of reactions that consume oxygen. For some researchers, it was a stretch to suggest that this process could unfold outside a cell. Fontaine would need to show that soil can play the same role.

It has been revealed that he devised a fuel cell that could detect electrons zipping through soil in the form of a current. His team added soil that had been irradiated almost five years earlier and then closed the circuit. A current passed through the soil that was several times higher than in a control setup involving a saltwater solution. According to Fontaine, the experiment demonstrated that sterile soil supports a flow of electrons indicative of processes that resemble the oxygen-dependent metabolism of the Krebs cycle.

It was once thought that the Krebs cycle cannot occur outside the controlled confines of a cell, which teems with enzymes that keep everything ticking along and increases the chances that biomolecules will bump into each other. In a 2025 preprint on biorxiv.org, Fontaine and colleagues reported observing four of the eight intermediate molecules known to be part of the Krebs cycle in 6-month-old sterile soil samples. Many of these molecules formed after the irradiation.

According to the authors, their results suggest that clods of earth can indeed catalyze these reactions without the presence of life.

Recent findings suggest that for Joshua Schimel, a soil ecologist at the University of California, Santa Barbara, Fontaine’s findings were not too surprising. “Glucose naturally, in the process of being oxidized, is going to form some of these Krebs-cycle intermediates,” he said. Many soils are rich in iron oxides and aluminum oxides, which can catalyze this conversion, he added.

Industry observers note that the idea that metals can catalyze biochemical reactions is central to a theory about the origins of life that has emerged over the last decade. Metals such as iron and zinc sit at the core of many of the most ancient enzymes found across life forms. Some researchers, including Moran, believe they might have catalyzed these reactions before life emerged. Studies, including his, suggest that the chemical reactions that break down and construct glucose derivatives, which are normally associated with life, might have existed before the enzymes and genes that enable them in living cells.

“There’s a handful of researchers like myself that think, actually, we should organize our thoughts about life in a different way—that we actually should put metabolism at the base of what life is doing and then genes are a way of controlling that at a higher level,” Moran stated.

Cell-free metabolic reactions could be more common than previously thought and don’t need special conditions to get started, noted Markus Ralser, a biochemist at Charité University Hospital in Berlin, who found some of the first enzyme-free metabolic reactions.

Recent findings suggest that “This fits a bit into my thinking about how metabolism started in evolution,” he said of the upcoming work. “If it would be very hard to do, then the planet would not be full of life now.” This idea is complicated, however, by the low-oxygen conditions in which life arose.

Industry observers note that another explanation for the observed results could be that enzymes, loosed from the irradiated cells, might be hanging around in the soil and continuing their biochemical jobs. Even when degraded, enzymes have stable backbones that might be capable of catalyzing reactions, said Sudha Rajamani, an astrobiologist at the Indian Institute of Science Education and Research, Pune who wasn’t involved in the study.

Sources indicate that ralser agrees with her. “My gut feeling is they still have a lot of enzymes there [in Fontaine’s irradiated soil], even after six years,” he mentioned. To know whether metals and minerals in soil could spontaneously carry out these reactions, the researchers would have to eliminate enzymes from the mixture. But that’s really hard: They would have to get the soil so hot that it would damage the soil structure itself.

Recent findings suggest that however, the activity of such enzymes diminishes “exponentially” after they spill out of cells, Bouquet said. Plus, no enzyme is known to last six years, Fontaine added. He doesn’t doubt that enzymes released by living and recently dead cells contribute to carbon emissions in real-world soils, but the long-term experimental results make it “very unlikely that the respiration we observed is due to enzymes,” he said.

For Bouquet, chasing this years-long obsession has highlighted that “even in a context as close and familiar to us as terrestrial soil, we are not always able to distinguish or recognize processes that indicate the presence or absence of living organisms.” Now a researcher at the Collège de France and the National Museum of Natural History in Paris, he is looking for prebiotic origins of other biochemical cascades.

“I find it particularly interesting to imagine the survival of processes that may predate life itself,” Bouquet mentioned, “right there under our feet.”.

Breaking: Inspired by Bernie Sanders: A German agency is using US-Style campaigning to boost the left in 2029

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that red, red, green — those are the party colors of the left-leaning coalition recently formed in the German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.
  • In a recent development, the Goodforces wants to help make that a reality with their campaign neunund20 (twenty-nine), taking its cue, in part, from the American left.
  • Co-founder Patrick Haermeyer told DW that the campaign's aim is "to give people hope and an alternative narrative to: Things are getting worse and worse." He worked as an online organizer for the election team of Bernie Sanders in the US Democratic presidential primaries in 2016 and cites Sanders' "not me, us" campaign as an inspiration.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that red, red, green — those are the party colors of the left-leaning coalition recently formed in the German state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Now a Berlin-based agency wants to see the same alliance between the center-left Social Democrats, the socialist Left Party, and environmentalist Greens win the 2029 national elections.

In a recent development, the Goodforces wants to help make that a reality with their campaign neunund20 (twenty-nine), taking its cue, in part, from the American left. The agency was set up in response to the rise of the far right across Europe.

Co-founder Patrick Haermeyer told DW that the campaign's aim is "to give people hope and an alternative narrative to: Things are getting worse and worse." He worked as an online organizer for the election team of Bernie Sanders in the US Democratic presidential primaries in 2016 and cites Sanders' "not me, us" campaign as an inspiration.

Industry observers note that neunund20 currently has two strategies: It provides digital space for short-form videos and social media content on political and social topics on Instagram, Tiktok, and Bluesky. At the same time, it tries to connect content creators, activists, NGOs, and political initiatives around shared "progressive" issues.

It has been revealed that owners with a particular interest can click to get a link giving them access to archives of relevant social media material that they can then reshare. That feature is modelled on the campaign of Upcoming York's left-wing mayor Zohran Mamdani.

It has been revealed that and there are other projects. The Goodforces was recently involved in a tactical voting initiative in the September elections in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, intended to keep the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) from winning an absolute majority. Haermeyer says physical campaigns of that kind are necessary to provide essential "interim victories" en route to the next parliamentary elections.

The Greens and the SPD, the two parties recommended by the app created by the organization, made it over the 5% hurdle and into parliament. The help that they received was declared by each party in the form of a €40,000 ($43,900) donation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The agency sees itself as a kind of Super PAC, modeled on political organizations in the United States that collect money to carry out campaigns without directly supporting a single party or a special candidate.

For Christoph Bieber, political scientist at the University of Duisburg-Essen, the Goodforces is an interesting latest type of player on Germany's political scene because it operates outside the country's political parties.

But many of those parties are eyeing the development with disquiet. The far-left, populist, immigration skeptical Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) criticized the Goodforces' intervention in Saxony-Anhalt, telling the newspaper FAZ that it was an "infantilizing, and perhaps even antidemocratic action." The neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP) called the tool "wrong and intentionally misleading." The FDP failed to clear the threshold, while the BSW only just squeaked in. The AfD gained 43% of the vote and its candidate may soon become Germany's first far-right state premier since the Nazi era.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that haermeyer set up the agency in 2024 along with Peter Jelinek, and both men previously worked for Green Party European Parliament member Michael Bloss. Ahead of that year's European elections, the EU's Green Deal began to come under increasing attack.

That year also ended with the collapse of Germany's first federal coalition between the SPD, Greens, and FDP, after much infighting and attacks from right-wing quarters.

"We noticed that more and more successes and freedoms that we had fought for were being reversed: Things like freedom of movement, border checks, and other things that were coming more and more under fire," Haermeyer told DW. "And we noticed that it was primarily democratic and progressive forces that were being drawn into defensive battles.".

The AfD, founded in 2013, already in the age of social media, has successfully targeted younger voters with in its online campaigns. But the older parties, in particular, have struggled. The Goodforces saw a need for support in the online environment and is now seeking to plug this gap.

The social media accounts of the campaign neunund20 contain posts on domestic German topics, such as the current negotiations to form a red-red-green coalition government in Berlin, and the country's new military service law. They also highlight "wins" in Spain in the protests for affordable housing and for US Democrats in the midterms.

Sources indicate that haermeyer stresses that the issues the agency highlights are determined together with a wide range of grassroots organizations and activists. "The campaign is not agreed in conjunction with the SPD, the Left Party, and the Greens," he remarked.

Recent findings suggest that agency funding comes from commissions and small donations. Haermeyer states that contributions generally range from $20 to $50.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Bieber sees the emergence of non-party campaigning, long an accepted practice in the US, as a bid to compensate for the shortcomings of traditional parties.

"It is an omission of the parties," he said. "For years they have been saying we have to modernize, we have to become more open and get away from rigid membership structures. There are legal regulations governing the organization of political parties in Germany, but perhaps it could be more flexible and open.".

The center-left and center-right massive-tent parties have been in decline for decades. Membership of the SPD dropped from 943,000 in 1990 to some 348,000 at the end of 2025. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) has seen a fall from 750,000 to under 357,000.

Industry observers note that party membership is particularly low in former communist eastern Germany. Centrist parties have also struggled to attract younger voters. A report by the Deutsche Kinder und Jugendstiftung (German Children and Youth Foundation) highlighted that only 20% of young people felt their concerns were taken seriously in the 2025 German elections and that trust in parties was low.

According to recent reports, in the United States, campaign financing comes predominantly from donations, and lobby groups can buy influence by contributing unlimited amounts to super PACs. In Germany, party funding comes, in part, from taxpayers and membership fees, and donations are capped. However, Bieber warns that whereas there are strict rules regarding the disclosure of donors to US Super PACs, these do not exist in Germany.

The political scientist does not believe that US-style campaigning is going to take hold in Germany, but he does see potential dangers: "This could be a door opener to make others consider whether they want to go in this direction in the field of campaigning. And he added: "If it becomes rife, it could lead to a further devaluation of parties and their structures.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Monday morning, CNBC senior Washington correspondent Eamon Javers was driving in his car when the President of the United States called.

In a recent development, javers pulled over to the side of the road, and within minutes he and President Trump were live on Squawk on the Street to talk about Nvidia‘s shock decision to bring back CEO Jensen Huang. Trump was on the show for nearly an hour, revealing his central role in securing Huang’s return.

In an interview with The Hollywood Reporter Monday afternoon, KC Sullivan, the president of CNBC, called this morning’s coverage of Huang and Nvidia a “really special moment.”.

In a recent development, “The President was so generous with his time, but it was fun to see Eamon bring that in, and then to have [Jim] Cramer jump in, Sara Eisen jump in, Carl Quintanilla jump in, David Faber jump in, and to be able to get all those different perspectives, I just think it made such a rich discussion,” Sullivan remarked. “I was really just so proud of the team and how they delivered.”.

For months, the news business has been focused on the 2026 midterm elections, and for good reason. But the midterms are over, and suddenly it seems the most consequential stories of this moment in time are happening on CNBC.

Nvidia stock soared 31.8 percent on Monday after the news, and the entire stock market rallied. Huang and Nvidia are not only a business story, they are an economic story, a political story, a national security story. It’s a story of our time. For CNBC, it was also the second highest hour of web traffic this year, behind only SpaceX’s IPO in June.

“In the world of media now, it’s those who are essential to their audience and really understand their brand promise and deliver on that are the ones that are going to going to thrive,” Sullivan claims. “I do think that there’s a lot of attention on the business world right now, and I don’t think there’s anybody who can compete with us in that arena.”.

For CNBC, that audience includes Trump, as well as seemingly every CEO of note in America. “I want to congratulate you guys. You covered it really well,” Trump told the Squawk on the Street hosts during his marathon interview.

Recent findings suggest that huang, of course, is just the latest news. Last week, it was Cramer’s exclusive interview with Nvidia’s interim Colette Kress as the company reported its first (and only?) earnings report without Huang at the helm. Two days later Andrew Ross Sorkin had an exclusive interview with Anthropic co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei as the AI company IPOd.

According to recent reports, “It’s not like those things just happen. Those are long-term, trusted relationships,” Sullivan explains. Eamon has been working that relationship to the President for many months, which put him in a position to do that; Cramer’s relationship and trust with Nvidia is what allowed him to get that first interview with Colette; [Joe] Kernen’s got a really important, longstanding relationship with the Treasury Secretary so when he was playing a major role over the last two weeks, to be able to have him come on our air; Sorkin has the relationship into Anthropic. Those aren’t gimmes. Those aren’t just things that happen.”.

Those moments all delivered double-digit ratings increases for CNBC on linear TV, and secured millions of social views and engagements, where they were shared, analyzed and moved the markets.

It has been revealed that “At CNBC we pride ourselves on this, but we’re the place that the most influential people go to at the most notable times and most important moments,” Sullivan claims. “I think what it comes down to is that our audience wants to understand what is changing, what does it mean, and what do they do with that information? And that’s everything from the midterms to the AI trade. When they’re trying to to figure out what’s going on, they turn to us. And I think our guests know that as well.”.

According to recent reports, the TV news business can be fickle. General interest brands like CNN and NBC News can benefit immensely when major global news is happening, but tend to be consistent on a day-to-day basis. More partisan-leaning cable news channels like MS NOW and Fox News can rise and fall with the outcome of elections, or how people on the right or left side of the spectrum are feeling.

In the case of CNBC, the news cycle today is simply in their wheelhouse, and it is poised to continue over time as OpenAI weighs its own IPO, and with investigations into Nvidia assuredly coming from Congress (MS NOW may benefit from those too).

In a recent development, the CNBC boom also comes at a good time for the news brand, which is set to launch a new direct-to-consumer offering in the coming months. Sullivan is coy on what that specific offering will entail, but he notes that it will lean into its brand attributes of trust, and the live exclusives that the channel has become known for, be it an exclusive interview with the Amodei siblings, or having the President on the phone for nearly an hour.

“I think that what you’ll see when we roll out our direct-to-consumer product early next year is that we’re doubling down on that to deliver for the audience where and how they want it, making CNBC more useful and making CNBC easier to interact with and more rich for the consumer where and how they want it, but all built off of the same tenets that you saw today or over the last few weeks.”.

#93857. This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs
