This strange creature lived 309 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (935 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A fossil discovered in Illinois years ago has turned out to belong to a previously unrecognized species that lived 309 million years ago, long before dinosaurs appeared.
  • In a recent development, during the Carboniferous period, the region surrounding present-day Chicago looked dramatically different.
  • Industry observers note that the newly identified species, Jeanerpeton mazonensis, resembled a salamander with the short, stocky body of a frog.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A fossil discovered in Illinois years ago has turned out to belong to a previously unrecognized species that lived 309 million years ago, long before dinosaurs appeared. The strange animal, an early relative of modern amphibians, has also received a name with a personal connection to the two student scientists who helped identify it.

In a recent development, during the Carboniferous period, the region surrounding present-day Chicago looked dramatically different. Instead of a modern city, the landscape was a warm, swampy river delta populated by giant insects, early animals adapted to life on land, and unusual creatures swimming through its waterways. This environment supported an extraordinary variety of life, leaving behind fossils that now provide a remarkable glimpse into Earth's prehistoric past.

Industry observers note that the newly identified species, Jeanerpeton mazonensis, resembled a salamander with the short, stocky body of a frog. Its name means "Jean's crawler from Mazon Creek," honoring the mothers of the two student researchers, both of whom are named Jean. The discovery is described in the Journal of Vertebrate Paleontology.

A 309-Million-Year-Old Fossil With Extraordinary Detail.

The Mazon Creek fossil deposits are among the world's most important sources of Carboniferous fossils, in large part because of the conditions that existed when the animals were alive.

As plants and animals died in the ancient river delta, layers of sediment swiftly covered their remains. This rapid burial created ideal conditions for fossilization, sometimes preserving delicate structures that would ordinarily disappear long before they could become fossils.

"What's really cool about Mazon Creek is that it preserves all of these unusual details -- things like toe pads and body outlines," states Allison Sefcovic, co-lead author of the paper and 2025 Women in Science intern at the Field.

According to recent reports, "In the fossil of Jeanerpeton, we can see some of the scales on its back and tiny 'belly ribs' called gastralia. You can even see the eye impressions! It's so cool to see.".

These exceptionally preserved features offer valuable evidence of what early amphibian relatives looked like. They also indicate that several anatomical characteristics associated with modern frogs and salamanders were already present approximately 309 million years ago.

A Prehistoric Species Hidden in Plain Sight.

Although Jeanerpeton mazonensis has only recently been formally described, its fossil was discovered many years earlier. An amateur fossil collector originally found the specimen and later donated it to the Field Museum.

It has been revealed that when researchers first examined it, they classified the animal as Amphibamus grandiceps, a previously established species known from the Mazon Creek area. However, closer examination eventually revealed that the fossil represented a distinct animal.

Sources indicate that misidentifications like this can occur when scientists have limited information about ancient species. Fossils that appear similar are sometimes assigned to an existing species even when key differences have not yet been recognized.

Paleontologists refer to such broad classifications as a "waste bin taxon." The term describes a category in which multiple fossils are grouped together because they seem related, even though their true identities and evolutionary relationships remain poorly understood.

"What we're finding from the Field Museum's collection are a bunch of things that historically were grouped together into this waste bin taxon known as Amphibamus grandiceps," says Cam So, co-author on the study and postdoctoral researcher at the Field Museum.

Recent findings suggest that "Jeanerpeton is one of those species. And now, we've found enough evidence to support it being an anatomically distinct animal. With this publication, we officially pull Jeanerpeton out of this waste bin taxon.".

The finding highlights how museum collections can continue to produce discoveries long after fossils are first collected. In this case, a specimen already held by the Field Museum provided enough anatomical evidence to establish a separate species.

Two Student Scientists Make a Remarkable Discovery.

According to recent reports, the research was co-led by Payton Kohlberg and Allison Sefcovic, who participated in the Field Museum's Women in Science internship program in 2025. The initiative encourages young women to explore careers in scientific research and museums.

Both students worked alongside So as members of the research group led by Arjan Mann, the museum's assistant curator of fossil fishes and early tetrapods in the Negaunee Integrative Research Center.

For Kohlberg, the project offered an opportunity to enter an unfamiliar scientific field and gain confidence through hands-on research.

According to recent reports, "Before working in the Mann Lab, I didn't know much about paleontology," states Kohlberg. "My experience at the Field and in the Women in Science program has made me more confident in my abilities to try something newly introduced. It is scary to take on a project when you feel like you don't know as much as you should, but I learned with my practical experience that it is possible to overcome that fear with hard work.".

Recent findings suggest that the identification of Jeanerpeton mazonensis adds another species to the growing record of ancient life preserved at Mazon Creek. As researchers continue examining fossils from the region, each discovery helps reveal more about the extraordinary diversity of animals and plants that inhabited Illinois more than 300 million years ago.

The 20th annual LA Skins Fest concluded on Sunday following the five-day celebration of Native American cinema and special screenings at the TCL Chinese Theatre.

Industry observers note that since its founding, the festival has become a platform for Indigenous filmmakers to showcase their work, connect with entertainment industry professionals and reach upcoming audiences. It also extends its mission outside the annual festival through its partnership with the Native American Media Alliance, supporting year-round professional development initiatives that includes writing labs, animation programs, showrunner training, development workshops and youth media education. This year’s LA Skins Fest featured a line-up of narrative features, documentaries, short films and special screenings that recognize Indigenous artists. This year’s festival opened with films presented by Amazon MGM Studios and also included a Netflix screening of “North of North” with actress Anna Lambe and a Cherokee-language screening of “The Rings of Power” followed by a discussion with the actors and Cherokee Film’s language revitalization team.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The art of making a sandwich has been revered since John Montagu, the fourth Earl of Sandwich, was so engrossed in a game of cards in 1762 he demanded meat between slices of bread to fuel his playing — it was a deeply espresso martini-coded move which saw all of his jealous mates also ask for one.
  • Over 250 years later, the subtle craft of 'wich is championed once again in an online sandwich-making simulator that threatens to eat into my GTA 6 time.
  • Created by German developer Gregor Weichbrodt with music by Scott Hühnerkrisp, a latest sandwich simulator is exactly that.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The art of making a sandwich has been revered since John Montagu, the fourth Earl of Sandwich, was so engrossed in a game of cards in 1762 he demanded meat between slices of bread to fuel his playing — it was a deeply espresso martini-coded move which saw all of his jealous mates also ask for one.

Over 250 years later, the subtle craft of 'wich is championed once again in an online sandwich-making simulator that threatens to eat into my GTA 6 time.

Created by German developer Gregor Weichbrodt with music by Scott Hühnerkrisp, a latest sandwich simulator is exactly that. "You make a sandwich. That's all," reads the simulator's about page. Notably, it's not the same as FiftyEight Studios' 2026 game Sandwich Simulator or Sandwich Squad's 2024 Sandwich Sim.

Sources indicate that each sandwich gets a serial number and a permalink, so you can revisit your creation later for reasons I can't quite conjure here beyond lunch inspo. To date, 42,375 unique sandwiches have been made on the simulator since it launched in Oct. 2026. For example, my tower of power sandwich will probably live on the internet after I shuffle off this mortal coil.

But there's more going on here, with the developer promising "realistic cucumber behavior" (if you put a slice too far on the edge it'll fall off) and "soft body physics" (slices of cheese, salmon, or ham will drape themselves over what's already on the sandwich).

To make a sandwich, all you need to do is add toppings from the array provided in the bottom menu. To add spreads, you tap the pot and a virtual knife will appear; holding your mouse down will drag that butter across the bread. For other toppings like cheese, radishes, crisps, eggs, tomatoes, and whatnot, you just drag your pick from the menu onto your bread.

Sources indicate that if you want to get rid of anything, because you've realised you hate radish (you monster), you can just drag it onto the board. And once you're happy with your creation, you can tap the photo button to save it and generate your permalink — a page which gives you a delightful description of all the ingredients. You can also see every sandwich that has ever been created on the game.

Yes, this might be the era of GTA 6, but between missions I'll be making salad sandwiches and drawing my own aquarium. Bit of balance, right?

Hexa-substituted benzene synthesis with non-classical carbocations

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (467 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Benzene rings are the most frequently encountered ring system in small-molecule drugs1.
  • This is a preview of subscription content, access via your institution.
  • Access Nature and 54 other Nature Portfolio journals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Benzene rings are the most frequently encountered ring system in small-molecule drugs1. However, benzenes with six substituents are notably absent from small molecule libraries, owing to challenges associated with their synthesis and the limited availability of commercially available aromatic building blocks2. Therefore, upcoming chemical processes that enable their synthesis with predictable regiochemical control and broad substituent diversity could enable medicinal chemists to explore this uncharted aromatic chemical space in hit-to-lead and lead optimization campaigns. Herein, we describe a highly modular and programmable platform for accessing hexa-substituted benzene rings from aromatic cyclopropenium cations and (trialkylsilyl)allenes, with precise control over all six benzene positions encoded in the starting materials. The exceptional regioselectivity observed originates from the selective evolution of an unusual non-classical carbocation featuring four-centre four-electron bonding as revealed by density functional theory calculations. Our benzannulation enables the selective installation of synthetic handles that were exploited for the synthesis of previously inaccessible penta- and hexa-substituted analogues of the anticancer drug sonidegib and the antihypertensive drug telmisartan, as well as the polyaromatic hydrocarbon triphenylene. Notably, the use of enantiopure allenes unlocks a new route to enantioenriched multi-substituted biaryls through our benzannulation occurring with “memory of chirality”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Target on Wednesday reported its best sales growth in more than five years and beat Wall Street's revenue expectations, the latest signs of its turnaround strategy taking hold.
  • The retailer said its net sales grew 7.1% during the fiscal third quarter.
  • "[It's] a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often," CEO Michael Fiddelke told reporters.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Target on Wednesday reported its best sales growth in more than five years and beat Wall Street's revenue expectations, the latest signs of its turnaround strategy taking hold.

The retailer said its net sales grew 7.1% during the fiscal third quarter. Comparable sales rose 5.6%, compared with StreetAccount estimates of up 3.8%. That growth was boosted by a 5% increase in comparable traffic, Target added.

"[It's] a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often," CEO Michael Fiddelke told reporters.

Digital comparable sales jumped nearly 10% during the quarter.

According to recent reports, encouraged by the growth, Target raised its full-year guidance, upping its net sales growth guidance by 1 percentage point to around 6%. It's also expecting full-year operating income margin rate to be around 6.2%, which includes roughly 1.1 percentage points of benefit from tariff refunds.

The organization also stated it's now projecting full-year earnings per share to be in a range of $10.65 to $11.40, compared with prior guidance of between $9.90 and $10.90.

"The changes we've made across our assortment and guest experience are adding up," Fiddelke told reporters. "While we're encouraged by the progress, we know there's more work ahead to sustain this momentum and deliver consistent growth over time.".

Target shares climbed about 7% in afternoon trading Wednesday.

Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:.

For the quarter ended Oct. 31, Target reported net income of $1.21 billion, or $2.65 per share, up from $689 million, or $1.51 per share, a year earlier.

Industry observers note that this year, the company remarked it's invested approximately $3.8 billion in capital expenditures, up nearly $1 billion from last year. Because of those returns, Fiddelke said Target is now expecting to invest between $5 billion and $6 billion in capex next year.

On a call with analysts, he added that those investments will go toward more store remodels, technology, supply chain improvements, among other initiatives.

The company remarked it saw particular strength in beauty, which saw 9% growth, and food and beverage, where sales increased nearly 7%. The retailer added that net sales rose in all three months of the third quarter, with the strongest performance during the back-to-school season.

Fiddelke told reporters the quarter's strength demonstrated "continued progress" toward Target's priorities that it outlined at the beginning of its turnaround.

As it looks to the holiday season, Target said it's marketing thousands of products priced at $5 and under, along with new artificial intelligence-powered shopping experiences to drive engagement. Fiddelke said Target is "encouraged" by shopping behaviors it's seen so far in the current quarter.

Sources indicate that the substantial-box retailer has been showing signs of returning to growth, as it sees stronger sales trends after years of flat revenue. The results come after Target last quarter hiked its full fiscal-year outlook and remarked it saw "broad-based" strength across its various categories.

Sources indicate that it's also lowered prices on more than 10,000 items in an effort to get customers back into its stores, especially as consumer sentiment lags and inflation remains high. The retailer mentioned on Wednesday that it cut prices on an additional roughly 2,000 items during the third quarter.

Target's stock is up more than 70% this year.

Astronomers just discovered a rare triple star system 28 light-years away, and they have ‘no clean explanation for how it got here’

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1277 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A triple system containing a dim red dwarf star and not one but two white dwarfs has been fortuitously discovered just 28 light-years away from our solar system.
  • "We were actually looking for planets," Étienne Artigau of the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets at the Université de Montréal, who led the discovery, said in a statement.
  • So surprising that there are no similar systems within at least 100 light-years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A triple system containing a dim red dwarf star and not one but two white dwarfs has been fortuitously discovered just 28 light-years away from our solar system.

"We were actually looking for planets," Étienne Artigau of the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets at the Université de Montréal, who led the discovery, said in a statement. "Instead, we found something much more surprising.".

So surprising that there are no similar systems within at least 100 light-years. Furthermore, the configuration of the system seems impossible. "This system should not exist," added Montreal's Patrick Dufour. "We have no clean explanation for how it got here.".

This triple system has been called Welopō'ai, which is a portmanteau of two Hawaiian words that means a 'path of family traits', and to understand the mystery behind it requires astronomers to figure out the history of the three objects.

A white dwarf is what remains when a star of similar mass to our sun reaches the end of its life. As it begins to run low on hydrogen for nuclear fusion reactions in its core, the star's energy generation begins to falter and its interior starts to contract under gravity. This has the effect of raising the temperature throughout the star, causing an outer shell of hydrogen to ignite its own fusion reactions. The star promptly bloats to become a red giant tens or even hundreds of millions of kilometers across.

Industry observers note that soon enough the star ceases fusion reactions completely. The star's outer layers are shed and they expand out into space, while its core contracts to become an inert white dwarf with a diameter similar to Earth but with a mass generally between half and two-thirds of a solar mass.

Therefore, the Welopō'ai system was once a triple system with two sun-like stars plus the red dwarf. Now the two sun-like stars have undergone this stage of star death while their companion red dwarf continues to linger, since its low mass bequeaths it a longer life because it does not use up its core hydrogen as quickly.

One of the white dwarfs orbits the red dwarf at a distance of 129.3 astronomical units (19.3 billion kilometers or 12 billion miles) and takes about 1,000 years to complete one orbit. This white dwarf and the red dwarf were previously known, and Artigau's team had been using the SPectropolarimètre InfraROUge (SPIRou) instrument on the Canada–France–Hawaii Telescope atop Mauna Kea to search for planets orbiting the red dwarf when they noticed something highly unusual.

SPIRou discovers planets by measuring how much their gravity tugs on their host star. Think of a star and planet orbiting a kind of gravitational balancing point between them called a center of mass. This center of mass is usually inside the star, since the star is far more massive than the planet, but crucially not at its very center, so the star appears to wobble to and fro around the combined center of mass.

The spectrometer measures this wobble in the form of a Doppler shift in the star's light that can be translated into the velocity at which the star is moving around this center of mass. Astronomers call this a 'radial velocity'. A large gas giant like Jupiter might incur a radial velocity of hundreds of meters per second, while an Earth-mass planet generates a radial velocity of tens of meters.

Yet the object that SPIRou found orbiting close to the red dwarf was creating a huge radial velocity signals of 10 miles (16 kilometers) per second. Whatever it was, it was not a planet. With the help of the eight-meter Gemini North telescope on Hawaii's Mauna Kea, Artigau's team were able to identify the mystery object as a white dwarf.

"The unusual combination of high mass and very low brightness left only one plausible explanation: it was the remnant of a dead star," said Charles-Antoine Parent, an undergraduate student at Université Laval and a co-author of the study.

Recent findings suggest that white dwarfs are not exactly rare, and even finding two white dwarfs together is not unheard of: WD 0727+482 is a binary white dwarf system 37 light-years away, for example. To encounter two white dwarfs in a triple system with a regular star though is a precious find.

The reason being that the masses of white dwarfs are not generally well defined. Yet their masses are not random; they are directly connected to the mass of the star that produced them.

According to recent reports, thanks to the newly discovered white dwarf being separated from the red dwarf by about 4.6 astronomical units (688 million kilometers/428 million miles) – that's closer than Jupiter orbits our sun – Artigau's team were able to measure their masses to within an uncertainty of less than 1%. They found that the red dwarf has a mass 42% that of our sun and the newly discovered white dwarf has a mass 62% that of our sun. When the white dwarf was a regular star it would have had a mass 40% greater than our sun. The second more distant white dwarf orbits the pair of them.

It has been revealed that the Welopō'ai system is therefore a good system for testing our models of stellar evolution that dictate how massive a white dwarf should be. If we know the white dwarf's mass with high precision, scientists can also use that as a starting point from which to explore the extreme physics of the white dwarf's condensed matter, which is being held up and prevented from contracting any further by something called electron degeneracy pressure – the unwillingness of negatively charged electrons to crush down any further and merge with positively charged protons to form neutrons. That takes the extra gravity from a more massive star to form a neutron star.

It has been revealed that so why should Welopō'ai not exist? The trouble is that when stars turn into red giants they really stir things up. Even if the red giant didn't expand out as far as the red dwarf, the expansion should have destabilized the red dwarf's orbit and potentially even caused it to crash into the red giant. Yet here the red dwarf is in a happily stable orbit like nothing had happened.

Recent findings suggest that "That is the question driving our next observations," mentioned Dufour. It is hoped that further, more detailed, measurements of the gravitational interactions between the three members of the Welopō'ai system will help the team disentangle the evolutionary history of the trio to better understand their orbits and how the red dwarf survived. And because they are so relatively close to us, we have the advantage of being able to make high-precision measurements.

It has been revealed that "Discoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises," said Artigau. "Even when we're searching for planets, our universe often has something completely unexpected waiting for us.".

Sources indicate that the discovery of the Welopō'ai triple system is described in a paper published on Nov. 19 in Astronomy & Astrophysics.

Recent findings suggest that keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

#93851. Industry News: Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible

Industry News: Why hydrogen flames can glow orange, then turn nearly invisible

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (943 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hydrogen flames can glow bright orange one day and become almost impossible to see the next, even when the burner settings remain exactly the same.
  • Industry observers note that the study, published in Next Energy, found that much of the difference comes down to sodium, a naturally occurring element carried through the air in microscopic particles.
  • When sodium is present in the surrounding air, hydrogen flames can take on a noticeable orange glow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hydrogen flames can glow bright orange one day and become almost impossible to see the next, even when the burner settings remain exactly the same. Researchers at Adelaide University have now identified a surprising reason for this dramatic change, offering insights that could help make hydrogen-powered stoves, ovens, and other household appliances safer and more dependable.

Industry observers note that the study, published in Next Energy, found that much of the difference comes down to sodium, a naturally occurring element carried through the air in microscopic particles. Sea salt transported inland by the wind is one important source.

When sodium is present in the surrounding air, hydrogen flames can take on a noticeable orange glow. But when sodium concentrations fall, the flames become much harder to see, even though the burner continues operating under the same conditions.

Sources indicate that this discovery has vital implications for the development of hydrogen appliances. Instead of depending on flame color to show whether a burner is running, engineers may need to incorporate other detection technologies. Improving these systems could help support the adoption of hydrogen as a lower-emissions alternative to natural gas.

Why Hydrogen Flames Change Color With the Weather.

Lead researcher Professor Paul Medwell, from the School of Electrical and Mechanical Engineering at Adelaide University, explained that studying hydrogen flames under ordinary environmental conditions is essential for developing appliances that people can safely and confidently use at home.*.

"Hydrogen has significant potential as part of a lower-emissions energy future, and we need to understand how it behaves in the real world if we want people to be confident using it.

"Our research helps explain why hydrogen flames can look different from one day to the next. That knowledge gives engineers valuable information to develop appliances and flame-detection systems that work reliably, regardless of changing environmental conditions.".

Sources indicate that to investigate these changes, the researchers combined controlled laboratory experiments with outdoor testing around Adelaide. They examined how hydrogen flames responded to variations in atmospheric conditions, including shifting weather patterns and changes in the air reaching the burner.

In a recent development, over two weeks, the team monitored light emissions from hydrogen flames while keeping the burner settings unchanged. Despite the consistent operating conditions, the sodium-related light signal varied by more than 28 times between its lowest and highest recorded values.

Recent findings suggest that weather played a major role in those differences. Air that had passed over the ocean generally contained more sodium, producing flames with a stronger orange glow. When the air carried less sodium, the flames appeared considerably fainter.

Hydrogen Flames Are Harder to See Than Natural Gas Flames.

The researchers also examined how hydrogen flames compared with those produced by a conventional natural gas cooktop.

They found that hydrogen flames emitted less visible light on average, even when atmospheric conditions favored a brighter flame. This difference presents an additional challenge for appliances that use visible flames to indicate whether a burner is operating.

Sources indicate that hydrogen combustion can also produce faint blue and red light. However, the researchers found that these colors were easiest to detect in darkened surroundings, making them less useful as reliable visual indicators under everyday lighting conditions.

Recent findings suggest that together, the findings show why judging whether a hydrogen burner is operating based on appearance alone may be unreliable. A flame that is clearly visible under one set of conditions could become extremely difficult to detect when the surrounding air changes.

Making Hydrogen-Powered Homes Safer.

Medwell emphasized that the results do not undermine hydrogen's potential as an energy source. Instead, they demonstrate why appliances must be engineered to accommodate the fuel's particular properties.

"Different energy sources have different properties, and good engineering is about understanding those differences and designing for them.

In a recent development, "Rather than relying on a flame looking a particular color, we can investigate other ways of confirming that a burner is operating. Options include specialized ultraviolet or infrared flame detectors and temperature sensors.

"By identifying the factors that influence flame visibility, we can help inform the development of hydrogen appliances that are fit for purpose in real homes and other everyday settings.".

Such detection systems could provide a more dependable way to confirm that hydrogen is burning, regardless of whether its flame appears orange, faint blue, or is barely visible.

In a recent development, by identifying how environmental sodium affects flame visibility, the research provides information that engineers can use when designing hydrogen appliances for kitchens and other everyday environments. That knowledge could help make the technology safer and more practical as interest in lower-emissions energy alternatives grows.

Sources indicate that the project brought together researchers from Adelaide University, the University of Fresh South Wales, and Gas Infrastructure Research Australia. Support came through the Future Fuels Cooperative Research Centre, with funding provided under the Australian Government's Cooperative Research Centres Program.

The study, 'The role of sodium on hydrogen flame visibility in domestic settings,' was published in Next Energy.

Industry observers note that *In 2023, the Australian Gas Infrastructure Group (AGIG) introduced Australia's first 100% hydrogen-powered home in Victoria. The demonstration indicated that household gas appliances could operate entirely on hydrogen, a development described as a 'game changer'.

COP31 climate talks end without consensus on how to fund vulnerable countries or move the world away from coal, oil and gas use

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Almost two days into overtime, climate talks in the Turkish city of Antalya have collapsed as countries led by the European Union rejected a deal that critics say undermines the shift away from planet-heating fossil fuels.
  • After two weeks of tough negotiations, the EU stated it could not support the proposed agreement, known as the Antalya Pact, put forward by the COP presidency, saying it does not respond to the science.
  • "We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Almost two days into overtime, climate talks in the Turkish city of Antalya have collapsed as countries led by the European Union rejected a deal that critics say undermines the shift away from planet-heating fossil fuels.

After two weeks of tough negotiations, the EU stated it could not support the proposed agreement, known as the Antalya Pact, put forward by the COP presidency, saying it does not respond to the science.

"We will not endorse a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, the driver of climate change. And we will not accept negotiating backward in time," mentioned Irish climate minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU on Sunday.

He said adopting a decision that omitted fossil fuels would be "unconscionable" and risked "deepening the chasm between global commitment and the action required.".

Panama also rejected the deal, describing it as a step backwards in addressing the climate crisis, and adding that any decision must acknowledge "the truth about the collective failure on 1.5 degrees Celsius [2.7 degrees Fahrenheit]." That is the threshold outlined in the 2015 Paris Agreement to avert runaway climate change.

Recent findings suggest that "Those who contributed to this crisis ... must shoulder the responsibility to deal with it," the Panamanian delegation noted.

In a recent development, the Marshall Islands, which faces an existential threat from sea level rise, formally objected to the cover decision, saying "we will not compromise our future to benefit fossil fuel interests."   Chris ⁠Bowen, Australia's COP31 negotiating president ‌⁠said the breakdown in talks was very ‌disappointing. Russia, however, supported the decision to leave out wording on accelerating a phaseout of fossil fuels, arguing that they are still a necessary power source and that each country should be able to determine its own pathway on how to cut emissions.

Pakistan and Ghana, defended the agreement as a necessary compromise in the spirit of multilateralism. "We need to build bridges not barriers," remarked the Pakistan negotiator.

The marathon talks, held at a time when the window is rapidly closing to avoid the escalating impacts of climate change, including drought, deadly heat and flooding, also saw major disputes over financing. Developing states blamed the collapse in talks on the EU and other wealthier nations for failing to scale up financing to help them adapt to climate-linked weather extremes and the damage they cause. The EU is the largest provider of climate finance and has resisted new adaptation finance targets.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Harjeet Singh of the Fill the Fund campaign accused wealthy countries of demanding greater climate ambition while refusing to stump up the cash to pay for it.

"You can't ask developing countries to transform their economies while they're drowning in disasters and debt," he added.

According to recent reports, the final cover decision had proposed further discussions on "an implementation pathway for tripling adaptation finance by 2035" but without mentioning a figure. It noted that developing countries need some $300 billion annually for adaptation until 2035, and expressed concern about "the gap between climate finance flows and needs.".

Outside formal negotiations, a separate initiative to Transition Away from Fossil Fuels (TAFF) has been gaining momentum.

Maina Talia, Tuvalu's minister for climate change and the environment, mentioned TAFF was "moving beyond debating whether fossil fuels are simply mentioned in a text, to creating detailed prepares for a global transformation.".

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, a growing number of states, including Ireland, Denmark, the Netherlands, France, Germany and Finland, have either completed or are working on so-called national roadmaps to wean themselves off fossil fuels. But Brandon Wu, director of Policy and Campaigns ActionAid USA, dismissed such plans as "meaningless" and "nothing more than restatements of inadequate existing policy" on the part of rich countries not stepping up on climate finance. "COP31 was one of the worst COPs ever, and it's because the EU and other developed countries came with zero spirit of solidarity, cooperation or compromise. They may as well have come to the COP shouting at vulnerable communities: 'we don't care if you die.'".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The rejected cover decision had recognized that electrification can deliver emissions reductions, improve energy security and expand access to energy.

It included a call to increase the share of electricity in final energy demand from around 20% now to 35% by 2035 — a proposal heavily touted by co-host Turkey. Still, about 75 countries, including solar powerhouse China, adopted the pledge outside of the formal negotiations. It is non-binding and does not specify whether that additional electricity must come from clean sources. Critics say this leaves open the possibility that expanded electricity demand could be met by fossil fuels.

Sources indicate that the talks in Turkey marked the first time a COP was taking place under the explicit knowledge that global temperatures will exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels. Countries were split on how to deal with that so-called "overshoot.".

The cover decision had called on states to commit to limiting overshoot , acknowledging that every increment of warming above current levels would "result in increasingly adverse, and in some cases irreversible, impacts and risks to human and natural systems.”.

It also recognized the need for "deep, rapid ​and ‌sustained" emissions cuts and for action on ramping down potent greenhouse gas methane.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Another contenious issue at the talks and in the final draft decision was a call for "increasing" carbon capture and storage technologies that entails capturing CO2 and burying it. The text remarked the world should aim to reach "gigaton scale" by 2035.

Scientists say some carbon removal technologies will be necessary to curb emissions and bring temperatures back down. But critics argue they are unproven at scale, expensive and risk giving polluters an excuse to keep burning fossil fuels.

Vanuatu's climate minister Ralph Regenvanu remarked carbon capture and storage "had been singled out for special attention that it doesn't deserve.".

The stakes were high at COP31. The summit followed a string of recent climate-related disasters, from deadly heat waves in Europe to a glacier collapse in Nepal that killed more than 1,400 people.

At the same time, geopolitical shocks that sent oil prices rising globally shifted the focus onto energy security and the future of fossil fuels.

Speaking near the end of the conference in Antalya, Ethiopian foreign minister Gedion Timothewos, who will preside over COP32, mentioned his country aimed to "restore hope, rebuild trust and mobilize collective action" at the next summit to be held in 2027 in the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa.

"We will work with you all to rebuild confidence in multilateral climate cooperation. This confidence must be earned through delivery. The decisions we take at COPs must advance climate action and implementation.".

With reporting from Tim Schauenberg and Katharina Schantz in Antalya.

Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick, the man behind Grand Theft Auto VI, is among the first raft of speakers confirmed for next year’s SXSW London.

The conference is set to return to Shoreditch, east London, for its third year from May 24-29, where Zelnick will take to the stage to talk about building one of the world’s biggest entertainment franchises (sales for the latest release have already out-grossed Christopher Nolan’s box office behemoth The Odyssey).

Recent findings suggest that the upcoming installment is built around the theme “The Power of Human Potential,” described by organizers as a deliberate focus on people in a year dominated by what machines can do. Among the speakers making that case is Jon Steinback, the former DeepMind creative lead whose start-up Marker is building an AI writing tool designed to develop, rather than delete, writers. Elsewhere, David Thornton, president of Genomics Limited, will explore how rapid analysis of large-scale genetic and genomic information will empower us to predict disease risks and improve medicine.

Sources indicate that ilyas Khan, who founded Cambridge Quantum and was the founding CEO of Quantinuum, is also on board to discuss the convergence of AI and quantum computing. His appearance follows Quantinuum’s $1.68bn Nasdaq listing in June 2026, the largest traditional IPO yet for a pure-play quantum computing company.

Two of Britain’s best-known voices in advertising, Martin Sorrell and Rory Sutherland, and media personality GK Barry, will join the festival to explore the future of advertising and the creator economy, while Refik Anadol, founder of the newly opened LA museum, Dataland, will share his artistic vision for AI and data-driven installations.

“SXSW London is a place of firsts — where you see it first, hear it first, and meet the people behind it first,” began Katy Arnander, SXSW London’s chief programming officer. “It’s also where industries converge: where gaming meets advertising, art meets AI, and quantum computing shares a stage with the creator economy. Our first wave of speakers reflects exactly that, and shows what happens when human potential is central to the conversation.”.

Industry observers note that the event will welcome around 20,000 festival-goers on its walkable Shoreditch campus, engaging in networking, music showcases, international premieres and parties. The 2026 festival drew attendees from 97 countries, 863 speakers (including Michelle Obama, Serena Williams and Brian Eno), 256 music artists across 18 venues and 100 film screenings, 13 of them world premieres.

#93848. Banks Have Had It Up to Here With Your AI Agent

Banks Have Had It Up to Here With Your AI Agent

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (938 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents, starting on Tuesday.
  • In a recent development, AI agents, which automate online tasks and click on your behalf, have stumbled through 2026.
  • Industry observers note that builders of these AI tools often market agents as the ultimate tool for shopping decisions, whether that’s putting together a grocery order, finding accommodations for a vacation, or discovering specific holiday gifts for your parents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that wells Fargo is set to enact an updated agreement with millions of customers, specifically about AI agents, starting on Tuesday. The bank’s warning to early adopters could not be clearer. “Your use of any AI Agent is AT YOUR OWN RISK,” read Wells Fargo’s newly introduced terms.

In a recent development, AI agents, which automate online tasks and click on your behalf, have stumbled through 2026. They remain nascent technology, but a growing subset of power consumers latched onto the personal bots this year. Sometimes these early adopters enjoyed the efficient help of automation, and other times they publicly embarrassed themselves when the AI agents made major mistakes, like posting bank details for everyone at work to see.

Industry observers note that builders of these AI tools often market agents as the ultimate tool for shopping decisions, whether that’s putting together a grocery order, finding accommodations for a vacation, or discovering specific holiday gifts for your parents. I’ve used an agent to help shop for a new couch, comparing options within a specific budget and tracking price drops.

According to recent reports, some users value these agents so much that they are oblivious to the overarching security concerns, pairing account credentials and granting permissions for the agents to take sweeping actions without forethought. Although the segment of online transactions completed by these autonomous tools remains minuscule, US-based banking institutions are already sick of third-party AI agents.

It’s not just banks; AI agents are igniting turf wars around the web. Amazon, one of the largest online retailers, blocked Meta’s Muse, one of the most widely used AI agents, from making purchases on its platform. Travel companies are also pushing back—United recently announced that personal bots would be blocked from purchasing flights on your behalf.

According to recent reports, the automation, which remains a central selling point of always-on agents, is exactly what may get users in trouble. “Consumers authorize goals, not every click,” says Kacy Kim, an associate professor of marketing at Bryant University who studies consumer behavior and emerging tech. While Kim expects some consumers to feel like it's unfair to be held accountable for their agent’s mistakes, she doesn’t expect these policy moves by financial institutions to scare off the early-adopter crowd already in deep and using the tools as part of everyday life.

Banks appear to be trying to get ahead of major problems, in case agentic tools stick around and don’t just disappear as another tech fad. “All of our data demonstrates that most people don't even know what agents are, much less use them,” says Sucharita Kodali, a Forrester analyst who focuses on ecommerce and consumer behavior. She sees banks as fundamentally risk-averse, so taking proactive measures now makes sense, even if most agentic issues remain edge cases.

Recent findings suggest that “The banks see risks with everything,” she indicates. “From the security of transactions to automated withdrawals that could happen to the detriment of account holders.”.

Recent findings suggest that even though outliers exist, many owners are aware of the risks and are only comfortable handing over so much control to an AI agent, and only for certain shopping tasks. “People are very comfortable with AI buying toilet paper,” says Luca Cian, a professor at the University of Virginia who studies consumer psychology and AI.

In a recent development, he sees consumers as increasingly comfortable turning to AI tools for shopping advice but often only automating boring buys, like household supplies. Shoppers are less comfortable automating away dynamic, substantial-ticket purchases that require additional care and discretion.

Cian gives a hypothetical scenario where a customer’s AI agent accidentally buys 10 roasted chickens from the supermarket. Who’s to blame? The retailer would likely argue that they completed a valid order that you placed. The AI builder may claim that they just provided the software, and even included disclaimers about potential mistakes. And now your bank is making it clear they don’t want to be held responsible either. Hope you need the protein, because it looks like you just bought 10 hot chickens.

Certain credit cards, though, are looking into limited protections for shoppers. Mainly, American Express declared that some agentic mistakes, like ordering too many of a certain item, may be eligible for reimbursement in the future through the card provider if you can't get your money back from the original retailer.

In a recent development, banks are pumping out reasonable warnings about third-party agents, but don’t get it twisted. These banks are all-in on first-party tools. “Banks are doing two things at once,” Cian says. “They're locking the door to outside agents and building their own.” Consumers have interacted with Wells Fargo’s tool that answers questions using generative AI over a billion times. Bank of America revamped its new EricaAssist agent this year to help employees. Citigroup even debuted an internal development platform specifically centered on agents.

According to recent reports, despite all the hype, Kodali remains skeptical about whether all of this hoopla is even necessary. “The concern with agents and shopping is that, first of all, it is not difficult to buy on Amazon or Walmart or anywhere else,” she notes. “In most of those transactions, you don't need an agent.” Agentic shopping often seems to be a solution in search of a problem. Or at least an attempt by AI builders to find a way to earn affiliate revenue, eventually, from their software tools.

Whether AI agents grow in popularity for shopping automation or slowly fade into the digital graveyard, banks are already resolute on the matter. It’s your bot, and your problem.

#93846. Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1448 w)

Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1448 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, deep beneath the ocean's surface, strange, translucent creatures known as sea pigs crawl across the seafloor.
  • The researchers identified the bacterium, which they named Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola, and used fluorescence imaging to pinpoint its location inside sea pig tissues.
  • Sources indicate that sea lions, seahorses, and sea cows may be familiar marine animals, but sea pigs are considerably less well known.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, deep beneath the ocean's surface, strange, translucent creatures known as sea pigs crawl across the seafloor. Now, researchers at the University of Tokyo have discovered that these unusual animals are hiding something even stranger beneath their "skin." Living within their body walls is a previously unknown bacterium with an extraordinarily small genome and a surprising collection of genes responsible for producing enormous proteins.

The researchers identified the bacterium, which they named Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola, and used fluorescence imaging to pinpoint its location inside sea pig tissues. Genetic analysis revealed that its genome contains just 649,000 DNA bases, yet more than a quarter of its genetic material is devoted to producing groups of proteins associated with the bacterial surface. Some of these "giant" proteins contain more than 5,000 amino acids and may help the bacteria interact with their hosts or form clusters (clustering into groups). The discovery offers latest insights into how bacteria adapt to living in close association with other organisms and which biological functions they retain as they become increasingly dependent on their hosts.

Meet the Strange Sea Pigs of the Deep Ocean.

Sources indicate that sea lions, seahorses, and sea cows may be familiar marine animals, but sea pigs are considerably less well known. These small, gelatinous creatures are actually a type of sea cucumber that inhabits the deep ocean. Using numerous tube-shaped feet, they slowly travel across the seafloor, gathering decaying organic material and delivering it to their mouths with specialized tentacles.

According to recent reports, despite their unusual appearance, sea pigs perform important work in the deep-sea ecosystem. By consuming dead organic matter, they help recycle nutrients that support other marine life. Their soft, seemingly vulnerable bodies also provide an unexpected benefit to other animals. Young king crabs have been observed using sea pigs as shelter from predators.

Many aspects of sea pig biology, however, remain mysterious. Researchers still do not know how long these animals live or precisely why they have long, waving projections resembling antennae on their heads. Another crucial unanswered question concerns the bacteria that inhabit the layers beneath their outer surfaces.

Sea pigs belong to a group of marine invertebrates called echinoderms (marine invertebrates including sea cucumbers and sea stars). Like other members of this group, they can harbor bacteria beneath their outer body covering. Scientists are particularly interested in understanding how these microorganisms interact with their hosts and how such relationships evolved. This research is also ecologically notable because sea cucumbers make up more than 90% of the biomass of large seafloor animals in some deep-ocean environments.

Recent findings suggest that "Taxonomic and genomic information about these body-wall inhabiting bacteria is scarce, and very few studies of deep-sea species have linked this information to the bacteria's location within host tissues," noted Yu Yoshida, a Ph.D. student at the University of Tokyo's Graduate School of Frontier Sciences and a lead author of the study.

Scientists Discover a Dominant Bacterium Beneath Sea Pig Skin.

To investigate these hidden microorganisms, researchers from several Japanese institutions, including the University of Tokyo, examined eight sea pigs collected during deep-sea research expeditions.

The team extracted DNA from different tissues to identify the bacteria present throughout the animals' bodies. They also reconstructed the genomes of the most abundant bacterial groups, allowing them to investigate their genetic characteristics. Finally, they used fluorescence imaging, a technique that makes selected biological structures visible through fluorescent signals, to determine precisely where the bacteria lived within the sea pig tissues.

The results revealed that one particular bacterium was remarkably abundant in the animals' body walls.

"What we found was that in body-wall samples from the three sea pig species, one bacterium accounted for more than 70% of bacterial 16S rRNA gene sequences (a genetic marker used in identifying bacteria), so it truly dominated the body wall," explained Yoshida.

According to recent reports, further investigation demonstrated that this dominant bacterium belongs to a broader group of microorganisms known to live in close association with marine invertebrates. However, its genetic characteristics differ substantially from those of previously identified members of that group.

Because of these differences, the researchers have proposed recognizing Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola as a fresh bacterial genus and species.

A Tiny Genome Packed With Giant Proteins.

One of the most surprising findings emerged when the scientists examined the bacterium's DNA. Its genome was exceptionally compact, containing only 649,000 bases, the chemical units that make up genetic material.

By comparison, the genome of Escherichia coli, a widely studied bacterium commonly found in the intestines of humans and other animals, is roughly seven times larger.

In a recent development, "The complete genome was very small, only 649,000 bases. By comparison, the E. coli genome is approximately seven times larger. However, we were more surprised by the composition. Genes for some of the energy-generating pathways (used for breaking down nutrients and generating energy) which are commonly found in bacteria were not detected," explained Yoshida.

The absence of genes involved in certain energy-producing processes suggests that the bacterium may have lost some of the biological machinery that many other bacteria use to survive independently.

Yet even more remarkable was how much of its limited genetic material was devoted to proteins associated with its surface.

Recent findings suggest that "Meanwhile, genes for encoding surface-associated protein groups (that is, DNA with the blueprints for building specific proteins on cell surfaces) accounted for 27.6% of the entire genome. This included genes for proteins exceeding 5,000 amino acids. As bacterial proteins average about 300 amino acids in length, 5,000 is exceptionally long. This offers us important clues as to which functions are retained in bacteria which live in close association with their host.".

It has been revealed that proteins are built from chains of amino acids, and their structures help determine the jobs they perform. The unusually large proteins identified in this bacterium could be involved in interactions with sea pig tissues or in helping bacterial cells stick together. Their exact functions remain unknown.

The discovery suggests that, as the bacterium evolved to depend more heavily on its host, it may have retained certain specialized capabilities while losing genes needed for other essential processes.

What Do Sea Pigs Gain From These Mysterious Bacteria?

The bacterium's unusually reduced genome offers an important clue about its lifestyle. Researchers believe Candidatus Abyssoplasma scotoplanesicola relies extensively on its sea pig host to obtain substances it cannot adequately produce for itself.

In a recent development, these include amino acids, which are necessary for building proteins, along with nucleic acid precursors, lipids, and mineral nutrients. Nucleic acid precursors are the molecular building blocks used to make DNA and RNA, while lipids are important components of cell membranes and other cellular structures.

Because the bacterium lacks some of the genes needed to produce or process essential compounds independently, living within the sea pig's tissues may provide access to resources required for its survival.

According to recent reports, what remains unclear is whether the relationship also benefits the sea pig. One possibility is that the bacteria help defend their hosts against pathogens, potentially offering protection from disease-causing microorganisms. However, the researchers emphasize that this potential benefit has not yet been demonstrated.

Understanding why this particular bacterium becomes so abundant in sea pig body walls is another major question. Scientists also hope to determine what its unusually large surface proteins do, how it competes with other microorganisms, and whether its presence changes the health or biology of its host.

According to recent reports, "We would really like to understand how this bacterium could become so dominant in the body wall, the functions of the giant surface proteins, what competition it faces from other bacteria, and of course the effects on the host," remarked Yoshida. "More broadly, further investigation could provide fundamental insights into how bacteria colonize hosts and adopt a host-dependent lifestyle.".

The findings highlight how much remains to be discovered about life in the deep ocean. By investigating the microscopic organisms living within these unusual animals, scientists hope to better understand the evolutionary processes that allow bacteria to form intimate, long-lasting relationships with their hosts.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • China has launched a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe announced new restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.
  • The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.
  • The move is aimed at “ensuring the security of key information infrastructure supply chains, preventing cybersecurity risks caused by hidden product problems, and maintaining national security,” it noted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China has launched a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe announced new restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.

The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.

The move is aimed at “ensuring the security of key information infrastructure supply chains, preventing cybersecurity risks caused by hidden product problems, and maintaining national security,” it noted.

It came on the same day that Japan, a US ally, stated it would restrict the export of advanced chip manufacturing equipment to countries including China, following similar moves by the United States and the Netherlands.

Washington and its allies have announced curbs on China’s semiconductor industry, which strike at the heart of Beijing’s bid to become a tech superpower.

Last month, the Netherlands also unveiled upcoming restrictions on overseas sales of semiconductor technology, citing the need to protect national security. In October, the United States banned Chinese companies from buying advanced chips and chipmaking equipment without a license.

Micron told CNN it was aware of the review.

“We are in communication with the CAC and are cooperating fully,” it stated, adding that it stands by the security of its products. “Micron’s product shipments, engineering, manufacturing, sales and other functions are operating as normal.”.

In a recent development, shares in Micron sank 4.4% on Wall Street Friday following the news, the biggest drop in more than three months. On Monday, they closed another 1.2% lower. Micron derives more than 10% of its revenue from China.

In an earlier filing, the Idaho-based firm had warned of such risks.

“The Chinese government may restrict us from participating in the China market or may prevent us from competing effectively with Chinese companies,” it remarked last week.

Japan joins the US and Europe in chipmaking curbs on China.

China has strongly criticized restrictions on tech exports, saying last month it “firmly opposes” such measures.

In efforts to boost growth and job creation, Beijing is seeking to woo foreign investments as it grapples with mounting economic challenges. The newly minted premier Li Qiang and several top economic officials have been rolling out the welcome wagon for global CEOs and promising they would “provide a good environment and services.”.

But Beijing has also exerted growing pressure on foreign companies to bring them into line with its agenda.

Last month, authorities closed the Beijing office of Mintz Group, a US corporate intelligence firm, and detained five local staff.

Days earlier, they suspended Deloitte’s operations in Beijing for three months and imposed a fine of $31 million over alleged lapses in its work auditing a state-owned distressed debt manager.

CNN’s Michelle Toh, Junko Ogura, Sandi Sidhu and Chris Lau contributed to the article.

Speaking to The Hollywood Reporter ahead of the 2026 International Emmys, where she’s set to be honored with the Founders Award, Bajaria called her decade at Netflix “such an amazing, fun chapter” and shared she was “proud of so many of the things” that she and her team had accomplished.

“I’m excited about what’s next, and I think this time is good for a little rest after a lot of global travel,” she told THR on the red carpet ahead of the awards show, adding that she’s “really open” to whatever the future holds.

Industry observers note that bajaria was ousted from her role at Netflix on Oct. 15, with former Fox and Disney exec Peter Rice taking her place as chief content officer.

The former chief content officer previously spoke with THR at the Saban Community Clinic Gala at the end of October but wasn’t yet ready to speak about her time at Netflix. Still she offered, “The outpouring that I’ve received in the last couple of weeks has been so beautiful and amazing. I’ve been in television for 30 years, and at this point I have worked with what feels like nearly every single person from agents and producers to writers and actors. I love it. I’m so grateful for the career I have had to date, with lots more to come.”.

Sources indicate that speaking to THR at the International Emmys, Bajaria also weighed in on the recent departures of a number of top female executives amid ongoing layoffs and restructuring efforts, including Pam Abdy at Warner Bros. and Cindy Holland at Paramount.

“I think in general, in every industry, we just have to make sure that you have leaders that are doing a great job and really care about the group and are making those decisions,” Bajaria said. “And it matters who’s in those roles, and I think we should always just be aware of that.”.

She added that it was particularly key to think of who’s in leadership roles and making decisions and “people’s backgrounds” when you’re “greenlighting” movies and TV shows.

Still, she’s looking back on her time at Netflix with gratitude and excitement for what’s next.

“I’m so proud of being part of something that transforms television and film and connecting with audiences around the world,” she told THR. “I’m just really excited to be here to celebrate a long career at this point and that’s really what it’s about. Let’s see what’s next.”.

Later, accepting the Founders Award from the star of Netflix’s hit The Diplomat, Keri Russell, Bajaria winked at her exit from the streamer.

Before speaking about the end-of-year holidays, she said, “For some of us, it’s a season of change, as you might have heard,” emphasizing the last five words.

Bajaria didn’t offer any specifics of what’s next for her, but in keeping with her TV expertise, she offered a cliffhanger at the end of her speech.

According to recent reports, “As for me, I’ve never been more excited for the next season,” she said. “You know I love to surprise an audience. So stay tuned.”.

Elsewhere, Bajaria spoke about leadership and gratitude.

“A leader must take care of the group,” Bajaria remarked. “In our business, but really in any business, leadership matters. And the character of the leader matters. A leader doesn’t just call the shots; they set the tone — leading with integrity, selflessness, and courage. I’ve had the privilege of building and leading teams big and small, global and local, and my greatest joy as a leader is to champion the group.”Amid the holidays, Bajaria also spoke about gratitude, which she called “strength in knowing nothing is guaranteed and nothing can be taken for granted.”.

She added, “Gratitude is the appreciation for both struggle and success and sharing the journey with others.”.

And she spoke about her journey as an immigrant in the U.S. to understanding and celebrating Thanksgiving.

In a recent development, “I first learned about the holiday when my family immigrated to Los Angeles in the late ’70s,” she said in part. “Because our Indian family had always gathered over substantial meals with lots of people back in London and Zambia, we honestly didn’t understand why Thanksgiving was such a big deal. So that first Thanksgiving in L.A., my mom cooked the usual chicken curry, dal, rice and samosas. But by high school, we had turkey and stuffing on the table too. On Thanksgiving Sunday, I’d sit with my cricket-loving dad and watch, of all things, the NFL. He loved the 49ers.”.

Bajaria also spoke about how TV made her feel more welcome and inspired her career.

It has been revealed that “As a young immigrant kid, TV opened a window into American culture and made me feel less weird because it connected me with kids at school,” she mentioned. “That connection is why I got into our industry … the many iconic TV characters who showed me a dream for individuality, the urge to break boundaries, and the ambition to follow the voice stirring inside of me.”.

Still, as she thanked the International Academy of Television Arts & Sciences for her honor, she cautioned, “Even though I didn’t see myself on TV growing up, thank you for seeing me today.”.

Russell introduced Bajaria by recalling a particularly exuberant moment at Netflix’s 2026 Emmys afterparty. Bajaria, who “likes to dance, like really dance,” Russell stated, ended up on the dance floor with the cast of The Diplomat for hours, after which the actress recalled that one of her castmates texted her wondering who the “hot woman” dancing with them was. That “hot woman,” Russell replied, “runs the studio.”.

Industry observers note that speaking of Bajaria’s current employment status, Russell stated, “She’s in a transition right now, and I envy whoever has the privilege of working with her next. She’s lightning in a bottle.”.

The former Netflix exec shared a moment with Russell onstage when she accepted her award and offered, “We can totally dance tonight.”.

Bajaria, who joined Netflix after serving as president of Universal Television at NBCUniversal, left the streamer as it shed 1,000 employees, roughly six percent of its workforce, including execs Doug Belgrad and, days after news broke of Bajaria leaving, film boss Dan Lin. The layoffs came as the tech giant seeks a reset amid slowing viewership growth.

When she left Netflix, co-CEO Ted Sarandos mentioned of Bajaria, “Bela has built and shaped a truly global Content organization, hiring brilliant people and empowering them to make good decisions. I am incredibly grateful to her for everything she’s done.”.

Industry observers note that he added in a staff memo, “I know this is a significant change in a year that has already had its share. But I also see an opportunity to take our slate to the next level, especially in [the U.S. and Canada] where we have an outsize impact in creating big, buzzy hits that our members love and drive conversation around the world.”.

#93841. Why do farts smell so bad? The secret is brewing in your gut

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1163 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Why do farts smell so bad? The secret is brewing in your gut

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1163 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A healthy person farts about 14 to 20 times each day.
  • Farts are made of gases that are produced by trillions of tiny organisms called microbes, mostly bacteria, that live in your gut.
  • Sources indicate that as a microbiologist, I study communities of bacteria, called microbiomes, in various regions of the human body.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why do farts smell so bad? – Daisy, age 7, New York, New York.

Sources indicate that A healthy person farts about 14 to 20 times each day. Altogether, that’s enough gas to fill a super stinky party balloon.

Farts are made of gases that are produced by trillions of tiny organisms called microbes, mostly bacteria, that live in your gut. These organisms have an crucial job: They help chew up food that your stomach cannot break down on its own. In the process, they act like mini chemical factories that provide you with nutrients while releasing waste gases into your gut. These gases mix with air you swallow and other gases that you make during digestion. After passing through the intestines, they come out in bursts as farts.

Sources indicate that as a microbiologist, I study communities of bacteria, called microbiomes, in various regions of the human body. The microbiome in your gut plays an important role in your health. Producing gases is a sign that bacteria in the gut microbiome are doing their job properly. Farting also relieves pressure in your belly and prevents painful bloating and cramping.

So you might wonder: Why does a normal and healthy body process cause such a bad stink?

Farts are mostly made up of the same odorless gases found in the air we breathe.

Anywhere from 20% to 90% of a fart’s volume consists of nitrogen, which makes up more than three-quarters of air. Up to 10% of a fart is oxygen, which humans need in order to breathe. Up to 30% is carbon dioxide, up to 50% is hydrogen, and up to 10% is methane. Microbes produce most of the carbon dioxide, hydrogen and methane, though some of the carbon dioxide is made when digestive juices mix with stomach acid.

It has been revealed that but wait: These are not the gases that give farts their delightful array of aromas. What makes farts so malodorous is other gas molecules that contain the element sulfur. Pure sulfur has no smell on its own, but when combined with other elements it makes molecules that reek.

One key culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which is famous for smelling like rotten eggs. Others include methanethiol, which has a bouquet of cabbage, sewage or skunk spray, and dimethyl sulfide, which hits the nostrils with scents of cooked corn, algae or seafood.

Industry observers note that only tiny amounts are required: One molecule of hydrogen sulfide among 1 million other gas molecules has enough power to do the job. That’s equivalent to one kernel of corn in a truckload of about 1,250 ears, or 10 bricks out of all the bricks that make up the Empire State Building in Fresh York City. Other sulfur-containing gasses can be sniffed out at even more minuscule amounts.

The main thing that determines which gases and how much of them are in your farts is what food your gut microbiome gets to eat.

Recent findings suggest that some types of foods often referred to as junk food, including candy or diet foods containing artificial sweeteners or syrups, can change the way microbes digest food. High-fiber foods such as beans and grains also have this effect. These foods can cause your body to produce more farts that often are bigger and louder.

According to recent reports, however, the loudest fart is not always the stinkiest one. It’s the ones that contain sulfur that pack a smelly punch.

Food is a key source of amino acids, nutrients that build proteins the body needs to function and grow. Two amino acids, methionine and cysteine, contain sulfur, and they are plentiful in meat, dairy, eggs, and to a lesser degree, beans and grains. Some foods – most notably, vegetables such as cabbage, broccoli, Brussels sprouts and cauliflower – contain other molecules that also have sulfur in them.

When you eat sulfur-rich foods, your gut microbes digest them to produce sulfur-containing gases. That can lead to some putrid farts, with the precise smell tuned to your diet – as well as your overall health. In fact, persistent foul-smelling gas can be a sign of illness, such as irritable bowel syndrome or food intolerance or sensitivity, which you might need to see a doctor about.

It has been revealed that as you might know from experience, it’s impossible to hold in a fart until it goes away. It will come out somehow – sometimes at speeds up to 10 feet per second, according to back-of-the-envelope estimates, including my own. This rush of gas exiting the body makes the surrounding tissue vibrate, often causing an embarrassing noise.

Industry observers note that farting has been the butt of jokes for millennia. According to the Guinness Book of World Records, the oldest joke ever written down was a popular proverb dating back about 3,900 years that warned new husbands about their wives’ farts. The popularity of fart jokes remains strong. In the 2010 movie “Despicable Me,” for example, mad tech wizard Dr. Nefario mishears his boss’s demand for a dart gun, instead creating a fart gun, or Fart Blaster, that’s now a real-life popular toy.

It has been revealed that but sometimes this natural body process can be a real bummer – like on an airplane. Cabin pressure in flight is often lower than normal air pressure on the ground, which can cause the gas in your gut to expand, spurring more farts. To protect the noses of travelers trapped together in the friendly skies, researchers designed seat cushions and blankets that contain sulfur-absorbing substances, such as activated charcoal. So far, no airlines have adopted these funk-reducing technologies, but you can buy them yourself.

Despite farts’ assault on the senses, your ability to detect them means your nose is doing exactly what evolution designed it to do: act as a chemical sensor for sulfur-containing gases. People can detect hydrogen sulfide and methanethiol at minuscule concentrations, even when there is less than one molecule of these compounds amid billions of other molecules.

These smells can signal the presence of rotting substances and bacterial activity that might harbor pathogens that can make you sick, or deadly environments such as swamps, stagnant caves and volcano vents that can suffocate and kill you.

So the next time you lay a fart that’s pungent enough to clear the room, don’t apologize – just say you’re conducting a live demonstration of natural chemistry that took eons of evolution to perfect.
