8 Best Travel Adapters (2026): 20+ Models Tested

📅 27 Jul 2021 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3847 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, whether planning a country-hopping odyssey or a quick business trip, your journey will go more smoothly with the best travel adapters that allow you to safely charge all your gadgets wherever you land.
  • The best adapters make great gifts for travelers and deserve a place in your carry-on, but check out our other travel guides, like the Best Travel Essentials, Best Travel Tech for Families, Best Travel Pillows, and Best USB-C Cables.
  • Updated November 2026: I added a Mukiya travel charger and a Mophie Travel Kit, removed some discontinued devices, and updated links and prices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, whether planning a country-hopping odyssey or a quick business trip, your journey will go more smoothly with the best travel adapters that allow you to safely charge all your gadgets wherever you land. After many work trips and family vacations I’ve tested several—both universal and basic options—and my favorites will work in most parts of the world.

The best adapters make great gifts for travelers and deserve a place in your carry-on, but check out our other travel guides, like the Best Travel Essentials, Best Travel Tech for Families, Best Travel Pillows, and Best USB-C Cables.

Updated November 2026: I added a Mukiya travel charger and a Mophie Travel Kit, removed some discontinued devices, and updated links and prices.

There’s a ton to like about this 100-watt universal travel adapter from reliable travel brand Ceptics. It covers more than 200 countries and can charge multiple gadgets in a hurry. The classic slider design pushes out EU, UK, and US plugs, and you can rotate the pins for sockets in Australia and China. I love how securely the plugs lock into place; you must press down firmly to slide them back. You have a universal input socket, an additional side socket for US or Japan plugs, and two USB-C ports and two USB-A ports on the bottom. But what makes this travel adapter my favorite is the retractable USB-C cable. It’s around 25 inches long, the end sticks to the adapter magnetically, and it saves you from having to pack an extra cord. The cable can deliver up to 100 watts in total. The USB-C ports support up to 15 watts, and the USB-A ports go up to 12 watts.

For all of its strengths, though, it does provide an unfortunate lack of any grounding. Grounding is meant to reduce the risk of an electric shock if there’s a fault, such as a loose wire inside a device with a metal case. (This video explains grounding well.) Thankfully, there’s overload protection with a 10-amp fuse, and it also comes with a spare. But you should not use this adapter with any device with a third metal ground pin on its plug.

Sources indicate that I also tested the 140-watt Ceptics 6-in-1 model ($51), which omits the cable but has three USB-C ports and one USB-A, and the excellent 70-watt model ($40), which has the retractable cable but fewer ports and loses the extra outlet. Both are great alternatives.

Industry observers note that perhaps the smallest travel adapter that's still practical to use, the Epicka Air measures 3.46 x 1.97 inches and is just 1.19 inches thick, with the prongs folded away. It’s easy to pack but still feels reasonably sturdy in use. You get one USB-A and three USB-C ports. The first three ports offer up to 15 watts apiece, and the last USB-C port on the right can go up to 65 watts. But 65 watts is also the maximum output across the four ports, so it gets divided if you plug in multiple devices. But if you use the AC outlet too, and you can charge up to five devices at once.

According to recent reports, when I first tested the 40-watt version ($25), I wasn’t sure about this travel adapter, but after using the 65-watt model for a while, I’ve grown to like it. I still think this style of folding design can be a bit fiddly to use, and the prongs sometimes fold back if you bump them while plugging in. But the placement of the EU prongs in the middle helps it stay plugged in more reliably than some larger sliding cube adapters; the US prongs lock into place, and I didn’t have any issues with the UK prongs.

Industry observers note that this budget Ceptics device proves that you don’t need to spend that much money to snag one of the best travel adapters. It covers more than 150 countries, with sliders you push to reveal the three most common international plugs—EU, UK, and US. You can rotate the pins for sockets in Australia or China. The sliders lock into place securely, and there’s a button on the side for retracting them. This plug’s universal outlet can recharge your power-hungry devices, like laptops and camera batteries. Two USB-C and two USB-A ports on the bottom, plus a USB-C port on the side, can handle phones, tablets, smartwatches, and Kindles. Each USB-C port can deliver up to 15 watts, and each USB-A port up to 12 watts. While it's not as fast as some of my picks above, you won't care if you tend to charge your gadgets overnight.

There’s no grounding, so don’t plug devices with a third metal ground pin into this adapter. There is an 8-amp fuse for safety, and it comes with a spare. It is also certified by RoHS and CE.

What I love about this sturdy, compact plug adapter is the lack of sliding pins or moving parts to worry about. It stays put in the outlet. Offered in several versions (Type C, Type E/F, Type G), this adapter enables you to charge up to six gadgets. I’ve been testing the Type G model in Scotland, and it plugs into a single outlet, giving you three US outlets, a USB-A port, and two USB-C ports. The USB-C can output up to 15 watts, and the USB-A ports are limited to 12 watts—not especially speedy, but fine for overnight charging. The adapter is grounded and has various safety features.

Sources indicate that on the downside, it can be tough to use all the outlets simultaneously, as larger plugs, like the MacBook power adapter, tend to block one of the other US outlets. It does not offer surge protection, and the Type G adapter maxes out at 3,250 watts (250 volts, 13 amps), while the EU and other versions top out at 2,500 watts.

According to recent reports, if you only need USB-C and USB-A ports for charging your mobile gadgets on the go (and no outlet), I recommend this clever, compact travel adapter. I’ve never seen a mechanism like this before, where you twist to extend the prongs. It's a neat feature. The standard US prongs can be angled for Australia, and there are EU and UK prongs (types A, C, G, and I). The USB-C ports can deliver up to 70 watts, enough to charge a laptop (slowly), and there’s a USB-A port. You could charge up to three devices at once, though the wattage is divided between them, and it got a little warm when I did this. It uses gallium nitride (GaN) technology to keep the size down. This is a fresh brand to me, but I’ve been testing it on various devices for the last two weeks, and so far, so good.

Recent findings suggest that universal adapters don't always work properly everywhere, and most don’t have grounding. The cheaper and more reliable alternative is to buy individual adapters. The 12-piece international set from Ceptics is my favorite. It includes types to cover most of the globe, and each is properly grounded. Only visiting a single destination? Just pack the relevant type. These adapters don't have USB ports, so you’ll need the respective charging adapter for your gadgets.

This set is especially good for Europe because it includes Type C, E/F, and G adapters, so you’re covered for any socket. Ceptics offers an even cheaper and smaller five-piece set, but I don’t recommend it. The adapters are flimsy, there’s no grounding, and the European plug’s design doesn’t work well with the recessed sockets you will sometimes encounter. The drawback of plug adapters is that they’re easy to lose, but at least Ceptics includes a small bag for storage.

According to recent reports, this kit includes multiple plug attachments that slide and lock into place to keep you powered across most of the world. It is bulky and much bigger than the average adapter but provides two grounded US AC outlets. There is also a built-in USB-C cable, two USB-A ports, and two USB-C ports. The USB-A ports and built-in USB-C cable offer a combined maximum charging rate of 15 watts. The USB-C ports support Power Delivery, with up to 20 watts each. The top charging rate for all of them simultaneously is 55 watts.

Recent findings suggest that there is built-in surge protection, but since this is not a voltage converter, don’t plug in hair dryers or other non-dual-voltage electronics. While the two AC outlets are handy, their proximity means that the shape and size of some plugs can make it tricky to use both simultaneously. But with the ability to charge up to seven devices, this kit is handy. I also like the original Ceptics World Travel Adapter Kit ($35), though it lacks the two USB-C ports.

Recent findings suggest that this cute kit comes in a zippered pouch and includes everything you need for a trip. There’s a fold-out charger with a tiltable magnetic Qi2 25W pad for your iPhone or Qi2 Android phone, a 7.5W pad for an Apple Watch, and a 5W pad behind for wireless earbuds. It also includes a 40W power adapter with switchable plugs for the US, UK, EU, and AU—plus a 5-foot USB-C cable. Everything inside comes in color-matched black or cream, unless you opt for the bolder orange-and-teal special edition.

It’s not the most compact option, but I love that everything slots neatly into the included pouch. You can find some great alternatives in my Best Apple 3-in-1 Travel Chargers guide.

What Type of Adapter Do You Need?

There are 15 plug types in use across the world. Universal adapters tend to cover all of these types.

Some countries are not usually covered by universal adapters, such as India (Type D), Israel (Type H), and South Africa (Type M or N). You'll need to buy specific plug adapters for those places. To avoid any surprises when you land, double-check what type you need before you travel.

If you're visiting just one destination, a basic plug adapter that caters to one plug type is all you need. For trips to multiple destinations or for frequent flyers, a universal travel adapter can prove more versatile. The universal adapters I recommend here have the bonus of including multiple USB ports for charging several mobile devices from a single outlet.

Do You Really Need a Voltage Converter?

Recent findings suggest that voltage converters are big, heavy, and expensive, and they don’t always work—so it’s probably best to avoid them. The reason you might think you need one is that the AC sockets on all of our recommended travel adapters do not convert the voltage coming from the socket. This means plugging into a UK socket will deliver 220 volts at 50 hertz, which is very different from the 120 volts at 60 hertz you can expect in the US. Don't worry! Your gear won’t get fried. You just need to make sure anything you plug into one of these universal travel adapters has something like this printed on it:.

Industry observers note that that should include most modern gadgets. If your device or charger can’t handle a variable voltage, it’s probably best to leave it at home. Most places provide hair dryers, irons, and kettles, so there’s no need to take them with you. It’s also often cheaper to buy a set with the correct plug at your destination and save the luggage space and hassle.

If you are determined to try a voltage converter (again, I don’t recommend doing so), the Ceptics 2,000-watt Travel Voltage Converter ($70) seems to work well. It has a special 2,000-watt outlet for hair dryers, but only ones that work via a mechanical switch (anything with an electronic circuit board for automatic switch-off or temperature control won’t work and is at risk of being fried if plugged in). It also has two outlets that go up to 200 watts, one USB-C port, and three USB-A ports, though the ports do not support fast charging.

According to recent reports, travel adapters and chargers usually state the wattage they can deliver for USB-C and USB-A ports, retractable cables, and wireless charging. If you're interested in getting the fastest rates possible, you’ll want a charger and cable that can deliver the maximum wattage to your device. A laptop might want 100 watts, while a phone only needs 30 watts. There's no need to worry if the charger can deliver more wattage than is required because the device will dictate how much power to draw. If the wattage is lower than required, most devices will simply charge slowly. You can find out more about charging standards like Power Delivery (PD), Quick Charge (QC), and others in my guide on how to fast charge your phone.

Can Travel Adapters Go in a Suitcase?

Sources indicate that yes, you can pack travel adapters in your suitcase. It may be wise to bring one in your hand luggage for easy access should you need to charge up a device when you arrive at your destination. In fact, devices like power banks with lithium batteries (must be capped at 27,000 mAh) must go in hand luggage, not checked bags.

Can I Buy Travel Adapters at the Airport or Hotel?

You certainly can buy travel adapters at the airport, but like all other goods you buy at kiosks between connecting flights, they will be far more expensive than necessary, and your choice will be limited.

Some hotels have travel adapters, and some even have wall outlets for other countries (or USB-A and USB-C ports), but most do not, so don’t bank on it. You can always check with your hotel or accommodation before you depart, but it’s safer to bring a travel adapter with you.

Should You Test Your Travel Adapter Before You Go?

According to recent reports, seriously, nothing is worse than thinking you’re being very clever by packing light only to get to your hotel and discover that your gadgets refuse to charge. Between the adapter, cable, and your device, plenty can go wrong, so do a quick test on your wall outlet at home with everything you are taking before you set off on an international trip.

According to recent reports, anytime I fly for work or vacation, I take a few travel adapters and chargers with me to test. I also test them for longer periods at home in the UK. I have power stations and power strips with US and EU outlets to test those plugs. I test each charger with a variety of devices (iPhone, Pixel, iPad, MacBook, AirPods). I try charging with every port and outlet simultaneously to see if the charger gets warm. I assess the charging rates, durability, size, weight, and usability of each device. If there are any special features, I test them too.

There is an endless amount of travel adapters out there you could buy. While I wholeheartedly recommend one of the options above, there are some other travel adapters I've tested that just barely miss the mark.

Epicka Pulse for $30: The beveled edges of this travel adapter from Epicka make it more comfortable to hold. The sliders work well and lock in place securely to cover you in around 200 countries. A pair of USB-C and two USB-A ports provide a good mix of port options. This adapter can deliver up to 45 watts from either USB-C port, while the USB-A ports top out at 18 watts. I also tested the newer Epicka Pulse Duo ($130), which can deliver up to 140 watts across three USB-C and one USB-A ports, has an extra US or Japanese socket in the side and boasts a smart display that indicates you the current charging status, wattage, and temperature. Cool as it is, it's overkill for most folks and kinda pricey.

Sources indicate that tessan Travel Adapter 009 for $20: This is a similar design to the Epicka Air I recommend above, but the prongs don’t stay in place as securely when unfolded, and you can only draw a maximum of 20 watts from the one USB-A and two USB-C ports. But it is affordable and compact. Tessan also makes good, traditional, slider universal adapters: There's a 140-watt model ($70), and the most powerful travel adapter I’ve tested, the Voyager 205 ($128), which has six USB-C ports and one USB-A to deliver up to 205 watts. If you don’t care about charging speed, Tessan's 20W model ($23) is very reasonably priced and offers two USB-A and two USB-C ports in a small package.

UGreen Travel Plug Adapter for £17: This travel adapter is for UK folks visiting Europe, and it’s a solid option with a fixed plug (no mechanism). It has only two USB-A and one USB-C port for smaller devices, and it’s very bulky. I prefer the OneBeat above for this type of design.

In a recent development, statik SmartCharge Pro for $80: This is a nice combo device that includes a 15,000 mAh power bank and a 60-watt wall charger. There are fold-out US prongs and slide-on adapters for the UK, EU, and AU. You also get one USB-A port, one USB-C port, a fold-out USB-C cable, and a wireless charging pad on top that works with your iPhone or Apple Watch.

It has been revealed that D-Link 65W Multi-Port GaN Charger (DCP-651) for $30: If two USB-C ports and a USB-A port are enough for your travel needs, this affordable D-Link charger could be for you. It comes with interchangeable plugs for different countries. The 65-watt limit is enough for overnight charging a laptop and a couple of smartphones.

Arsmel VisaPro All-in-One Travel Adapter for $80: This chunky power adapter can charge laptops or multiple small devices with a whopping 170-watt maximum output. It works with any outlet in the US, UK, or EU, thanks to sliding plugs that slot in securely, and you can spin the prongs on the US plug to support the total number of countries (more than 200). I love the mecha-inspired paint job, too. There are four ports along the bottom: two USB-C ports rated at 140 watts, with the third USB-C and USB-A ports rated at 18 watts. It supports PD 3.1, QC 3.0, PPS, FCP, and SCP, and has a 10-amp fuse.

According to recent reports, satechi GaN Travel Charger for $120: If you only take small gadgets with you when you travel, a compact, multi-port wall charger is all you need and a great way to pack light. It plugs directly into the wall and comes with four interchangeable travel adapters for the EU, UK, and Australia, plus a mesh bag to store them. There are four USB-C ports that you can plug your gadgets into, including laptops like the MacBook Pro, tablets, phones, and wearables. With support for Power Delivery 3.1, the first two ports can supply up to 140 watts, and the bottom two ports up to 45 watts. However, the maximum output when all four ports are in use is 145 watts.

In a recent development, baseus 70W Universal Travel Adapter With Retractable Cable for $40: This excellent travel adapter is almost identical to our top pick from Ceptics, offering up to 70 watts, sliding prongs to cover more than 200 countries, and a built-in retractable USB-C cable, not to mention a USB-C port and two USB-A ports. It also has a snazzy black-and-yellow finish. It only misses out because it’s slightly more expensive, but if you can snag one on sale or prefer the colors, it’s a solid option.

Epicka Universal Travel Adapter for $20: This travel adapter from Epicka is still a solid option. The sliding plugs cover 150 countries, and there are four USB-A ports on the bottom and a 15-watt USB-C port on the side. There’s also an 8-amp fuse with a spare, and this adapter is RoHS-, CE-, and FCC-certified.

Masterplug Visitor to UK Travel Adapter (3 Pack) for £12: For visitors to the UK, this simple trio of adapters accepts European, American, Australian, and Asian plugs. They are single-outlet adapters with 13-amp fuses inside, and they work perfectly. These are the adapters I use for long-term testing of devices from the US and elsewhere that lack UK plugs. If you forgot to buy an adapter before arriving in the UK, you can find this affordable three-pack at any Argos store.

Anker European Travel Plug Adapter for $16: One of our favorite portable charger brands, Anker, also makes travel adapters. This one plugs into most European outlets to provide a single grounded US outlet, a USB-A port, and two USB-C ports. Unfortunately, the three USB ports max out at 15 watts total, so it’s best for overnight gadget charging, but I appreciate the temperature and overload protection. There is also a UK version ($16).

Epicka Hybrid European Travel Plug Adapter for $26: This handy adapter turns one outlet into four and includes four USB ports (two A and two C). It has fold-out Type A prongs, but you can also slide on a fold-out Type C plug for use in Europe. While the USB ports support QC 3.0 or PD 3.0, they max out at 20 watts in total. I prefer the OneBeat adapters recommended above.

You can do better than these travel adapters.

Recent findings suggest that EZQuest WorldTravel GaN 5 Port With PD Wall Charger: This travel adapter has a generous four USB-C ports and one USB-A port with a familiar slide-out prong design that covers more than 150 countries. There’s also a built-in 10-amp fuse and a spare. It has RoHS, CE, and FCC certification. It works fine, but it's kinda boxy, and the sliders don't lock in place as securely as some of our other picks. There's also a 65W version ($60).

Rolling Square Pocket Travel Adapter: I admire any attempt to shrink down travel adapters in size, but the three-pronged UK plugs are usually the obstacle. Rolling Square’s solution is to have a flip-out third prong, but you’ll need a good fingernail to unhitch it. This charger has a single USB-C port capable of delivering up to 30 watts and is a compact option that covers the US, UK, and Europe.

Ceptics 65W World Travel Adapter.

Sources indicate that ceptics 65W World Travel Adapter: This versatile adapter comes with Type A, B, C, E/F, G, and I slide-on plugs. They fit onto the rectangular brick and plug directly into the outlet, or you can attach them to the optional five-foot cable. The brick has one grounded US outlet and a second non-grounded outlet, with one USB-A (30-watt) and two USB-C (65- and 33-watt) ports at the other end. It works fine, and it's affordable, but it's bulky and ugly.

CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1464 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that after more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have finally found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that occurs only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles.
  • The evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC).
  • The elusive process, called 'Bd to mu mu', has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that after more than four decades of searching, physicists at CERN have finally found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay that occurs only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The long-awaited result could help scientists investigate a largely unexplored realm of physics where unknown particles and forces of nature may exist.

The evidence comes from the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Researchers at the University of Manchester played important roles in the international effort, contributing to the advanced technology that made the measurement possible.

The elusive process, called 'Bd to mu mu', has a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. That is strong enough to qualify as evidence, but physicists will need additional data before they can officially declare a discovery. Even so, the finding marks a major milestone in a search that has lasted more than 40 years.

Industry observers note that it also creates fresh opportunities to test the Standard Model, the leading scientific framework describing fundamental particles and how they interact. By examining this exceptionally rare decay in greater detail, researchers hope to uncover subtle clues that could eventually point toward physics beyond our current understanding.

Why Rare Particle Decays Could Reveal New Physics.

It has been revealed that the LHCb experiment specializes in studying particles that contain beauty quarks. These are heavier relatives of the up and down quarks that make up much of the ordinary matter around us.

Sources indicate that when particles collide inside the Large Hadron Collider, enormous numbers of beauty quarks are produced. However, they survive for only about one and a half trillionths of a second before decaying into other particles.

Recent findings suggest that scientists study these transformations because they may reveal the influence of particles that cannot be directly observed at the collider. By measuring exactly how frequently different decays occur, physicists can search for unexpected effects that might indicate previously unknown physics.

Industry observers note that particularly rare decays offer an key advantage. Because they happen so infrequently, their rates can be especially sensitive to contributions from undiscovered particles. Even small differences between predicted and observed decay rates could provide valuable evidence of new forces or particles.

A One in 10 Billion Particle Decay.

The newly observed signal involves a process known as 'Bd to mu mu'. During this decay, a particle containing a beauty quark transforms into two muons, which are heavier relatives of electrons.

According to theoretical predictions, this transformation should occur only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. Despite decades of investigation, no individual experiment had previously produced convincing evidence that it occurs.

The upgraded LHCb experiment has now achieved a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma. Although this meets the standard for reporting evidence, particle physicists generally require a significance of five sigma before announcing a confirmed discovery.

Industry observers note that professor Chris Parkes, Head of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Manchester, led the international LHCb collaboration during construction of its major upgrade. He also oversaw the collaboration's approval of the new findings.

He explained: "The upgraded LHCb was a major undertaking -- a fifteen-year design and construction project from a 1900 international member collaboration.

"The UK made the largest national contribution to the project, pioneering upcoming technologies that have made today's result possible, where we probe nature at a new scale. But this is also just the start; we are planning the construction of an experiment that will exploit the capabilities of the next-generation High Luminosity LHC, probing physics at an even smaller scale.".

Parkes, who became a Fellow of the Royal Society earlier this year in recognition of his contributions to LHCb, offered a memorable comparison to illustrate just how improbable the decay is.

"This decay is remarkably unlikely; the chance of it happening is roughly like going on a romantic date and, on your very first try, finding the one perfect match for you among everyone on Earth.".

Advanced LHC Detectors Make the Breakthrough Possible.

Detecting such an uncommon event requires instruments capable of following the movements of particles with extraordinary accuracy.

One of the most important components of the upgraded LHCb experiment is a silicon pixel detector developed with major contributions from researchers in the United Kingdom. Called the Vertex Locator, it measures the paths of particles generated during collisions inside the collider.

Positioned just five millimeters from the LHC beams, the detector allows researchers to determine precisely where particles originate and where they subsequently decay.

Dr. Stefano De Capua, who directed detector construction at the University of Manchester, described the extensive collaboration behind the technology.

Sources indicate that "We worked with nearly 90 UK companies to construct this detector and trained the next generation of scientists and engineers on the novel technologies we are using. It is these detectors that we use to locate where the beauty meson was produced and pinpoint where it decayed into two muons.".

It has been revealed that the wider LHCb upgrade also allows the experiment to gather information at up to five times its previous rate. This greater capacity, together with improvements in tracking technology, is helping physicists identify events that were previously too difficult to measure reliably.

Exploring the Mysterious Zeptoverse.

Beyond confirming an exceptionally rare particle process, the result could help scientists investigate what they call the 'Zeptoverse'.

Industry observers note that this name refers to an almost unimaginably small scale, measured in zeptometers. A single zeptometer is just a billionth of a trillionth of a meter. Physicists suspect that effects from presently unknown particles and forces could become apparent when nature is examined at these extreme scales.

According to recent reports, for now, the fresh measurement agrees with the Standard Model. Researchers have not found evidence that the established theory is wrong, but increasingly precise measurements could reveal deviations that current experiments cannot yet detect.

Such differences would be especially significant because they could indicate where the Standard Model stops providing a complete explanation of the physical world.

Professor Conor Fitzpatrick of the University of Manchester, who serves as Deputy Physics Coordinator of the international LHCb collaboration, emphasized the importance of finally obtaining the long-sought signal.

It has been revealed that "There has been a more than forty year long search by physicists worldwide to observe this decay. It is a golden channel to observe the effects of new physics from beyond our current knowledge.

"The results from this experiment are expanding our understanding of nature at its most fundamental level. We are excited to have finally seen this elusive signal and looking forward to the future discoveries that will come from our data.".

What Comes Next for CERN's Particle Research?

According to recent reports, the upgraded LHCb experiment is expected to continue gathering a substantially larger collection of measurements into the early 2030s. With more data, physicists should be able to determine the frequency of this rare decay with much greater precision.

According to recent reports, researchers are also planning another major upgrade that could increase data collection rates by an additional factor of ten. This would improve their ability to investigate extremely rare particle processes and search for the effects of unknown particles at even smaller distance scales.

Professor Brian Cox, a particle physicist at the University of Manchester who did not participate in the experiment, highlighted how improvements in scientific instruments can lead to important advances in understanding nature.

Sources indicate that "This is an important result and a beautiful example of how science advances. We upgrade our instruments, and we see nature in greater detail. Occasionally we see something we don't understand, and then progress is made. We cannot know whether this progress will be incremental or genuinely world-changing -- that's science! LHCb is a major scientific success.".

The experiment receives funding from the Science and Technology Facilities Council, which operates within UK Research and Innovation. The UK LHCb collaboration brings together scientists from ten universities across the United Kingdom and the STFC Rutherford Appleton Laboratory.

According to recent reports, although the newly detected decay has not yet revealed any unknown particles or forces, it gives physicists a powerful latest way to search for them. After more than 40 years of effort, an extraordinarily elusive process is finally becoming accessible to detailed study, potentially bringing researchers closer to understanding some of the universe's deepest mysteries.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apurv Gaikwad is presnting his debut feature “Hurda – That Tight Green Top,” a Marathi-language crime drama adapted from Atharva Pandit’s novel, to the Co-Production Market at WAVES Film Bazaar.

The film follows Chitranshu, a journalist investigating the mysterious deaths of three young sisters in a village in Maharashtra. When he returns to the village six years later, his search for the truth takes an unexpected turn, forcing him to confront uncomfortable realities. Related Stories Grammy Nominations 2027: Raye Leads With 11 Noms as Rosalía, Olivia Rodrigo, Ella Langley and Other Female Artists Dominate Noah Kahan Deserved a Lot More Grammy Love Than Just One Minor Nomination. Here's Why He Didn't Get It.

Gaikwad states he was drawn to the story because he “was fascinated by its polyphonic narrative, the way multiple characters coexist, each with their own distinct voice.” He adds, “Even months after reading the novel, there was one particular aspect of it that refused to leave me – the protagonist, Chitranshu.”.

“It is as much a mystery as it is a character study and an exploration of the society we live in. While the audience may find the answers they initially seek, I hope they leave the film with an entirely different set of questions,” says Gaikwad, who previously made the short mockumentary “The Last Auteur.”.

Gaikwad hopes to challenge the binary understanding of masculinity and “the comfortable distinction we make between good men and bad men. I hope the film encourages audiences to question their own prejudices and examine how caste, gender and social hierarchies shape their understanding of truth, justice and morality,” he says.

The film is being produced by brothers Apurv and Akshay Gaikwad and Nina Bhatt of Disha Cinema and Khan & Kumar Media (“Songs of Forgotten Trees”). In an advanced stage of pre-production, the film is scheduled to start shooting in January 2027. Akassh Ghosalkar leads the cast, which also includes Rohit Kokate, Jitendra Lad, Gayatri Bansode and Gauri Deshpande.

Recent findings suggest that producer Nina Bhatt states she was drawn to Gaikwad’s examination of ordinary masculinity. “The contradictions between how men see themselves and how they exercise power in everyday relationships, his exploration of the entitlement and complicity that can exist within familiarity, affection and even empathy, felt particularly compelling to me. What made me want to back the project was his willingness to turn that examination inwards, rather than simply locate violence in others.”.

According to recent reports, producer Vikas Kumar says Khan & Kumar believes in nurturing and supporting new and vital voices in cinema, and that he strongly believes Gaikwad is one of them. “Supporting ‘Hurda’ felt like a natural progression of that belief.”.

At Film Bazaar, the team hopes to engage with programmers, sales agents and other industry professionals and explore potential pathways for the independent production.

WAVES Film Bazaar runs as the market component of the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa.

The final trailer for Avengers: Doomsday just landed, and it finally puts the spotlight on our boy Steve Rogers.

Avengers: Doomsday has been promising the scale and excitement the MCU has often been lacking since the Infinity Saga. Previous trailers played it safe, mostly setting up the conflict and introducing Victor Von Doom. Now it’s time for one last explosive look at the film before it tries to conquer cinemas next month.

Disney and Marvel Studios have just released a "final trailer" that puts the focus back on Steve Rogers — no longer Captain America but still ready to use Mjolnir — and Thor as the veterans leading the Fresh Avengers, former colleagues, the Fantastic Four, and even Fox's X-Men (after some first-encounter fights, of course) against Doom and his followers.

A few dodgy CG shots aside, it looks grand, and if you're a substantial X-Men fan, it's hard not to get goosebumps when Cyclops (James Marsden) finally gets to say the thing.

The multiverse-spanning story is still largely kept a secret in this trailer, but at least we get a better sense of what the emotional stakes are for Rogers and how all these heroes can realistically work together against the greatest threat they've faced so far (even if most of them won't get more than a few lines).

As for Robert Downey Jr.'s Doctor Doom, this isn't his trailer, but the mysterious Latverian witches — who have fueled many theories online for months — are finally seen in motion.

It has been revealed that doom has, however, received a simple but evocative poster that mirrors one of the original Iron Man ones. Even though Marvel Studios' honcho, Kevin Feige, has shot down the theory that this Victor Von Doom is a Tony Stark variant, you can't stop marketing from doing the obvious things, it seems. We won't complain.

Avengers: Doomsday won't fix all of the Multiverse Saga's shortcomings, but at the very least, it looks like a proper fun time with more toys being mashed together than ever before and proper stakes.

Right before Christmas, it's hard to resist such a pitch.

#93803. Tech Report: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along

Tech Report: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1249 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For more than 50 years, scientists have debated a provocative idea about evolution: Could organisms protect their most important genes by making them less likely to mutate?
  • Industry observers note that in a study published in PLOS Biology, Dr.
  • The findings challenge the claim that natural selection can reduce mutation rates in genes essential for survival.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For more than 50 years, scientists have debated a provocative idea about evolution: Could organisms protect their most important genes by making them less likely to mutate? First proposed in 1972, the hypothesis challenges the traditional understanding of how genetic changes arise. Now, latest research from the University of Bath suggests that the evidence supporting this idea has been misleading.

Industry observers note that in a study published in PLOS Biology, Dr. Sofia Radrizzani and Professor Laurence D Hurst of the University of Bath's Centre for Evolution examined the largest collection of spontaneous genetic mutations assembled to date. Their analysis focused on two microorganisms: the bacterium Escherichia coli (E. coli) and the single-celled fungus baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae).

The findings challenge the claim that natural selection can reduce mutation rates in genes essential for survival. Although this theory has repeatedly attracted scientific attention since its introduction, including a renewed debate in 2023, the researchers say their results undermine its central premise.

Recent findings suggest that "The claim that mutation is slower for important genes is a triumph of hype over substance," stated Dr. Radrizzani, who co-wrote the upcoming paper as part of her PhD. "It's a really old suggestion and is reinvented in various forms routinely.".

How Mutations and Natural Selection Drive Evolution.

The conventional explanation of evolution involves two main processes. Genetic mutations first introduce variation among organisms. Natural selection then influences which of those variations become more common, favoring traits that improve survival and reproduction. This process can be compared to a sieve that separates different kinds of material, allowing some genetic changes to persist while others disappear.

Recent findings suggest that A familiar example comes from Darwin's finches, which Charles Darwin first encountered on the Galápagos Islands in 1835. These birds have different beak shapes that help them feed on different foods. Random mutations contribute to variations in beak size and shape, and when certain food sources become more plentiful, birds with better-suited beaks are more likely to survive and reproduce. Over many generations, these advantageous traits can spread through the population.

However, an alternative hypothesis suggests that mutations may not occur as randomly as the conventional model assumes. According to this idea, organisms have evolved ways to reduce mutations in their most critical genes (such as those involved in replicating DNA or maintaining basic cellular machinery). Meanwhile, genes in which changes might provide useful adaptations (such as those in which mutations give bacteria resistance to antibiotics, or change beak dimensions) could experience higher mutation rates.

Industry observers note that at first glance, protecting essential genes seems like an obvious evolutionary advantage. Mutations affecting these genes can disrupt vital biological processes, cause genetic diseases, or even kill an organism. If such changes are so dangerous, why wouldn't natural selection favor mechanisms that prevent them?

Industry observers note that the problem, researchers explain, is that mutations in individual genes are already relatively rare. Reducing those rates even further would provide only a tiny additional benefit, making it difficult for natural selection to favor such a protective system.

The Mystery of Disappearing Genetic Mutations.

Sources indicate that another problem lies in how scientists have measured mutations in earlier research. Notable genes may appear to mutate less frequently not because they are better protected, but because harmful mutations in those genes are quickly eliminated from populations.

Professor Hurst said: "We'd expect natural selection to rapidly remove mutations when they occur in more key genes, because these mutations are more likely to be harmful to the organism. This can create the illusion that important genes have fewer mutations when, in reality, some mutations have simply disappeared before we have a chance to analyze them - what you can think of as 'ghost mutations'.".

This distinction is crucial. When scientists examine the genetic changes remaining in a population, they may miss mutations that occurred but were subsequently removed by natural selection. As a result, the apparent stability of essential genes could reflect the disappearance of damaging mutations rather than a lower likelihood of those mutations occurring in the first place.

A Major Test of the 50-Year-Old Evolutionary Theory.

To investigate the question more directly, the University of Bath team analyzed data from experiments designed to record mutations while minimizing the influence of natural selection. These experiments, known as mutation accumulation studies, allowed researchers to examine genetic changes in E. coli and baker's yeast without the usual strong filtering effects of selection.

The scientists also performed three independent tests to determine whether natural selection might still have significantly distorted the data. None revealed evidence of substantial bias.

Dr. Radrizzani said: "This looks like the largest and cleanest sample of mutations assembled to date.".

With this extensive dataset, the researchers investigated whether genes that are more crucial for survival actually experience fewer mutations.

They assessed gene importance using experiments in which individual genes were removed from organisms. Some genes are indispensable, meaning that cells die without them. Others can be deleted with little or no noticeable effect.

Recent findings suggest that if the protective mutation hypothesis were correct, the most essential genes should have shown consistently lower mutation rates. Instead, the researchers found no such relationship in either microorganism.

Professor Hurst stated: "Analyze the data any which way and we found nothing. In neither species did these key genes have a lower mutation rate.".

What Really Determines How Often Genes Mutate?

The team also examined whether other measures of gene importance could explain differences in mutation rates. These included the amount of protein produced by each gene and how strongly natural selection had shaped genes over thousands of years.

Once again, the results failed to support the idea that more vital genes receive special protection.

Industry observers note that dr. Radrizzani remarked: "We found that genes producing more abundant proteins don't have lower mutation rates. Nor does the way genes evolve over thousands of years predict how frequently they mutate.".

It has been revealed that that does not mean every gene has exactly the same chance of mutating. The researchers identified features of genome structure and DNA replication that influence mutation frequency. For example, genes copied later during DNA replication tend to accumulate mutations more frequently than those copied earlier.

These findings indicate that mutation rates can vary across the genome, but the differences do not appear to reflect a system that specifically shields essential genes from genetic changes.

Professor Hurst noted: "While we see known causes of variation in mutation rates, we found no evidence for the effects that have been proposed as a challenge to the conventional model. None predicted which genes would have high or low mutation rates, and there are certainly no grounds for a shift in paradigm.".

Industry observers note that the research therefore provides upcoming support for the conventional distinction between mutation and natural selection. Although mutations do not occur at identical rates everywhere in the genome, the evidence from bacteria and yeast offers no indication that evolution systematically protects its most crucial genes by reducing how often they mutate.

Israeli military veterans, a backbone of protest movement, vow to keep demonstrating

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a sea of Israeli flags, Yiftach Golov holds one that looks a little different.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a sea of Israeli flags, Yiftach Golov holds one that looks a little different.

Among the hundreds of thousands of protesters who took to the streets for the 13th week in a row on Saturday, Golov hoists a brown flag that represents a group called “Brother and Sisters in Arms.”.

They are veterans – many, like Golov, from elite forces – who now feel they are fighting on a latest battlefield: To save Israeli democracy.

“We believe this is our responsibility to go once again called to the flag of the nation to stop this madness to defend Israel,” Golov stated, as he weaved his way through the protesters on Tel Aviv’s Kaplan street, between the high-rises that house many of Israel’s high tech companies.

During the second intifada, in the early 2000s, Golov served in a special forces reconnaissance unit. He was never before particularly political, focusing more on getting his PhD in biophysics from Tel Aviv University.

But when the protest movement against the Israeli government’s judicial overhaul plan began in January, Golov attended one a demonstration and soon became one of thousands of veterans, and now military reservists, who have taken up the cause as their fresh mission.

Some, including elite Air Force reservists, have taken it a step further, threatening not to heed the call to train or even serve in protest of the government’s looks planned judicial changes, which would give the governing parties more control over Israel’s judiciary.

Others have taken to becoming some of the most active organizers and demonstrators. Last week, a group from Brothers and Sisters in Arms protested by carrying a figure wrapped in the Israeli flag on a stretcher, the way they would carry a wounded comrade off the field.

While Golov states he has not taken the drastic step to refuse service, he understands the motivation.

In a recent development, “We’re fighting for justice and liberty, just like the American story, that’s the values that that are being represented symbolized back when we look at our flag, that’s something that was lacking lacking for the last few decades. So basically, we reclaim the flag,” he mentioned.

Palestinian taxi driver recounts surviving attack by right-wing protesters.

Fellow members of the group, all wearing brown shirts with the organization’s logo, come up and say hello. They’re sprinkled all throughout the protests. One is even leading the “Pink Front,” a group of coordinated drummers who look like they are dressed for a rave, and often lead the chants at the protests.

They’re using skills they learned in the military – how to organize, how to mobilize – now for the protests. But more importantly, they say they have the same type of motivation.

“The very deep feeling that you are part of something bigger than yourself, that (you’re) allowed to sacrifice anything that is needed, whether it’s your career, health, seriously mental health,” Golov mentioned. “We all have a mission, you’re willing to do it at any cost. You’re very determined, you know that you are on the right side, you’re carrying the torch of light. That keeps us being highly motivated despite the fact that we’re not sleeping for days.”.

Israel’s protest movement is made up of many disparate groups, but the pressure from Israel’s much vaunted veterans has been seen as a key to moving the needle.

Last Monday, after weeks of sustained protests and the largest general strike in Israeli history, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a pause to the legislation, to allow time for negotiations with the opposition.

Recent findings suggest that but despite the announcements, protesters are still out in the streets in large numbers. CNN affiliate Channel 12 in Israel estimated the size of Saturday’s demonstration in Tel Aviv at about 150,000 people. Organizers claimed it was 230,000.

Last week’s mass protests and widespread strike action came after Netanyahu said he had decided to fire Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for advocating a delay in passing the legislation – a move that Netanyahu has since delayed, sources told CNN, due to “the present security situation.”.

Sources indicate that in his televised speech calling for a delay, Gallant had mentioned the pause in the legislation was needed “for the security of Israel,” citing the refusal of some Israel Defense Forces reservists to train in protest of the government aims. He said pressing ahead with the proposals could threaten Israel’s security.

Under pressure at home and from allies abroad, Netanyahu remarked he would delay votes on the remaining legislation until after the Knesset’s Passover recess in April “to give time for a real chance for a real debate.”.

“Out of the responsibility to the nation, I decided to delay … the vote, in order to give time for discussion,” he added.

But Netanyahu indicated that the delay was only temporary. He insisted that the overhaul was necessary, and reiterated criticism of refusal to train or serve in the military in protest at the planned changes. “Refusing is the end of our country,” he remarked.

Many protesters don’t believe that the pause is real, or say it’s simply a stalling tactic to give Netanyahu some breathing room and get the protesters to go home before he plows on with the reforms.

“We will start doing deactivation only when we will know 100% that Israel state will stay a functional democratic country. Whatever needs to be done for that,” Golov said.

While a certain generation might associate Woody Harrelson most with his role as Haymitch Abernathy in the billion-dollar “Hunger Games” franchise, the actor has admitted he needed convincing to sign on for the dystopian film.

According to recent reports, during a recent Vanity Fair interview alongside his “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” co-star Joseph Zada (who plays a younger Abernathy in the prequel), Woody told the actor he “turned it down twice,” referring to the role. Related Stories Taylor Swift Ties Grammy Record for Consecutive Album of the Year Nominations Beyoncé Makes Grammys History as First Artist With 100 Nominations.

“Turned it down?” asked Zada. “Yeah, it’s stupid,” responded Harrelson. “I thought it was good, I read the books, really good, but I just don’t think there’s enough to do. I don’t know if there’s enough to do. It’s an arbitrary, odd way of assessing it.”.

Sources indicate that he continued, explaining that director Gary Ross ultimately convinced him to do it. “[I] Can’t imagine not having had this experience in my life and knowing these people and then Gary calls me and he’s like, ‘Woody, you have to do this part. I don’t have a second choice. You have to play Haymitch.’ And he just talked to me for about 10 minutes on the phone. I’m like, ‘All right, okay, yeah, let’s do it.'”.

Industry observers note that released in 2012, Ross directed the first “Hunger Games” film, while Francis Lawrence went on to direct “Catching Fire,” “Mockingjay – Part 1,” “Mockingjay – Part 2,” “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes” and “Sunrise on the Reaping.” The recently released prequel takes place 25 years before the original “Hunger Games” series and follows the origin story of Abernathy as he’s forced to compete in the second Quarter Quell. McKenna Grace, Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons, Elle Fanning and more also star.

In addition to Harrelson, who returned for the film, original cast members Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson also made small appearances. On an episode of “Call Her Daddy,” Lawrence told host Alex Cooper it was “unbelievable” to return as Katniss. “It was so crazy. It was the same crew. It was the same AD, who I’ve worked with a million times because I love him. And with Josh [Hutcherson] and Woody [Harrelson] … it was so emotional.”.

“Sunrise on the Reaping” opened to $120 million at the box office last weekend, and is presently in theaters.

Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists dedicate their careers to uncovering how the world works, yet they have surprisingly different opinions about what science actually means.
  • It has been revealed that the study, published in Royal Society Open Science, examined 18 different descriptions of science and found that researchers rarely embraced any of them without reservations.
  • "What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield," indicates Marina Dubova, who led the research while working as a postdoctoral researcher at the Santa Fe Institute.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists dedicate their careers to uncovering how the world works, yet they have surprisingly different opinions about what science actually means. Newly introduced research reveals that scientists disagree about the nature and purpose of science even more than the general public does.

It has been revealed that the study, published in Royal Society Open Science, examined 18 different descriptions of science and found that researchers rarely embraced any of them without reservations. Even when scientists generally supported a particular definition, many questioned some aspect of it.

"What was surprising to me was that there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield," indicates Marina Dubova, who led the research while working as a postdoctoral researcher at the Santa Fe Institute.

It has been revealed that members of the public, by comparison, expressed more consistent views. They were more likely to regard science as a dependable way to discover objective truths about the world, placing less importance on the uncertainty and creativity involved in scientific research.

Industry observers note that these contrasting perspectives may have vital consequences. They could affect the questions scientists choose to investigate and influence how people evaluate scientific findings. They may also help explain why the public sometimes becomes frustrated when researchers cannot offer clear answers or change their conclusions in response to new evidence.

What Scientists and the Public Believe About Science.

Industry observers note that dubova, now an assistant professor of psychology at the University of California, Berkeley, worked with Princeton University researcher Qiawen E. Liu to investigate how people understand science.

The researchers surveyed 91 scientists and 99 members of the public. Participants were asked to assess 18 descriptions of science drawn from historical perspectives, including comparisons of scientific research to detective work, a pursuit of truth, and a mirror that reflects reality.

It has been revealed that both groups generally agreed that curiosity, exploration, and the desire to solve mysteries are central to science. Beyond those shared ideas, however, the scientists expressed strikingly different perspectives.

Some researchers viewed science primarily as a means of discovering objective truths. Others placed greater importance on imagination, personal judgment, and the creative decisions involved in research. Scientists also differed over whether scientific progress depends mainly on following established procedures or adapting and improvising as newly introduced challenges arise.

According to recent reports, dubova believes these disagreements may reflect the individual experiences that shape how researchers approach their work. Just as chefs can have very different philosophies about preparing food, scientists can develop distinct ideas about the best ways to investigate the world.

Why the Public Sees Science Differently.

Another intriguing finding involved differences among scientific disciplines. The general public's understanding of science more closely resembled the views expressed by physicists and biologists than those of psychologists and other social scientists.

It has been revealed that one possible reason is that physics and biology receive greater attention in science education, potentially shaping how people imagine scientific research. Dubova emphasizes, however, that this explanation remains tentative and will require additional investigation.

The differences between scientists and the public could also help explain misunderstandings about scientific uncertainty. People who expect science to produce firm, objective answers may have difficulty understanding why findings sometimes conflict or why scientific conclusions must be updated when newly introduced evidence becomes available.

What the Findings Could Mean for AI and Scientific Discovery.

The research also points to a potential challenge as artificial intelligence becomes increasingly involved in scientific discovery.

Sources indicate that with researchers developing AI systems that can carry out scientific investigations, Dubova is concerned that automation could favor a limited conception of how science should work. If those systems are built around one particular approach to research, other valuable methods of discovery could receive less attention.

The study received support from the Santa Fe Institute's Lou Schuyler Seed Grant Fund, which was created in 2022 to encourage exploratory projects by early career scientists. Dubova used the funding to pay participants for taking part in the research.

For Dubova, the findings represent an initial effort to understand how scientists' underlying beliefs about their profession might influence the research they conduct and the discoveries they make.

Industry observers note that "Don't take the common understanding of science for granted," she claims. "Always ask. Always be curious about what someone has in mind.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Engineers and analysts searching for the root cause of the technical issues behind Friday's nationwide ground stop by the Federal Aviation Administration have been able to replicate the situation that was overwhelming parts of the air traffic system, people familiar with the investigation told CNBC.

In a recent development, while replicating the glitch in a lab in Florida is progress, those investigating the matter have yet to determine exactly why two routers in question failed, according to the people, who requested anonymity to talk about an ongoing situation. Finding the root cause is critical to the FAA determining if there may be an issue with other routers that form the backbone of communications for the national air transportation network.

The ground stop lasted for more than four hours Friday, marking the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford have said there is no indication the routers failed due to a cyberattack.

The incident in question happened shortly after L3Harris Technologies, the primary contractor supporting the FAA telecommunications network, installed a new router at a facility in El Dorado, Arkansas.

L3Harris stated that it, in partnership with other tech companies, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber-optic system.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the statement mentioned. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.".

Investigators noted within eight minutes of its installation, the router began to transmit too much data within the FAA network.

That surge of data, 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, destabilized aircraft communications and radar feeds, Duffy mentioned.

It has been revealed that since the ground stop, Duffy has increased the amount of money he wants to upgrade the national air traffic system. After originally asking for $30 billion to build a digital network that will incorporate artificial intelligence, Duffy has now asked Congress for $50 billion.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Follow below for developments from the NATO Parliamentary Assembly on Monday, November 23:.
  • German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called on Russia to end its "dangerous provocations" after two Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone crashed in Poland on Friday.
  • Merz delivered those remarks after having met with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Berlin on Monday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Follow below for developments from the NATO Parliamentary Assembly on Monday, November 23:.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz called on Russia to end its "dangerous provocations" after two Russian missiles and a jet-powered drone crashed in Poland on Friday.

Merz delivered those remarks after having met with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in Berlin on Monday.

"Poland can count on our full solidarity. And if necessary, NATO will of course defend every inch of allied territory," Merz remarked.

Merz mentioned Europe and NATO must strengthen their defenses.

Drones have repeatedly strayed into NATO airspace in the year since Russia introduced its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The incident also came at a time as Poland was hosting a two-week military exercise by Ukraine's allies.

For delegates at the 72nd NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin on Monday, the question of Ukrainian membership of NATO wasn't fresh.

"It is a tragedy that, in 2008, Ukraine asked to become a member of NATO and who mentioned no? France and Germany," said Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, a German member of the European Parliament. "I think we have to fix it.".

Yet not all German delegates agree: "To become a member is a difficult question because it can also increase tensions," said Roman Poseck, interior mnister of the German state of Hesse. "Therefore, Germany in particular is not really in favor of this at the moment.".

According to recent reports, when pressed by delegates in a plenary debate, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul kept it vague, saying: "Ukraine is on an irreversible path towards NATO. I would say this is our position and let's see how and if it will work specifically.".

Other delegates were careful not to preempt any official processes.

"We have to make these decisions based on facts, based on [Ukraine's] readiness to become a member and, of course, after discussions with our own countries," cautioned Canadian delegate Cheryl Gallant.

"I think the most important thing for Ukraine, but also for all of the members of the alliance, is that there are durable security guarantees for the Ukrainian people," added Philipp Brickell, a delegate for the United Kingdom.

After last week's Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin saw US Special Envoy Jared Kushner float the option of "Article Five-like" security guarantees, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday again pushed for the real deal (see below).

In a recent development, "Wouldn't it be more effective to simply bring Ukraine into NATO?" he stated. "Why not say out loud what so many people think?".

He received support in particular from Nordic allies who, with the Russian invasion of Ukraine now well into its fifth year, are keen to strengthen Europe and NATO and boost security on the alliance's northern flank.

Ville Vayrynen, the Finnish President of the Nordic Council, remarked of Ukrainian NATO membership: "That's something that I would gladly welcome if that's the direction we're going to go, and I strongly support that idea.".

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Monday renewed his calls for full membership of NATO, arguing that Ukraine's hard-won combat experience, its cutting-edge defense industry and large military would be a benefit for the alliance.

"NATO is the answer – and with a strong Ukrainian army, NATO itself is guaranteed to be stronger," Zelensky told the 72nd NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin via video link.

A number of NATO leaders have expressed hesitation about bringing Ukraine into the alliance, with United States envoy Jared Kushner saying last week that Washington might consider offering Kyiv a security guarantee similar to that provided under Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty as part of a peace settlement.

But Zelenskyy stated major questions remain about how such guarantees would work without full NATO commitment.

"Which countries will support Ukraine if Ukraine is attacked again? What exactly will our partners do in response? Which troops will be stationed on our territory in advance? How much will all this cost? And will it really work?" he asked.

"All of this is not easy and so far we have not heard clear specific answers.".

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte underscored the alliance's support for Ukraine but noted that membership would require unanimous support.

"Not all NATO allies agree at this moment [on] letting Ukraine become a member," he stated, while also firmly rejecting the idea that outside powers like Russia could dictate who joins the alliance.

Sources indicate that "Who becomes a member of NATO is decided by NATO alone," he mentioned. "There is total clarity on that within the alliance.".

As for whether the prospect of Ukrainian membership of NATO could be part of talks with Russia, Rutte said: "In order to speculate about such talks, we would actually have to have the talks.".

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on Monday for fresh four-way negotiations with Russia – and involving European countries – to begin as soon as possible.

"We must do everything to make sure that the four-party meeting – Ukraine, Europe, America and Russia – happens as soon as possible," he told the 72nd NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin via video link.

Recent findings suggest that "We have heard from our partners that they want to try to make it happen before Christmas," he noted. "We hope it happens sooner. We are ready to do this literally tomorrow.".

The Polish government intends to summon the Russian ambassador in response to a violation of its airspace which saw three Russian cruise missiles crash on its territory on Friday, the Polish Foreign Ministry stated on Monday.

The security authorities and the military must first complete their investigations into the incident, a ministry spokesman told the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

On Saturday, Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski stated that Warsaw would convey its "strongest displeasure" to the Russians over the violation of Polish airspace.

Following examination of debris found in southeastern Poland, state prosecutors remarked that all three were Russian CH-101 cruise missiles.

The missiles are believed to have been manufactured in the fourth quarter of this year at an arms factory in Dubna, approximately 140 kilometers north of Moscow.

NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte remarked on Monday that Poland and allied countries were still working to establish whether the crossing of Russian missiles into Polish territory on Friday was intentional or not.

"It is ​clear ‌that this is a dangerous incident," he told ‌a ​meeting of the alliance's parliamentary assembly in Berlin.

"Whether it ​is intentional or not has to be ⁠decided, ​of course, by ​authorities," he ‌noted, adding he would only be ​able ⁠to comment once Poland and ⁠NATO allies ​had assessed what exactly had happened.

"I will never ​speculate," he noted.

Western military intelligence services believe Russia is planning to station a nuclear weapon in space by the end of this year, German media reported on Monday morning.

According to public broadcasters NDR and WDR, as well as the Süddeutsche Zeitung broadsheet, intelligence chiefs believe Moscow intends to fire a satellite armed with a nuclear warhead into orbit.

Intelligence regarding the plans was reportedly shared among NATO member states recently and German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius is noted to have been informed by experts from Germany's armed forces, the Bundeswehr.

A Bundeswehr spokesman reportedly declined to comment on the reports, acknowledging only that Russia does possess such capabilities and warning that a nuclear explosion in space would have devastating consequences for global satellite communications.

"It would effectively mean: back to the stone age," he said.

The German Ministry of Defense mentioned only that it was continuously observing global developments in space while the Russian embassy in Berlin said it had no information regarding such intends.

The United States Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) warned in October that Russia was developing a satellite capable of transporting a nuclear weapon and, according to the new report, a satellite codenamed "Sputnik-S" is believed to have been in storage in the Moscow area for several years.

Back in February 2022, the same month as the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia debuted its "Kosmos-2552" satellite into orbit, considered by western intelligence at the time to be a test designed to measure the effects of radiation in space.

Should Moscow indeed launch a nuclear weapon into space, it would constitute a breach of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty which prohibits the stationing of weapons of mass destructions in Earth orbit. Russia agreed to a continuation of the treaty at the United Nations General Assembly in December 2024.

Space is nevertheless becoming increasingly militarized, with the United States admitting in September 2025 that it had positioned offensive non-nuclear weapons in orbit.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the latest violation of NATO airspace on Friday an "intentional provocation.".

The incident occurred as Russia was carrying out a wide-ranging attack on Ukraine.

But it also coincided with European military drills in Poland, intensifying concerns about Moscow's intentions.

Following the most recent violations of Polish airspace by Russian weapons, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has emphasized NATO's determination to defend itself.

"We will defend every centimeter of NATO territory," he remarked on Monday as the 72nd NATO Parliamentary Assembly continued in Berlin.

Addressing Russian President Vladimir Putin, he added: "Don't be deceived: we may be a defensive alliance but we are prepared to defend our countries and our alliance.".

According to Polish state prosecutors, the three objects which crashed in southeastern Poland on Friday were Russian CH-101 cruise missiles.

Wadephul noted he was in close contact with Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski and assured Warsaw of his full solidarity.

Later, at approximately midday local time, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte is expected to address the assembly before heading to an official reception with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in the afternoon.

Parallel to the continuing NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin, representatives of the alliance's member states are also set to convene in Brussels on Monday to discuss the recent violations of Polish airspace by Russia.

Russian drones and missiles have frequently penetrated the sovereign airspace of Poland, a European Union and NATO member, in the course of air strikes against neighboring Ukraine over the past four years.

According to the Polish government, three Russian missiles entered Polish airspace on Friday, crashing in the south-east of the country.

Airspace violations have also been reported in other NATO and EU countries including Romania, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia.

On Saturday, Finland reported a suspected airspace violation by a manned Russian military helicopter near the southeastern town of Loviisa.

Moldova, which is not in the EU or NATO, has also reported airspace violations, most recently this weekend.

Hello and welcome to DW's coverage of the 72nd NATO Parliamentary Assembly which continues in Berlin on Monday.

Speakers in the German capital are set to include NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, joining by video link.

Later, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is to officially receive Rutte at the Chancellery in Berlin.

Meanwhile, in Brussels, representatives of the 32 NATO member states are due to discuss the recent violations of Polish airspace by Russia.

#93794. Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1097 w)
