Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mystery surrounding a skeleton discovered inside an ancient Roman coffin at Westminster Abbey may finally be approaching a solution, more than 150 years after the remains first attracted attention.
  • According to recent reports, the limestone sarcophagus, formally excavated in 1869, carries an inscription naming Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in London sometime between 300 and 400 AD.
  • Recent findings suggest that now, fresh archaeological research points to a surprising explanation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mystery surrounding a skeleton discovered inside an ancient Roman coffin at Westminster Abbey may finally be approaching a solution, more than 150 years after the remains first attracted attention.

According to recent reports, the limestone sarcophagus, formally excavated in 1869, carries an inscription naming Valerius Amandinus, a wealthy Briton who lived in London sometime between 300 and 400 AD. However, a large Latin cross carved into its lid dates to approximately the 10th or 11th century, suggesting that the person buried inside lived hundreds of years after the coffin was originally made.

Recent findings suggest that now, fresh archaeological research points to a surprising explanation. The remains likely belong to a prominent medieval monk, and researchers have narrowed the possible identities to two men who once led Westminster Abbey.

Two Medieval Abbots Emerge as Leading Candidates.

The latest findings, published in the peer-reviewed Journal of the British Archaeological Association, come from Professor Warwick Rodwell, Consultant Archaeologist at Westminster Abbey.

According to recent reports, rodwell identifies Aelfwig, an abbot who died around 1020, as the strongest candidate. At the time, Westminster Abbey was a Benedictine monastery, and Aelfwig had served there as a monk before becoming its abbot.

Another possibility is Wulnoth, who succeeded Aelfwig and died in 1049. Both men are believed to have been buried at the Abbey, making either a plausible match for the skeleton.

"We have two viable contenders for the occupant of the sarcophagus," says Professor Rodwell, Consultant Archaeologist at Westminster Abbey.

"We do not know the date of birth of either. But either would fit equally well if we assume the Abbot was in his early twenties when the appointment was made and close to fifty when he died.

"The fact Aelfwig was already a monk of Westminster might favor him.".

The elaborate burial provides another reason to suspect that the deceased held an vital position. Rodwell suggests that the individual was 'honored' with a 'fine sarcophagus', an unusual distinction that would be consistent with the status of an abbot.

It has been revealed that rather than commissioning an entirely new stone coffin, those responsible for the burial apparently reused an existing Roman sarcophagus. The man's wooden coffin was placed inside it, and the stone lid was modified with a prominent Latin cross. This may represent an early example of recycling a valuable object for an entirely different purpose.

Upcoming Excavations Reveal the Skeleton's Age.

Industry observers note that the Roman sarcophagus and its mysterious occupant have fascinated researchers for generations. Rodwell's latest conclusions draw on several investigations conducted with specialists over the years, including work associated with Channel 4's Time Team.

In 2009, the television program examined the archaeology and architecture of King Henry III's original sacristy, located along the north side of Westminster Abbey.

The same area was the scene of an earlier accidental discovery in 1820, when workers encountered the Roman coffin and broke its lid into six pieces. The damage was repaired around the time the sarcophagus was formally 'discovered' in 1869.

More recently, Pre-Construct Archaeology, one of the UK's largest commercial archaeological and heritage organizations, carried out another excavation of the sacristy. Completed in 2025, the project was undertaken to support construction of the King Charles III Sacristy, a upcoming facility at Westminster Abbey scheduled to open the following year.

As part of this investigation, human bone specialist James Young Langthorne of Pre-Construct Archaeology (PCA) conducted a fresh examination of the skeleton.

His analysis indicated that the deceased was a man between 35 and 49 years old who stood approximately 5 feet 9 inches tall. These findings differ considerably from an assessment made in the 1800s, which described the remains as those of a 'robust young man' no older than 30 and approximately 5 feet 7 inches tall.

Carbon Dating Confirms a 1,000-Year-Old Burial.

Industry observers note that one of the most important clues came from scientific dating of the remains. A bone sample was submitted to the Scottish Universities Environmental Research Centre for radiocarbon analysis, which produced a date range of 987 to 1052 AD.

This places the burial firmly within the late Saxon period, centuries after the Roman sarcophagus was originally created. The dates also align with the deaths of both Aelfwig and Wulnoth, strengthening the case that the skeleton belonged to one of these medieval abbots.

"This confirms that the reuse of the sarcophagus, and the associated remodeling of its cover, occurred in the late Saxon period.".

The results provide scientific support for the theory that an ancient Roman burial container was repurposed to honor an important religious figure nearly 1,000 years ago.

A Skeleton Thought Lost Was Hiding in Plain Sight.

It has been revealed that the investigation also brought renewed attention to an unexpected discovery made in 2016. For years, researchers had believed that the skeleton was missing, leaving an important part of the burial's history unresolved.

Sources indicate that that assumption proved mistaken when the sarcophagus was transported to a conservation studio. PCA researchers removed its lid and were surprised to find an almost complete human skeleton still inside.

In a recent development, the examination produced another clue that Rodwell describes as a 'remarkable new discovery'. Inside the stone coffin, researchers identified the rectangular outline of a structure that had disappeared long ago. Its shape was preserved by a white residue left behind by lime, a material historically used in burials.

Rodwell believes the outline marks the position of the original wooden coffin that held the deceased before it was placed inside the Roman sarcophagus.

"Although no physical traces of that feature remained, it can only have been a timber coffin, which has completely decayed over the course of the seven centuries that the sarcophagus was buried in the sacristy courtyard," writes Professor Rodwell.

Together, the rediscovered skeleton, evidence of a wooden coffin, and new scientific dating have transformed researchers' understanding of this unusual burial. Although the man's identity has not been established beyond doubt, the findings suggest that a medieval abbot may have been laid to rest in a Roman coffin already centuries old.

Visitors can see the sarcophagus today in the Queen's Diamond Jubilee Galleries at Westminster Abbey.

Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer.

Explanation: Cruising through the outer solar system, the Voyager 2 spacecraft made its closest approach to Neptune on August 25, 1989, the only spacecraft to visit the most distant ice giant planet. Based on the images recorded during its close encounter and in the following days, this inspired composited scene covers the dim outer planet, largest moon Triton, and faint system of rings. From just beyond Neptune's orbit, the interplanetary perspective looks back toward the Sun, capturing the planet and Triton as thin sunlit crescents. Cirrus clouds and a dark band circle Neptune's south polar region, with a cloudy vortex above the pole itself. Parts of the very faint ring system along with the three bright ring arcs were first imaged by Voyager during the fly-by, though the faintest segments are modeled in this composited picture. Spanning 7.5 degrees, the background starfield is composed from sky survey data centered on the constellation Camelopardalis, corresponding to the outbound Voyager's view of the magnificent Neptunian system.   • While their appearances may be unusual, these formations offer scientists something far more valuable than a collection of curious snapshots: clues to the geological processes that shaped Mars over billions of years.
  • In particular, the rocks and mineral deposits could help researchers piece together the planet's watery past and identify environments that may once have been capable of supporting microbial life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA's Curiosity and Perseverance rovers have spotted a bizarre assortment of Martian oddities, from potato chip-like rocks and ghostly white formations to mysterious patterns etched into the Red Planet's surface.

While their appearances may be unusual, these formations offer scientists something far more valuable than a collection of curious snapshots: clues to the geological processes that shaped Mars over billions of years.

In particular, the rocks and mineral deposits could help researchers piece together the planet's watery past and identify environments that may once have been capable of supporting microbial life.

In a recent development, NASA's Curiosity rover recently wrapped up a drilling campaign at a location nicknamed "Nazca," where scientists have been examining unusual disk-shaped crystal formations embedded in the surrounding bedrock. Some of the features are so thin and flat that the mission team likened them to potato chips, according to a statement from the space agency.

Curiosity used its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI), mounted on the end of its robotic arm, to capture detailed close-up images of the formations on Nov. 7 — the rover's 5,067th Martian day, or Sol 5067. The rover also used its ChemCam instrument to study the rocks' chemical composition, while samples from the Nazca drill site were delivered to its onboard Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) instrument for further analysis.

Meanwhile, NASA's Perseverance rover has been investigating a collection of unusually bright rocks in an area called "Idubi," located in the “Lac de Charmes” region outside Jezero Crater. The rover captured images of the formations on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023), revealing pale, ghostly-looking rocks that stand out dramatically against the darker, dust-covered Martian landscape.

In a recent development, data from Perseverance's SuperCam instrument revealed that the rocks are rich in hydrated silica rather than being typical igneous rocks. That discovery has scientists particularly interested. On Earth, hydrated silica can form in environments involving hydrothermal activity or groundwater. These deposits are also capable of preserving microscopic fossils, making them valuable targets in the search for evidence of ancient life, according to another statement from NASA.

Perseverance is now conducting a closer investigation of the formations, using its instruments to gather detailed chemical and mineralogical data that could help scientists determine how the rocks formed and whether they preserve potential signs of past microbial activity.

Back at Mount Sharp, Curiosity has also spotted another geological curiosity: the return of distinctive polygon-shaped patterns across the Martian bedrock.

Sources indicate that the rover's latest images, captured on Nov. 13, 2026 (Sol 5073), show small, regularly shaped polygons outlined by raised ridges, resembling patterns the rover encountered earlier in its climb up the layered mountain, whose rocky slopes preserve a record of Mars' changing climate and ancient watery environments. Scientists say these formations could have developed through several processes, including mineral shrinkage as water evaporated, temperature changes or the expansion and compaction of buried sediments, according to a statement from NASA.

By studying the composition of the rocks and the material cementing the raised ridges around the polygons, researchers hope to determine which processes shaped the terrain.

Together, these discoveries highlight how much Mars' seemingly barren landscape can reveal about its past. As Curiosity continues climbing Mount Sharp and Perseverance investigates ancient terrain beyond Jezero Crater, both rovers are helping piece together the planet's unique features and complex geological history.

Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1006 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, upcoming observations and computer simulations have revealed a surprising possible source of mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole.
  • Recent findings suggest that the center of our galaxy is an extraordinarily crowded and active environment.
  • Over the past two decades, infrared observations have revealed several small, dense gas clouds traveling close to Sagittarius A*.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, upcoming observations and computer simulations have revealed a surprising possible source of mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole. An international research team led by MPE has traced these compact clouds to a massive pair of stars whose powerful winds appear to produce material that could eventually help feed the black hole, known as Sagittarius A*.

Recent findings suggest that the center of our galaxy is an extraordinarily crowded and active environment. At its core sits Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), a supermassive black hole surrounded by stars, gas, and dust moving through a region dominated by intense gravitational forces. This extreme setting gives astronomers an opportunity to investigate how matter moves near black holes and where the material that sustains their activity comes from.

Over the past two decades, infrared observations have revealed several small, dense gas clouds traveling close to Sagittarius A*. These mysterious "clumps" may provide notable clues about how material makes its way toward the black hole. However, scientists have struggled to determine where the clouds originate and what causes them to form.

Mysterious Gas Clouds Near the Milky Way's Black Hole.

One of the first major discoveries came in 2012, when astronomers identified a compact cloud of ionized gas called G2. Containing several times Earth's mass, the cloud produces emissions from hydrogen and helium, consistent with hot gas mixed with dust. It follows a highly elongated orbit around Sagittarius A* and has a faint extension trailing behind it, known as G2t.

According to recent reports, soon afterward, researchers examining older observations recognized another similar object, G1, traveling along a closely related path. The similarities suggested that G1, G2, and G2t might not be independent objects. Instead, they could represent concentrations of gas within a larger, continuous stream.

Even relatively small differences in gas density can make such a stream appear broken into separate clouds. This happens because the brightness of the gas increases in proportion to the square of its density, making denser regions stand out much more strongly.

Industry observers note that more recently, astronomers observed gas in G2's trailing material gathering into another compact cloud that follows a similar orbit. Although this newly formed object might naturally be called G3, that designation had already been assigned to a different object. Together, the related clouds trace a connected flow of material through the Galactic Center, known as the G1-2-3 streamer.

These clouds could play a surprisingly important role in sustaining the black hole. Calculations suggest that if approximately one Earth mass of gas reaches Sagittarius A* every ten years, it could provide enough fuel to maintain the black hole's current level of activity. Discovering how the clouds form could therefore help explain how the black hole receives its supply of matter.

Astronomers Trace the Gas Clouds to Their Source.

Researchers have considered several possible explanations for the clouds, including powerful winds from massive stars, stellar explosions such as novae, and gas pulled away from objects by the black hole's gravity.

According to recent reports, to investigate, the MPE-led team used two advanced infrared spectrographs, SINFONI and ERIS. Both instruments employ adaptive optics to produce sharper observations. By examining a specific hydrogen emission feature called the Brackett‑γ line, the astronomers measured the clouds' positions and velocities and reconstructed their paths around Sagittarius A*.

It has been revealed that the results revealed a striking pattern. G1, G2, and G2t all follow orbits with nearly the same shape and orientation. It would be extraordinarily unlikely for three unrelated clouds to share such closely matching orbital characteristics, strongly suggesting that they originated from the same source.

Two Massive Stars May Be Creating the Clouds.

By working backward from the clouds' observed motions and their velocities along our line of sight, the researchers identified a promising source: IRS 16SW, a massive contact binary system consisting of two stars in extremely close proximity.

Recent findings suggest that the stellar pair belongs to a disk of young stars that revolves clockwise around Sagittarius A*. Its location and motion provide a plausible explanation for the gas stream. Even the slight differences between the clouds' orbital paths can be accounted for by the movement of the two stars around one another.

Recent findings suggest that computer simulations of how gas flows and interacts provided additional support for this explanation. The models indicate that powerful stellar winds from the binary system can collide with surrounding material, creating a shock in the region between the stars. Gas then accumulates and becomes compressed, forming dense concentrations that can eventually separate from the system.

Once released, these compact clouds can travel inward along paths resembling those observed in the G1-2-3 streamer. This provides a physical explanation for how one binary star system could produce several distinct clouds moving along closely related orbits.

A Latest Clue to How Supermassive Black Holes Are Fed.

The findings suggest that massive stars near the Galactic Center may provide a continuing supply of gas capable of fueling Sagittarius A*. Rather than relying only on material already circulating around the black hole, the system could receive fresh gas from the powerful winds generated by nearby stars.

The discovery also brings together several notable processes in astronomy. The evolution of massive stars, the movement and compression of gas, and the supply of material to supermassive black holes may all be closely connected. By identifying a possible source of the mysterious clouds near Sagittarius A*, researchers have uncovered a newly introduced way in which stars could help sustain black hole activity at the heart of our own galaxy.

In a recent development, explanation: What creates the colors in Jupiter's clouds? No one is sure. The featured image was taken by the robotic Juno spacecraft in 2018 during its 14th low pass over Jupiter. #93787. Interstellar solar sails hit a bizarre problem at 75% of light speed

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1242 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Interstellar solar sails hit a bizarre problem at 75% of light speed

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1242 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Reaching another star will require spacecraft capable of traveling far faster than anything humanity has built so far.
  • In a recent development, some proposed interstellar missions would take this concept even further by using powerful lasers to push sails to extraordinary speeds, potentially reaching a substantial fraction of the speed of light.
  • In a recent paper available on arXiv, Chao Shen and Jiaze Li of the Harbin Institute of Technology investigate how light interacts with a rapidly accelerating solar sail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Reaching another star will require spacecraft capable of traveling far faster than anything humanity has built so far. Conventional rockets powered by chemical fuel simply cannot achieve the enormous speeds needed to cross the distances between stars within a practical amount of time. One promising alternative is the solar sail, a vast, lightweight reflective surface that uses the momentum of light to propel a spacecraft through space.

In a recent development, some proposed interstellar missions would take this concept even further by using powerful lasers to push sails to extraordinary speeds, potentially reaching a substantial fraction of the speed of light. However, latest research suggests that this approach comes with an unexpected complication. At extreme speeds, some of the very light driving the spacecraft forward could begin acting against it.

In a recent paper available on arXiv, Chao Shen and Jiaze Li of the Harbin Institute of Technology investigate how light interacts with a rapidly accelerating solar sail. Their findings reveal a surprising source of resistance that emerges as the spacecraft approaches 75% of the speed of light.

How Light Can Push a Spacecraft Through Space.

In a recent development, although light has no mass, it carries momentum and can transfer that momentum to objects it strikes. This creates a tiny pushing force known as radiation pressure. Under ordinary conditions, the effect is extremely weak, but in the vacuum of space, a large reflective sail can gradually build up speed as light continues to strike its surface.

In a recent development, for spacecraft traveling between stars, powerful lasers could provide a much more concentrated source of light than the Sun. By directing an intense beam at a sail, engineers hope to accelerate extremely small probes to speeds that conventional propulsion systems cannot approach.

According to recent reports, the researchers examined three ways that photons, the individual packets of energy that make up light, transfer momentum to a sail. These interactions are incident light (that raw momentum of the photons hitting the sail), specular reflection (momentum imparted when photons bounce perfectly off the sail), and diffuse scattering (momentum from photons that are absorbed by the sail then reemitted in random directions).

Sources indicate that according to the study, these three contributions affect the sail's motion with different levels of efficiency. Incident light provides the strongest contribution in the researchers' breakdown, followed by specular reflection and then diffuse scattering.

A Strange Problem Emerges Near the Speed of Light.

The situation becomes considerably more complicated once a solar sail reaches relativistic speeds, meaning speeds high enough that the effects predicted by Einstein's theory of relativity become important.

In a recent development, as the sail accelerates away from its laser source, it experiences an increasingly strong Doppler effect. This is the same basic phenomenon that changes the apparent pitch of a passing ambulance siren, except that light experiences a change in frequency rather than sound.

Industry observers note that for the accelerating sail, the incoming laser light becomes progressively redshifted, meaning its frequency decreases from the sail's perspective. As a result, the light transfers momentum less effectively, reducing the thrust generated by all three contributions examined in the study.

Industry observers note that in other words, the faster the spacecraft travels, the less effective its laser propulsion becomes. Even with a powerful beam continuously striking the sail, gaining additional speed becomes increasingly difficult.

Various concepts for interstellar exploration have been proposed over the years, including Breakthrough Starshot, which envisioned using powerful lasers to accelerate tiny spacecraft toward nearby stars. The new findings highlight another challenge that such ambitious missions would need to consider.

At 75% of Light Speed, Light Starts Working Against the Sail.

The researchers identified an especially unusual effect once the sail reaches approximately 75% of the speed of light.

At this point, a phenomenon known as relativistic light aberration changes how the scattered light is distributed. Relativistic aberration describes how the apparent directions in which light travels are altered by motion at speeds approaching the speed of light.

From the viewpoint of an observer at rest on Earth, the diffusely scattered light becomes increasingly concentrated in the spacecraft's forward direction. Because emitting light carries momentum, the sail experiences a corresponding recoil in the opposite direction.

This means that diffuse scattering (admittedly the weakest of the three forces) begins producing drag rather than helping propel the spacecraft forward.

The result is a striking paradox: some of the light intended to accelerate an interstellar spacecraft actually begins resisting its motion.

According to recent reports, importantly, this does not mean the spacecraft suddenly stops accelerating or that its entire propulsion system begins pushing backward. The laser still generates a positive overall force, allowing the sail to continue gaining speed. However, the additional resistance reduces the efficiency of the system, making further acceleration more challenging.

Advanced Materials Could Help Overcome the Challenge.

The study focuses specifically on the forces produced by light and does not attempt to model every obstacle a spacecraft would encounter during an interstellar journey.

For example, the researchers do not include resistance from interstellar gas and dust, which could become notable at extreme velocities. They also leave out the thermal challenges associated with directing extremely powerful lasers at a thin sail. If the material absorbs too much energy, intense heating could damage or even melt it.

Another vital simplification is that the calculations treat the sail as an idealized mirror. Real spacecraft would need materials capable of reflecting laser light efficiently while remaining lightweight, durable, and stable under extreme conditions.

Industry observers note that engineers are already exploring advanced metamaterials and photonic crystals that could help address these demands. These specially engineered materials can be designed to interact with particular wavelengths of light in ways that ordinary reflective surfaces cannot.

Intriguingly, such materials might even turn some of the relativistic effects identified in the research into an advantage. By carefully controlling how light scatters from the sail, future designs could potentially generate forces that automatically correct its orientation and position, helping it remain aligned with the laser beam throughout acceleration.

The Long Road to Interstellar Travel.

Despite the promise of laser propulsion, humanity remains far from building and testing a complete solar sail system capable of reaching another star.

Recent findings suggest that the physics becomes increasingly complicated over such enormous distances and at such extraordinary speeds. Additional effects, including the curvature of spacetime, would also need to be considered in a more complete description of an interstellar journey. These effects were simplified out of the latest analysis.

Nevertheless, understanding how light behaves when it interacts with a spacecraft traveling at a significant fraction of light speed is an important part of making interstellar exploration possible.

If humanity eventually sends robotic probes to another star, success will depend on solving countless engineering and physics challenges. Knowing that light itself can become an unexpected source of resistance gives researchers one more piece of the puzzle, and potentially a better understanding of how to design spacecraft capable of making the journey.

Tech Report: On this day in space! Nov. 23, 2015: Blue Origin sticks 1st-ever rocket landing from space with its suborbital Latest Shepard rocket

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (580 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 23, 2015, a Blue Origin rocket made a historic landing.
  • After launching the New Shepard capsule safely into space, the rocket started heading back to Earth.
  • The Blue Origin milestone meant that rockets could be reused for multiple missions, which saves money and reduces waste.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Nov. 23, 2015, a Blue Origin rocket made a historic landing. Before this time, all rockets were single-use only — even SpaceX's rockets. Blue Origin changed the concept forever.

After launching the New Shepard capsule safely into space, the rocket started heading back to Earth. It flew towards a landing pad, reignited its engine to slow down and touched down softly on the ground. This was the first successful vertical landing from space in history.

The Blue Origin milestone meant that rockets could be reused for multiple missions, which saves money and reduces waste.

Today, SpaceX may be the most well-known for landing its Falcon 9 rocket boosters from orbit. The company's triple-core Falcon Heavy boosters can also land vertically and its massive Starship megarocket can even return to the launch site to be caught by giant metal arms.

But in the end, Blue Origin did it first.

Industry observers note that blue Origin's Upcoming Shepard booster landing kicked off an era of vertical launch and vertical landings for rockets that continues to this day. It may have even outlasted the New Shepard rocket.

In a recent development, since that first landing, Blue Origin has released 17 suborbital astronaut flights with New Shepard, and 21 more uncrewed flights for a total of 38 missions between April 2015 and 2026. The company reused its New Shepard boosters repeatedly (though it did lose one during an uncrewed launch after a technical issue.) But in January 2026, the company revealed a pause in New Shepard flights for two years so that it could focus on moon lander projects.

Recent findings suggest that but Blue Origin did not abandon rocket landings. Indeed, the company's success with New Shepard led it to build vertical landing into its larger orbital rocket, New Glenn, which made its first successful landing 2025 — nearly 10 years after that first touchdown.

Blue Origin has since reflown a Latest Glenn booster, and is developing a new rocket engine called Northstar for even better performance.

#93785. Industry News: Goodbye, World: The End of Programmers

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2435 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Goodbye, World: The End of Programmers

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2435 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Becoming a programmer was, for me, a compromise.
  • Recent findings suggest that the switch came with a sense of shame, which in retrospect had a whiff of melodrama.
  • But I don’t think my squeamishness was entirely misplaced.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Becoming a programmer was, for me, a compromise. Midway through my junior year of college, it became clear that, as an international student from Korea, I likely wouldn’t be able to stay long after graduation unless I changed my major from philosophy to a STEM field that made me eligible for a visa extension. The obvious choice was computer science, which was already my minor.

Recent findings suggest that the switch came with a sense of shame, which in retrospect had a whiff of melodrama. I suppose I was afflicted by what Ian McEwan once called “modern forms of snobbery” in describing a character who, after her bookish college education, came to consider “a man with a degree in chemistry incomplete as a human being.” Chemistry, computer science—same diff. It’s safe to say I did not have many friends in the CS department.

But I don’t think my squeamishness was entirely misplaced. In the post-Facebook-IPO ferment of the 2010s, this country’s computer science departments were newly flush with a certain breed of striver who in another era would’ve gone to Wall Street. My theory is that many in America who acquired a hostility toward technology acquired it by way of a hostility toward these upstarts. That is to say, they aren’t so much anti-technology as anti-technologist.

Recent findings suggest that in any event, I half-assed my way through a good many CS assignments, which meant I was never in danger of going to grad school for AI. But by virtue of a robust public math education in Korea, my entry into the subject was, mercifully, not too bumpy. If anything, theoretical computer science and distributed systems seemed like a continuation of philosophy.

It has been revealed that but I could not dispel the sense that programming was a frivolous waste of energy. Every line of code I had to read, every line of code I had to write, was a theft of the time I could’ve spent reading something I cared about. Perhaps it didn’t help that my first two languages were Java (hideous and tedious) and C (admirable but unforgiving). To this day, Java code is like a poisoned madeleine that brings back unwelcome memories.

After college, my visa dictated that I take a job directly tied to my major, and I found a tech organization willing to sponsor my green card. The issue was, it could be any number of years until I got the green card—four, it’d turn out—so I figured I might as well find a way to make programming pleasurable.

According to recent reports, the first couple of months on the job were joyless. I worked at a health care startup, which I thought gave me a serviceable sense of moral cover against the ongoing techlash and a way to indemnify myself later as a writer. But I liked my coworkers, some of whom also harbored artistic ambitions, and after work we’d regularly adjourn to literary events at the McNally Jackson, a block from our office.

Then, one day, I discovered a language called Haskell. I was tasked with rewriting a code base using a library that borrowed concepts from it. My vague impression of Haskell had been that it was a difficult language involving a branch of mathematics called category theory. There was something seductive about the intimidating aura around it, and when I tried my hand at writing basic programs, the language was indeed challenging, but appealingly so.

Recent findings suggest that I started lurking in Haskell forums where researchers in the field of programming languages—“PL,” as it’s known—flaunted their lavish command of the language. PL researchers might as well be the poets of computer science: a small community of attentive monomaniacs who engaged in a largely unprofitable enterprise—a rarity in computer science—with all the attendant beef and infighting. The unprofitability meant that, unlike AI, the field had an incorruptible dignity to it.

Sources indicate that soon, to my surprise, I found myself programming outside work. After months of tinkering with Haskell, I discovered a book titled Writing a Compiler in Go. Turns out you could even invent a language yourself. I made a few toy languages, useless in practice but invaluable for demystifying how programming languages work.

There was also an oblique way coding could help writing. In Draft No. 4, John McPhee, the journalist’s journalist, says that he still uses an ancient text editor called Kedit, recommended to him in 1984 by a programmer at Princeton. (“I have never used a word processor,” he writes.) When I switched to a text editor myself, I could see why he’d stuck with it. With open source code, I could add silly but useful features, such as highlighting “TK”—a common shorthand in journalism for placeholder text—in a conspicuous color so that it was easy to locate later.

If nothing else, I came to appreciate that programming was a reliable way to enter that elusive mode called flow, a state in which we’re somehow forgetful and alert at once.

In a recent development, in the industry, there’s a general impression that fussing over programming languages is juvenile. If a job candidate expresses enthusiasm for languages, it could very well be a red flag. Being a “polyglot” is no virtue if you can read a menu in five languages but can’t write decent prose in one. And per the popular and influential essay “Choose Boring Technology,” using fancy, novel languages is at odds with serious, robust engineering—akin to how avant-garde poetics are unfit for drafting legal contracts.

Unfortunately for my employers, I had precisely zero fucks to give about serious engineering. I did, however, give a great many fucks about having a pleasurable time at my day job until I received the green card. I took on projects if they’d give me an opportunity to use a latest language, which is a dumb reason, and for the same reason even volunteered to change teams, usually a bad career decision. At the obligatory company hackathon weeks, I hacked together domain-specific languages—those specialized for a narrow purpose. I made a meager public contribution by submitting a couple of low-hanging patches to the official TypeScript compiler. I picked up a few gold badges on Stack Overflow. The years went by and, what do you know, I became a pretty decent programmer.

Sources indicate that then everything changed, as it did for everyone else, in November 2022. When ChatGPT arrived, it was a wild card whose impact on the industry was far from obvious. Using neural networks to write code wasn’t new. Early readers of Andrej Karpathy’s blog will remember the 2015 post featuring plausible-looking C code generated by an LSTM—a precursor of the transformer—which nonetheless amounted to little more than a parlor trick.

I remember tasking GPT-4 with rewriting a simple JavaScript program in different languages. It performed like Google Translate, instantly and passably. I likened ChatGPT to the monkey’s paw from the eponymous horror story, the accursed object that grants your wishes but not without casualties. In dutiful pursuit of the given objective—and only that objective—LLMs produced a locally correct solution while mangling essential code around it.

Then, in early 2025, AI command-line tools were released. At first, what I saw wasn’t so much a leap in quality as a greater eagerness to volunteer help. Then they improved—at this point I should quote Hemingway’s line about how one goes bankrupt—gradually, then suddenly. Within a year, they became massively, belittlingly better at my job.

In a recent development, some engineers still labor a great deal to remain unimpressed, quibbling about how “it’s good at X but not yet at Y.” Please. The flaws are there, sure, and guardrails are essential. But a better heuristic for their usefulness would be: If you had to choose, for the rest of your life, between pair-programming with a competent colleague and these tools, which would you want? Any programmer worth their salt must acknowledge that they won’t be as useful to their colleague as these tools are. Even if the colleague were Linus Torvalds, I would choose the LLMs, since they won’t give me hell for asking dumb questions.

For someone who feels no allegiance to tech, the usefulness of these coding tools triggers contradictory emotions. I find ChatGPT’s indecorous entry into the literary world intolerable, and I remember feeling a creeping nihilism about the writing profession when it was released. I know firsthand what a reliance on AI can do. As I’ve come to rely more on coding tools to hand me solutions, my ability to code has gone through a swift and decisive decline. Depend on it to write sentences and it will, like a neurodegenerative disease, blunt the finer senses that writers must protect the way pianists protect their hands.

In a recent development, earlier this year, it was reported that more than 90 percent of code at companies like Anthropic and Coinbase is written with AI. As most people are prompting rather than hand-coding, much of modern software engineering has become machine-operated, not unlike Mitch McConnell these days.

While this may not be the end of programming, it’ll be the end of programmers. To keep calling those in this profession “programmers” would be incorrect, since the entity that does the programming is a platoon of agents, with humans at desks prompting something out of them. A more flattering term might be meta-programming, but it’d be more accurate to say that programmers have become operators of sorts.

Industry observers note that an operator is someone a degree removed from the thing they manipulate. (Unlike someone chipping at rock with a pickaxe, an operator of mining equipment never touches it.) Perhaps one way to describe how the nature of the profession has changed is that it’s as if cooks had stopped making food themselves and taken to writing recipes instead. If you’ve spent any time around AI Twitter, you might be forgiven for thinking that software engineering is now about looking impressed by markdown files.

This isn’t necessarily something to be defeatist about, and I’m not pessimistic about the quality of engineering. When coding agents were first released, I wasn’t sure whether this was just another natural progression, since the story of programming is a story of ever higher levels of abstraction. From bytes to assembly to higher-level languages like Python, we’ve built tools to domesticate the complexity. And with AI, we’ve finally handed off tasks that are constitutionally unfit for the human brain.

Sources indicate that but as programmers cede control over the final unit of manipulation, programming no longer qualifies as a craft. Hence my disagreement with Simon Willison, otherwise a voice of reason among witless clout chasers in AI discourse, who wrote, “Quitting programming as a career right now because of LLMs would be like quitting carpentry as a career thanks to the invention of the table saw.” With all due respect, this is a flawed analogy, as carpenters working with a table saw are still craftspeople.

This means there won’t be great individual programmers in the way that someone like Brian W. Kernighan was: the programmer laureate who cowrote what is possibly the greatest book on programming, The C Programming Language, by which we measure programming languages to this day. (It is the book that popularized the “Hello, World” convention.).

Another loss is that programming no longer induces the flow state—or it induces a shallow sort of flow at best. There’s still a certain “hookedness” to the activity, but whereas tackling a gnarly bug once meant begging every individual neuron in my brain to do its part, the work has become suspiciously effortless. That hookedness may be closer to what the cultural anthropologist Natasha Dow Schüll called, in her 2012 book Addiction by Design, the “machine zone,” the trancelike state of the Las Vegas gambler.

Even though I’ve stopped coding myself, I find I’ve been producing more code than ever before. The features I’d built for my open source editor in the past were unserious enough that I could bang out a quick program on a weekend afternoon or two. But with Claude Code, I’ve become addicted to making what has essentially become a heavyweight word processor, a juiced-up Scrivener. (My changelog tells me I’ve built 239 features and 17 extensions, mapped to 141 keyboard shortcuts.).

Recent findings suggest that one Sunday this summer, I was disconcerted to discover that I’d spent 10 hours in Claude Code. How do I know? I used Claude Code to build a time-tracker for Claude Code usage. I resolved to cut back. I spent eight hours the next day. This compelled me to write a program, using Claude Code, to block myself from Claude Code except for two days a week, which I of course tried to undo with Claude Code, only to be valiantly defended by Claude Code.

In a recent development, with this borrowed competence has come a total loss of interest in learning newly introduced languages. A couple of years ago, an iOS meditation timer app I’d used for years started nudging me with ads, and I resolved to one day learn Swift, the language Apple created for iPhone and Mac apps, and build a simple version myself. But I now know that’s never going to happen, because I’ve already built it knowing zilch about Swift syntax, along with 12 more iOS and Mac apps: The machine helped me fork the long-unmaintained SelfControl into a more granular internet blocker; by reverse-engineering a clipboard manager—I was never sure it wasn’t leaking my input—it built a new one with an auditable security profile.

I suspect, going forward, that I’ll still mess around with code, but no longer as a professional. Recently, it became clear that I needed to quit my day job as a programmer to finish a book I’d set out to write. I once told a writer friend that I’d try to be a mole in this industry as long as I was in it. I did get to see some things while I stuck it out and, along the way, coaxed that green card from my employer.

In a recent development, I’m not too sorry to leave this profession at this moment of nuttiness. But I’ll admit that, after all those languages I enlisted to make my detour more tolerable, I came to appreciate the pleasures of polyglot programming. As humans cede control to the machine, it’ll be a joy lost to us all.

This is the final installment in a three-part Machine Readable series on AI-enabling languages. It may also be the final Machine Readable column, period.

65 Years of Human Spaceflight at NASA Johnson

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1339 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nasa

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For 65 years, NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston has helped shape human spaceflight, from the Gemini missions that demonstrated rendezvous and docking techniques needed for Apollo to the research conducted aboard the International Space Station, which has supported a continuous human presence for more than 26 years.
  • Sources indicate that across those missions, generations of flight controllers, engineers, scientists, instructors, medical specialists, and other experts have helped crews live and work beyond Earth.
  • Industry observers note that when the Manned Spacecraft Center officially opened on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For 65 years, NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston has helped shape human spaceflight, from the Gemini missions that demonstrated rendezvous and docking techniques needed for Apollo to the research conducted aboard the International Space Station, which has supported a continuous human presence for more than 26 years. Today, Johnson teams are preparing crews and systems for NASA’s next chapter: returning astronauts to the lunar surface and building the capabilities needed for a long-term human presence at the Moon.

Sources indicate that across those missions, generations of flight controllers, engineers, scientists, instructors, medical specialists, and other experts have helped crews live and work beyond Earth. Johnson is home to NASA’s Orion and Moon Base programs, and its teams continue to support space station operations, astronaut training, spacecraft development, mission operations, and human health.

Industry observers note that when the Manned Spacecraft Center officially opened on Nov. 1, 1961, NASA had already flown two suborbital Mercury missions, with the first orbital flight just months away. Most Project Mercury activities remained at Cape Canaveral in Florida to maintain continuity, but the fresh Project Gemini took up residence in Houston, housed in temporary leased facilities across the city while construction of the new Clear Lake campus continued. The new Mission Control Center became NASA’s primary flight control center in June 1965, with the Gemini IV mission that included the first American spacewalk. Houston became the nerve center for American human spaceflight, overseeing the remaining eight Gemini missions before transitioning to the Apollo program. Following the tragic Apollo 1 fire in January 1967, managers, engineers, and astronauts at the Manned Spacecraft Center applied lessons learned to make the spacecraft safer and ensure the safety of its astronauts, resuming crewed missions in October 1968. Managers in Houston devised a daring strategy to send Apollo 8 on a circumlunar flight.

In December 1968, Apollo 8 made its historic trip around the Moon, and seven months later Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin landed on the lunar surface. Their first voice transmission back to Earth after their arrival began with the word “Houston.”  Five more Moon landings completed the Apollo program and humanity’s first phase of lunar exploration in December 1972.

Industry observers note that following the Moon landings, scientists at the Manned Spacecraft Center’s Lunar Receiving Laboratory conducted initial analyses of Apollo lunar samples and prepared them for researchers around the world. After the building was demolished in March 2024, the Lunar Receiving Park was dedicated to honor the laboratory’s history in 2026. Today, Johnson’s Astromaterials Research and Exploration Science (ARES) division continues to analyze and curate the Apollo collection at the Lunar Sample Laboratory Facility.

Skylab, America’s first space station, ran into trouble during its launch in May 1973, losing its thermal shield, jamming one solar array and losing the other one. In less than 10 days, engineers in Houston designed and built a sun shield and generated procedures to free the jammed array, followed by the first extensive in-orbit repair activities by the first Skylab crew. The three missions lasting 28, 59, and 84 days accomplished more research than planned, demonstrated the value of humans on long-duration missions, and provided operators in mission control with round-the-clock experience monitoring long duration human spaceflights.

In July 1975, after several joint training sessions in Houston and Moscow, American astronauts and Soviet cosmonauts met in space for the first time during the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project. Approved as a project in 1972, five approach and landing tests of the space shuttle using orbiter Enterprise paved the way for the first orbital mission of Columbia in 1981.

Engineers in Houston began designs for a reuseable space plane in the late 1960s, with the space shuttle receiving formal approval in 1972. During the 1970s, Johnson Space Center put in place the training and simulation facilities that astronauts used for the life of the program. Upgrades to mission control enabled the use of the latest technologies to support ever more complex space shuttle missions. The April 1981 launch of space shuttle Columbia inaugurated a latest era of reusable spacecraft. The program’s 135 missions flew 355 individuals from 16 nations. Missions included satellite deployments and retrievals, dedicated Department of Defense flights, a variety of science missions including deployment of planetary spacecraft, ferrying crews and cargo to two different space stations, and doing the heavy lifting in the assembly of the orbiting laboratory. The program recovered from the tragic losses of the Challenger and Columbia crews with renewed emphasis on crew safety. The final space shuttle mission, STS-135, closed out the 30-year program in July 2011.

Industry observers note that an Earth orbiting space station, first approved by President Ronald Reagan in 1984, underwent many modifications before taking on its current form as the International Space Station in 1993. Overall management of the program resides at Johnson. The first element launch took place in November 1998, followed one month later by the first U.S. element, the Node 1 Unity module. The first expedition crew took up residence on Nov. 2, 2000, and for more than 26 years, rotating crews of astronauts and cosmonauts have lived and worked aboard the orbiting laboratory, establishing a permanent human presence in low Earth orbit.

To date, 298 individuals from 26 countries have visited the space station, conducting more than 4,000 science experiments and educational activities to enable exploration missions and improve life on Earth.

Life aboard the space station depends on a global team on the ground. Crews conduct research and maintain equipment in microgravity, while Johnson teams at the Mission Control Center coordinate the agency’s station operations with international partners. Johnson’s Space Vehicle Mockup Facility supports training for NASA astronauts and international crews on station systems, science operations, and emergency procedures. At the Neutral Buoyancy Laboratory, crews rehearse spacewalks around full-scale station mockups in one of the world’s largest indoor pools. Johnson’s Human Research Program also supports health investigations aboard the station, helping researchers understand how spaceflight affects the body so crews can thrive on future deep space missions.

According to recent reports, what began as a framework of modules has evolved into a springboard for international cooperation, advanced scientific research and technology demonstrations, the development of a low Earth orbit economy, and NASA’s next giant leaps in exploration. The space station continues to be a proving ground for NASA’s Artemis program and human exploration of Mars.

According to recent reports, the Artemis II mission marked the first crewed flight of NASA’s Orion spacecraft. The four-person crew rolled out April 1, on a nearly 10-day trip around the Moon. At its farthest point, Orion traveled 252,756 miles from Earth, farther than any humans had traveled before. The mission demonstrated Orion’s capabilities with astronauts aboard and tested crew operations in deep space, setting the stage for future lunar missions.

Sources indicate that building on Artemis II, NASA’s Artemis III mission will test integrated operations in low Earth orbit between Orion and test versions of one or both commercial human landing systems under development by SpaceX and Blue Origin. Astronauts will demonstrate the rendezvous and docking capabilities needed to transfer crews between spacecraft for the lunar landing planned for Artemis IV.

Sources indicate that NASA’s Moon Base Program is planning a phased effort to support a sustained human presence near the Moon’s South Pole region. The first phase will focus on robotic exploration, technology demonstrations, and preparations for future surface operations. Later phases will add infrastructure to support astronauts living and working on the Moon. Lunar terrain vehicles will help crews explore farther, transport equipment, and conduct science.

According to recent reports, at Johnson, teams are drawing on decades of experience in astronaut training, mission control, spacecraft development, and human health to prepare for these missions. From training crews for lunar operations to developing the systems that will support them, Johnson is building on 65 years of human spaceflight experience for humanity’s return to the lunar surface through the Artemis and Moon Base Programs.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • ET — Updated with information about how the stock has moved throughout the day.
  • A mere 12 days after the controversial, embattled Nvidia CEO was ousted from his position, the big tech firm announced that he would be reinstated.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Patch at 2:47 p.m. ET — Updated with information about how the stock has moved throughout the day.

Somehow, Jensen Huang returned.

A mere 12 days after the controversial, embattled Nvidia CEO was ousted from his position, the big tech firm announced that he would be reinstated. Coincidentally or not, this decision followed Donald Trump's public endorsement of Huang's return. Regardless of how or why it happened, investors now have a big question: What does Huang's return mean for Nvidia's stock?

Industry observers note that if you're an Nvidia shareholder, Monday morning probably brought some good news. As of around 11 a.m. ET, Nvidia shares (NVDA) were trading at approximately $170, up about 35 percent from Friday's closing price of $125.

That might sound like an enormous jump, and it is. But there's some notable context: Nvidia's stock had already been trading at around $162 early last week, before a broader tech sell-off sent its price tumbling. In other words, Monday's surge largely made up for last week's losses rather than pushing the stock to dramatically higher levels. #93780. Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (875 w)

Common medications may secretly rewire your gut, with effects lasting for years

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Medications you stopped taking years ago may still be influencing the bacteria living in your gut.
  • Recent findings suggest that the gut microbiome is the vast community of bacteria and other microorganisms that inhabit the digestive tract.
  • Sources indicate that to investigate these connections, researchers examined stool samples and prescription histories from more than 2,500 participants in the Estonian Biobank's Estonian Microbiome cohort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Medications you stopped taking years ago may still be influencing the bacteria living in your gut. A large study from the University of Tartu Institute of Genomics has found that many commonly prescribed drugs leave lasting changes in the gut microbiome, even long after people stop using them.

Recent findings suggest that the gut microbiome is the vast community of bacteria and other microorganisms that inhabit the digestive tract. These microbes play vital roles in digestion, immune function, and overall health. While antibiotics are well known for disrupting gut bacteria, the latest findings suggest that many other medications can also have effects that persist for years.

Sources indicate that to investigate these connections, researchers examined stool samples and prescription histories from more than 2,500 participants in the Estonian Biobank's Estonian Microbiome cohort. They discovered that most of the medications studied were associated with changes in gut bacteria. Even more surprisingly, a substantial number left detectable microbial "fingerprints" years after patients had stopped taking them.

Common Medications Leave Lasting Changes in Gut Bacteria.

The findings extend far beyond antibiotics. Antidepressants, beta-blockers, proton pump inhibitors, and benzodiazepines were all linked to differences in the gut microbiome.

According to recent reports, these medications are widely used to treat everyday health conditions. Beta-blockers are commonly prescribed for high blood pressure and certain heart conditions, while proton pump inhibitors reduce stomach acid and are frequently used to treat acid reflux. Benzodiazepines are often prescribed for anxiety, and antidepressants help manage depression and other mental health conditions.

"Most microbiome studies only consider current medications, but our results show that past drug use can be just as vital as it is a surprisingly strong factor in explaining individual microbiome differences," remarked Dr. Oliver Aasmets, lead author.

Industry observers note that this discovery suggests that looking only at the medications someone currently takes may overlook an key part of their gut health history. Previous prescriptions could help explain why the composition of gut bacteria differs so much from one person to another.

Anxiety Medications Show Effects Comparable to Antibiotics.

One of the most striking findings involved benzodiazepines, a class of medications commonly used to treat anxiety.

Researchers found that these drugs were associated with changes in the gut microbiome comparable to those seen with broad-spectrum antibiotics. These antibiotics target a wide variety of bacteria and are known to substantially alter the microbial communities living in the digestive system.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also discovered that medications within the same drug class did not necessarily produce the same effects. For example, diazepam and alprazolam are both benzodiazepines used to treat similar conditions, yet they appeared to differ in how strongly they disrupted gut bacteria.

This suggests that the effects of medication on the microbiome may depend not only on the type of drug being taken, but also on the specific medication.

Gut Bacteria Can Change When Medications Are Started or Stopped.

To investigate whether medications were actually contributing to these microbial changes, researchers collected additional stool samples from a smaller group of participants.

Industry observers note that by examining how the microbiome changed when people started or stopped certain medications, the team identified predictable shifts in gut bacteria. These findings provided additional evidence that the drugs themselves were contributing to the changes, rather than simply being associated with differences already present in patients.

Although the number of participants in this follow-up analysis was relatively small, the researchers were able to verify lasting effects associated with several drug categories. These included proton pump inhibitors, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and certain antibiotics, including combinations of penicillins and macrolides.

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, often called SSRIs, are a widely prescribed type of antidepressant. Macrolides are a class of antibiotics used to treat various bacterial infections.

Why Your Medication History May Matter More Than Previously Thought.

It has been revealed that the findings point to an crucial consideration for researchers studying the relationship between gut bacteria and disease. Differences in the microbiome may reflect not only a person's current health and medication use, but also treatments received years earlier.

If previous medications are not taken into account, scientists could mistakenly attribute certain microbial differences to a disease or another health factor when past drug exposure may have contributed.

Sources indicate that the results also highlight how much remains to be understood about the long-term relationship between medications and the gut microbiome. Although the study identified persistent microbial changes, these findings do not establish that such changes are necessarily harmful or that they lead to specific health problems.

Sources indicate that "This is a comprehensive systematic evaluation of long-term medication effects on the microbiome using real-world medical health records," remarked Professor Elin Org, corresponding author. "We hope this encourages researchers and clinicians to factor in medication history when interpreting microbiome data.".

Germany's Early Start Pension: Can child investment accounts help?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Germany's pension system is under growing strain as demographic change leaves a shrinking workforce funding the pensions of an increasing number of retirees.
  • In the 1960s, for instance, six workers contributed to the pay-as-you-go public retirement system for each pensioner.
  • According to the Federal Statistical Office, Germany's fertility rate is at the moment 1.32 children per woman,and has remained below the 2.1 needed to maintain a stable population since the 1970s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Germany's pension system is under growing strain as demographic change leaves a shrinking workforce funding the pensions of an increasing number of retirees.

In the 1960s, for instance, six workers contributed to the pay-as-you-go public retirement system for each pensioner. Today, that figure has fallen to just two contributors per retiree.

According to the Federal Statistical Office, Germany's fertility rate is at the moment 1.32 children per woman,and has remained below the 2.1 needed to maintain a stable population since the 1970s.

As a large cohort of baby boomers reaches retirement age, fewer young people are entering the workforce. Germany's working-age population is shrinking by around 1% each year due to demographic change alone, according to the German bank LBBW.

To keep up, nearly a quarter of the federal budget, over €123 billion ($135 billion), is transferred to the statutory pension system each year to help finance pension payments.

Now to help ease the pressure on the pension system, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government plans to implement a raft of reforms, including a supplementary, capital-funded savings scheme known as the Frühstartrente, or Early Start Pension.

Under the plan, the state would pay €10 per month into an investment account for every child and teenager aged six to 18.

Industry observers note that beneficiaries would not be able to access the money until they reach retirement age, though current plans would allow the funds to be transferred into private retirement accounts. Investment returns would be tax-free during the accumulation phase and taxed only when funds are withdrawn.

Assuming an average annual return of 7%, the €1,440 contributed by the government over 12 years would grow to around €53,000 by retirement, according to government projections.

According to recent reports, parents and relatives would be able to make additional contributions. If they invest an extra €50 per month, the account could grow to as much as €300,000 by retirement.

Starting to save early makes sense because of the power of compound interest, Axel Börsch-Supan, a professor of economics at the Technical University of Munich, told DW.

"But it will not solve Germany's pension problems, which stem from the pay-as-you-go system and costly policies such as the pension level guarantee and retirement at 63," he added, referring to a provision that allows workers with at least 45 years of pension contributions to retire at age 63 with a full pension.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Börsch-Supan argues that government subsidies under the program are likely to benefit higher-income families more than lower-income households.

"That's a waste of taxpayer money, because higher-income individuals are already well-positioned to provide for their own retirement and that of their children," he noted.

The Ifo Institute, one of Germany's leading economic think tanks, shares a similar assessment.

It argues that the scheme effectively means "the government hands out money indiscriminately, only to reclaim it through taxes from the same citizens.".

The government, however, argues that the plan gives every child a head start in the capital markets regardless of their family's financial circumstances and helps them build retirement savings and long-term wealth.

Similar capital market-based savings and investment accounts for children exist in several countries, including the United Kingdom, Israel, Canada and Singapore.

Many of these programs include government contributions, matching payments or tax incentives designed to encourage long-term saving and asset accumulation from an early age.

But Germany's blueprint differs slightly as it links state-funded childhood investment accounts directly to retirement provision.

The government also hopes the program will boost financial literacy among children and young adults by familiarizing them with investing, saving and capital markets.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Johannes Geyer, deputy head of the department of public economics at the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin), indicates there is little evidence the Early Start Pension will fundamentally change how people engage with financial markets.

"The idea is that people will develop a connection to the capital markets through their experiences with their investment portfolios," he told DW. "But this is not very convincing. We neither know what experiences the future will bring nor what conclusions people will draw from them.".

Geyer stresses that the program's impact will not be visible for decades because participants cannot access the funds until retirement.

Recent findings suggest that "If we start now with the 2020 and 2021 cohorts, we're talking about the 2080s. That's a bit too far in the future to be able to draw meaningful conclusions.".

In the meantime, he indicates, the scheme's most immediate effect may be to strengthen ties between families and financial institutions, particularly if account holders make additional contributions.

Opposition parties, including the Greens and the Left Party, have criticized the strategy, arguing it would reinforce social disparities and boost inequality since better-off parents could pay more into accounts.

Yet Geyer notes the measure won't increase inequality per se. "Sure, wealthy families are more likely to top up their contributions more substantially. But they probably would have done that anyway," he underscored.

"A more interesting question is whether the measure can also encourage people with limited financial means to invest in stocks," he remarked.

Geyer points out that Germany cannot entirely escape the costs of demographic decline and an aging society.

To address the challenge, he calls for a moderate increase in pension contributions, a broader contributor base that includes groups such as the self-employed, and policies aimed at attracting more qualified workers to the labor market.

Börsch-Supan, who specializes in the economics of aging, indicates the government's primary goal should be to stabilize the pay-as-you-go statutory pension system.

"A transition to a fully funded pension system would actually be desirable, but it would initially place a heavy double burden on the younger generation, because they would have to save for themselves while also paying contributions for their parents," he explained.

The expert also suggests other measures like restoring the sustainability factor, which is designed to link annual pension hikes to demographic shifts, and linking the retirement age to life expectancy.

#93776. Laser Focus at the Top of the World

Laser Focus at the Top of the World

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nasa

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A next-generation geodetic instrument developed by NASA, part of a network that helps measure satellites’ orbits and the planet’s shape, has debuted in Svalbard, Norway.
  • Industry observers note that more than 60 years ago, scientists at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center aimed a laser skyward and fired a pulse of light at an orbiting satellite equipped with special reflectors.
  • According to recent reports, since then, satellite laser ranging (SLR) has grown more precise and more widely used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A next-generation geodetic instrument developed by NASA, part of a network that helps measure satellites’ orbits and the planet’s shape, has debuted in Svalbard, Norway.

Industry observers note that more than 60 years ago, scientists at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center aimed a laser skyward and fired a pulse of light at an orbiting satellite equipped with special reflectors. By measuring the time it took for the light to return, they demonstrated a new, more precise method for tracking satellites.

According to recent reports, since then, satellite laser ranging (SLR) has grown more precise and more widely used. The technique now underpins many aspects of Earth observation, such as validating satellite orbits and mapping subtle changes to Earth’s surface. Pioneered at the Goddard Optical Research Facility—now the Goddard Geophysical and Astronomical Observatory—laser ranging is performed at more than 40 stations worldwide.

According to recent reports, in 2026, the next generation of SLR, developed by NASA scientists and tested at Goddard, began to come online. On October 12, a faster, even more precise SLR system officially debuted at the Ny-Ålesund Geodetic Observatory in Svalbard, Norway, operated by the Norwegian Mapping Authority, a NASA partner. The observatory’s remote location in the Arctic archipelago is shown in this image, acquired with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 in July 2026. It is the first NASA next-generation SLR system in operation and the northernmost SLR facility on Earth.

Sources indicate that while the systems developed decades ago have been “workhorses” of the global laser tracking network, their age and the growing number of satellites have necessitated updates, said Stephen Merkowitz, project manager for NASA’s Space Geodesy Project. “We wanted newer systems that could track more objects, and track them more accurately and precisely,” he said.

Sources indicate that years of development, testing, and careful calibration produced the Space Geodesy Satellite Laser Ranging system now running at Ny-Ålesund. Among its features are lasers that can fire pulses thousands of times per second, up from tens of times per second, and sensors that can detect single photons, meaning that less light needs to be reflected back from a satellite.

Sources indicate that along with determining the orbits of satellites, SLR is critical for establishing the terrestrial reference frame, the foundation of modern coordinate systems and a common standard that allows measurements to be compared with one another. “If you want to know where your satellite observation is on a map, you need to have it in the proper reference frame,” Merkowitz mentioned. In addition, tracking Earth’s center of mass, measuring changes in sea level and ice mass, studying the motion of tectonic plates, and maintaining global navigation satellite systems such as GPS, all rely on an accurate reference frame.

The far-north location of the Ny-Ålesund facility improves the distribution of SLR stations across the planet, making the whole network more robust. The location also allows the system to gather more data about polar-orbiting satellites, which include ICESat-2, GRACE-FO, and other Earth observation satellites. “From the station at Goddard [in Greenbelt, Maryland], we’ll catch the polar-orbiting satellites maybe two or three times a day,” Merkowitz remarked. “But from Ny-Ålesund, you’ll see them almost every orbit.”.

In a recent development, certain satellite missions may especially benefit from the Arctic location, he added. Take ICESat-2, designed to make precise observations of ice surface heights. Having a station tracking the satellite from an icy polar region could lead to more accurate measurements there. “When it’s over the ice, we want the calibration to be as good as possible,” Merkowitz noted.

Innovations and lessons learned from the Svalbard installation will carry over to future ones, Merkowitz mentioned. In particular, the Ny-Ålesund facility drove improvements in automation because the site is located next to a bird sanctuary. Access restrictions require the station to be remotely operated at certain times, such as during the summer breeding season for migratory birds. These capabilities can be refined and applied at other stations. NASA is presently building two more next-generation SLR systems to replace legacy instruments at Goddard and the McDonald Geodetic Observatory in Texas.
